News.title: Charlie Kirk murder suspect pleads not guilty amid major death penalty update
News.content:
Charlie Kirk murder suspect pleads not guilty amid major death penalty update

Prosecutors say Tyler Robinson shot Mr Kirk from a rooftop more than 400 feet away and could have easily missed, injuring or killing other people

View Image Charlie Kirk was shot in the neck as he spoke to a crowd of thousands in Utah (Image: AP)

The murder case against the man accused of assassinating conservative activist Charlie Kirk last year is headed for trial and the defendant could face the death penalty if he is convicted.

Utah District Judge Tony Graf on Tuesday sided with prosecutors who said they had "overwhelming" evidence that Tyler Robinson shot Mr Kirk once in the neck as the ally of President Donald Trump spoke to a crowd of thousands last September in Orem, Utah.

One of Robinson's lawyers entered a not guilty plea on his behalf following Judge Graf’s decision. Robinson’s lawyers tried to block a trial, arguing prosecutors failed to show Kirk’s shooting placed others around him at risk of death.

That is an aggravating factor under the law that makes Robinson eligible for the death penalty. Mr Kirk’s family called the ruling "an important step in our family's pursuit of justice".

"Every step in this process carries the weight of all that Charlie’s murder has taken from his family, especially his children who will grow up without their father," the statement said."We are grateful to all who have continued to pray for us, support us, and stand with us through a year of unimaginable grief."

Prosecutors said Robinson shot Mr Kirk from a rooftop more than 400 feet away and could have easily missed, injuring or killing other people.

Judge Graf had the option to send the case to trial on a lesser charge of murder, which carries a minimum sentence of 15 years and a maximum of life in prison, said Steve Burton, director of the Utah Defence Attorney Association.

The judge said his decision to approve the aggravated murder charge was based on “the documented position of several individuals in and around the canopy area” where Kirk was speaking, among other factors.

“These circumstances support a reasonable inference that defendant was aware that other individuals were positioned near Mr Kirk when he fired,” the judge said.

The hearing on Tuesday in Utah state court came after prosecutors in July spent five days presenting what they said was “overwhelming” evidence that Tyler Robinson killed the conservative activist while he was speaking at an open-air event on a college campus.

The 23-year-old defendant turned himself in a day after the shooting at Utah Valley University last September.

Robinson’s lawyers have not offered alternative theories for Mr Kirk’s death and have focused instead on blocking the case from proceeding to trial and trying to get the death penalty taken off the table.

Article continues below

Mr Kirk’s parents, Robert and Kathryn Kirk, entered the heavily secured facility arm in arm before the hearing at the Fourth Judicial District Courthouse in Provo. Erika Kirk was seated beside them.

The family stepped out during part of a prosecutor’s argument that described the shooting. A few local members of Mr Kirk’s organisation, Turning Point USA, arrived with signs expressing their support for Erika Kirk but were told by security that they could not have them on the court property.

Robinson had no visible reaction to the arguments. His mother Amber Robinson watched from the courtroom gallery and his father Matt Robinson listened with his head bowed.

News.title: Missing man's body found metres from his car after he vanished more than two years ago
News.content:
Missing man's body found metres from his car after he vanished more than two years ago

Police found Richard Locker's car a day after he disappeared, but did not locate his remains for more than two-and-a-half years until August - when they found him in a property on the same road

View 2 Images Richard Locker, from Paignton, was found in Torquay in August - more than two years after he disappeared (Image: Devon and Cornwall Police)

The remains of a man who vanished two years ago have finally been found by police - just metres from where officers located his car the day after his disappearance.

‌



Richard Locker, from Paignton in Devon, was declared missing on January 4, 2024, and last spotted on a street in Torquay, four miles away. Police found his car parked on Mill Lane in Torquay the next day. However, a mystery surrounded what happened to Richard for the next two-and-a-half years.

‌



Tragically, his family's worst fears came true on Tuesday (September 1), as his step-daughter Nicola confirmed his remains were found at a property on Mill Lane last month - the same road his car was parked on, reports Devon Live.

‌



View 2 Images Mill Lane, where Richard's car and body were found (Image: Google)

Nicola said in a post on social media on Tuesday "finally after all this time, we have found you". Nicola added they never "stopped looking for him" and the last two years have been full of "wondering and pain of not knowing" whether he was safe.

‌



In a post in the Finding Richard Locker Facebook group, Nicola said: "After two years, seven months and 27 days of wondering where you were… we finally know.

"We wanted you home, we wanted answers, and more than anything, we wanted another chance to see you, hear your voice and tell you how much you are loved.

"But amongst all of the heartbreak, there is a tiny piece of peace in finally knowing where you are. You have never been forgotten, Rich. Not for one single day."

Article continues below

Richard left his home in Paignton in his vehicle on January 4, 2024. His vehicle was found the following day in Mill Lane, Torquay, during police searches; however, there was no trace of Richard.

His remains were found when police were called to a property on Mill Lane on Friday, August 7. The death is not being treated as suspicious, the force said.

A statement from Devon and Cornwall Police said: "Formal identification is yet to take place, but the family of a man reported missing in 2024 has been informed of this development. His death is not being treated as suspicious, and a file is being prepared for the coroner."

News.title: Brit pub landlady, 31, stabbed to death at German train station was 'breath of fresh air'
News.content:
Brit pub landlady, 31, stabbed to death at German train station was 'breath of fresh air'

Rebecca Bullock, 31, was attacked at the station in Rosenheim, Bavaria, in the early hours of Sunday before being rushed to hospital where she died from 'severe injuries'

View 3 Images Rebecca Bullock was attacked in Rosenheim, Bavaria

A British pub landlady who was stabbed to death at a railway station in Germany has been remembered as a "breath of fresh air".

Rebecca Bullock was attacked at the station in Rosenheim, Bavaria, just before 1am local time on Sunday, August 30. The 31-year-old was rushed to hospital where she died from "severe injuries," the Bavarian Police said.

Rachel, landlady at the White Swan pub in Whitchurch, Buckinghamshire, had been on her way to a funeral in Austria. Officers arrested a 27-year-old German man near the railway station shortly after the attack.

Richard Shuffill, 82, vice-chairman of the parish council in the village, said Ms Bullock had been "like a breath of fresh air" at the pub.

View 3 Images Rachel died from 'severe injuries' following the attack (Image: Facebook)

"Becca had only been here a couple of years but she was like a breath of fresh air and turned The Swan around," he said.

"It's the only pub in the village but she threw herself into her work to make it the centre of the community. It was impossible not to like her. She was always pleasant and friendly. No one can believe what’s happened and she will be terribly missed.

"Her death has come as a real shock and it's a huge loss to our community. I only saw her Saturday lunchtime and then 12 hours later - bless her - she is no longer with us."

Floral tributes were placed outside the pub where Rachel, a keen runner and horsewoman, held charity events - most recently to support a fundraiser for a seriously ill girl in the community.

View 3 Images Rachel was described in tributes as a 'caring' person (Image: Facebook)

One described Rachel as "such a caring person that will go out her way for others." Another said: "Heaven has gained the most beautiful angel."

A third tribute said Rachel "was an old soul and everyone in our local always felt safe and secure, and she turned the local around to modernise it but also keep it a welcoming safe space for our community.

Article continues below

"A true professional in hospitality with grace and dignity. [She] was so tolerant and non-judgmental. We are absolutely devastated for her loss and for the loss her family."

News.title: Augsburg live: 'Several injured' after explosion at German train station in 'major' incident
News.content:
Police have warmed members of the public to avoid the area widely after the explosion hit the city's main train station at 5am, officers confirmed

Augsburg live: 'Several injured' after explosion at German train station in 'major' incident

Several people have reportedly been injured in an explosion at a German railway station this morning.

Police have confirmed an explosion hit Augsburg's main train station at around 5am on Wednesday (September 2). Local news outlets report 'several' people have suffered injuries, but there are no reports of any deaths at this stage.

A statement from Schwaben North Police said: "A major police operation is currently taking place in Augsburg on Bahnhofstr.

"Halderstrasse / Hübnerstrasse, Bahnhofstrase / Hübnerstrasse, and Viktoriastrasse / Bahnhofstrasse are closed. Public transport is disrupted."

A second statement added: "An explosion of an unknown object occurred in a building passageway.

"There are disruptions to road traffic and public transportation. Please avoid the area widely."

This is a breaking news event, please check for updates below.

News.title: Woman loses home and pets in '10 minutes' after house fire caused by 1 common item
News.content:
Woman loses home and pets in '10 minutes' after house fire caused by 1 common item

A fire broke out and ravaged a woman's house and a 6,000-strong book collection in just 10 minutes – and she's urging everyone to check their drawers and cupboards for the common item that caused the blaze

View Image Roberta's home was devastated by a fire in just 10 minutes (stock image) (Image: Mike Beverley via Getty Images)

A woman who lost most of her possessions and her beloved pets in a devastating house fire has urged people not to keep hold of one common item which is likely tucked away, forgotten, in many drawers or cupboards in homes across the country.

‌



The woman posted images showing the extensive damage caused by the blaze, with flames "reaching the roof" in just 10 minutes, in the hope of preventing others from experiencing a similar ordeal.

‌



But what caused the fire in the first place? The devastating inferno was triggered by a lithium battery "spontaneously combusting," with the flames tearing through Roberta Mander Maghouin's property and destroying more than 6,000 books she'd collected over the years.

‌



Lithium batteries power countless electronic gadgets, from e-bikes and electric cars to mobile phones, laptops and beyond.

Are lithium batteries safe?

According to the British Safety Council, lithium batteries have been "increasingly linked to serious fires in workplaces and residential buildings," making it crucial to understand the dangers and proper disposal methods to prevent potentially catastrophic consequences.

Taking to Facebook, Roberta posted photos of her gutted room and wrote: "A few days ago we had a lithium battery spontaneously combust. In less than 10 minutes there were flames through the roof. Over 6000 books, likely total loss.

‌



"PSA [public service announcement]: Dispose/recycle unused phones and computers. They can combust simply from aging, need not be plugged in or anything."

Roberta and her partner were out when the fire broke out, fortunately escaping harm themselves, though tragically their cats died. It's understood the fire originated from a laptop combusting.

She maintains a "nearly complete inventory" of her book collection and "very good insurance" in an attempt to recover some of her possessions.

‌



In the comments section, fellow social media users rushed to share their sympathies and support - alongside their own similar experiences.

One person said: "I am so beyond sorry. This is devastating." Another said: "I am so sorry that this happened to you but thank you for sharing it and warning others. I have really been bummed by how many things you can ONLY get with lithium batteries anymore - for this very reason. This is my worst fear."

‌



A third commented: "I have like 2 old phones and computers that don't work just sitting in my closet. You're telling me they're a fire hazard?"

While a fourth shared: "I'm so sorry this happened. It's so scary because we have at least 10 old phones and a few laptops in a closet. I've got to figure out how to get rid of them!"

Someone else said: "[I've] had this happen to me too. 6 years ago." Another said: "I'm sorry for your loss. I have a friend in Oregon that lost her home too from a battery in their garage."

‌



And another added: "Wow I had no idea! I just don't know how to get rid of them."

How to safely dispose of lithium-ion batteries

According to the British Safety Council, these incidents are rare - but there are still risks.

It states: "Fortunately, Lithium-ion battery failures are relatively rare, but in the event of a malfunction, they can represent a serious fire risk.

‌



"They are safe products and meet many EN standards. However, when charged, Li-ion cells store a large amount of energy and are especially sensitive to high temperatures and damage, such as penetration and crushing.

"If a battery degrades, gets hot, or suffers a short circuit, heat and pressure build up inside. Warning signs that a battery is likely to fail include bulging or swelling, sometimes accompanied by other signs such as discharging too fast and/or the battery being hot to the touch."

When it comes to disposing of a lithium battery safely, it must be dropped off at a specialist recycling facility or collected through a hazardous waste disposal service, as placing them in ordinary household bins presents a serious fire risk.

Article continues below

The recent spell of hot weather has sparked a string of wildfires in some areas of the UK, with Brits encouraged to be more mindful regarding the risk of fires, especially in light of the ongoing hot conditions which could potentially heighten the risk of more blazes breaking out.

News.title: Mum books out restaurant for daughter's 5th birthday – then flees without paying £6k bill
News.content:
Mum books out restaurant for daughter's 5th birthday – then flees without paying £6k bill

The mum sparked outrage over her 'dine and dash' attempt, which left the owner of the barbecue restaurant £6,000 out of pocket – and now police are investigating

View 4 Images Carol had been suspicious, and demanded a €500 deposit (Image: La Voz de Galicia)

The owners of a barbecue restaurant Culleredo, northwestern Spain, have been left fuming after the organisers of a no expense spared birthday party disappeared – leaving a £6,000 bill.

‌



Carol Sao Luis explains that she received the initial booking in early August. "A woman called us wanting to organise a birthday party for her daughter. She told us it was important to have a big celebration because a family member had recently passed away, and the child was very sad.

‌



“She intended to invite a lot of people and wanted it all, so she booked every extra service we offered.”

‌



The customer was determined to spare no expense, Carol recalled: "It was 'yes' to everything, and she wanted more of everything: seafood, meat, cakes, appetisers, and an open bar. Admittedly, something about the booking seemed strange, but since I asked for a deposit [of €500] and she paid it, I decided not to overthink it."

The day of the event arrived, and some 80 guests arrived, determined to enjoy their day: "In addition to all the food, there were inflatables for the kids, personalised bottles, and non-stop alcohol service for nearly three hours," Carol says.

View 4 Images The restaurant was booked out for a family party (Image: Paxinas Galegas)

‌



But as the evening wore on, Carol was becoming increasingly concerned. "It was getting late, and I wanted to go home, so I told the woman we needed to settle the bill.

“We went to another area, and that’s when she told me she’d had an argument with her partner, who handled the finances, and couldn't pay me because she didn't have the money on her at the moment, though she promised to pay by the early hours of the morning at the latest."

Some of the group had left this point, and while Carol and her husband were discussing what to do next, the remaining 40 or so guests also disappeared.

‌



Realising that the party host was among them, Carol decided to gather some evidence: "I managed to snap a photo of the car's license plate because I knew I might need it if I wanted to file a police report, which is exactly what ended up happening."

View 4 Images The guests left suddenly while Carol was still trying to work out what to do (Image: TripAdvisor)

Carol tried to contact the party host via WhatsApp, to follow up on the promised payment, only to be told that the money wasn’t coming: “She simply replied that we hadn't provided the agreed-upon services,” Carol said.

‌



She added: ”The police have already located the person involved, and they told me it likely constitutes fraud. Now we’ll see what happens, because €7,000 is a huge amount of money for a business like ours, and things like this can't be overlooked."

She concludes: "Despite everything, I’d like my case to raise awareness, because 'dine-and-dash' incidents are all too common, though I hope no one else ever has to go through an ordeal as terrible as mine."

View 4 Images The bill totalled £6,000 (Image: TripAdvisor)

Article continues below

Dine and dash crimes appear to be on the increase, and the owners of restaurants not just in Spain, but around the world are in danger of losing their livelihoods thanks to incidents of this kind.

In the UK, Trade body UKHospitality reports that roughly one-third of its member venues have experienced a walkout. Of those affected, nearly 30% say the frequency of these events is increasing.

The cost of living crisis is not only increasing prices, but leading to fewer staff being on duty in restaurants to keep an eye on potential “runners”. Many restaurants are now considering pre-payment schemes to reduce the risk of being left out of pocket.

News.title: NHS full guide on what conditions make kids 'too ill for school'
News.content:
NHS full guide on what conditions make kids 'too ill for school'

Children might face these common health problems during the school year

View 2 Images The NHS says some health problems will not justify a day off school (stock pic) (Image: Getty)

Ahead of children returning to school after the summer holidays, or starting for the first time, the NHS posted a reminder online for parents. It can be hard to know what counts as being ill enough to stay home, and some conditions will not justify a sick day.

‌



In an Instagram post, the health service said: "With children heading back to school this week, it can be tricky deciding whether or not to keep your child at home if they are feeling unwell. If you're unsure, see our advice on when a child should be kept at home."

‌



Most schools will follow the UK Government guidance on what counts as an infectious disease. In some cases, conditions may not reach that standard and staying home is not excused.

‌



The health service added to its post: "If you do keep your child at home, it's important to phone the school or nursery on the first day. Let them know that your child won't be in and give them the reason."

For full details about specific conditions, see the NHS website here. For advice, consult a doctor or pharmacist, depending on the condition.

Content cannot be displayed without consent

‌



What does the NHS say about common illnesses in school?

The NHS has set out clear advice for parents on when children should stay off school with illness - and when it’s usually safe to send them in. The guidance is in place to help limit the spread of infections while avoiding unnecessary absences.

Chickenpox is one of the clearest examples of when children should be kept off school until all spots have crusted over, which is usually around five days after they first appear. For vomiting and diarrhoea, children should not return until at least 48 hours after the last episode.

Some illnesses need treatment before a return to the classroom. Impetigo often needs antibiotics from a pharmacist or GP, and children should stay off until sores have crusted over and healed, or for 48 hours after starting antibiotics. Ringworm can usually be managed with pharmacy treatment (a GP is recommended for scalp ringworm), and children can go back to school once treatment has begun.

‌



View 2 Images Some illnesses do not need time away from school, according to the advice

Measles requires a GP assessment and parents are advised to call the surgery before attending because it spreads easily. Children should stay off school for at least four days from when the rash first appears, and avoid close contact with babies, pregnant people and anyone with a weakened immune system. Scarlet fever also needs antibiotics, and children can return to school 24 hours after starting them.

What conditions can children still go to school with?

For everyday coughs and colds, the guidance is more flexible. Children can still go to school with mild symptoms such as a runny nose, sore throat or slight cough, as long as they feel well and do not have a high temperature.

Article continues below

Parents are encouraged to reinforce hygiene habits, such as disposing of used tissues and washing hands regularly. Several common conditions do not usually require time off from school, such as:

cold sores

conjunctivitis

head lice/nits

threadworms

slapped cheek syndrome (though schools should be informed if slapped cheek is suspected)

Children with mild COVID-19 symptoms who feel well can still go to school. They should stay at home if they have a high temperature or are too unwell for normal activities.

News.title: New 'fatal' warning for anyone on dapagliflozin, empagliflozin or canagliflozin
News.content:
New 'fatal' warning for anyone on dapagliflozin, empagliflozin or canagliflozin

More than a million people take the drugs every day

View 3 Images The pills are taken once a day

Researchers have issued a new alert over a common pill taken by more than 1million people in the UK. The medication is commonly prescribed to people with type 2 diabetes and a third of those with the condition have the drugs.

‌



New research has highlighted the link between ketoacidosis and SGLT2 inhibitors such as dapagliflozin , empagliflozin , canagliflozin , and ertugliflozin. Ketoacidosis occurs when harmful ketones build-up in the blood, triggering a life-threatening 'attack'. Swedish researchers say the complication could be more common in people taking the drug if they have low body weight.

‌



That could be around 10 per cent of those taking the pills. S eparate research found deaths from ketoacidosis are rising in the UK. Anyone concerned should not stop taking the pills - but talk to their GP.

‌



View 3 Images The pills help manage blood sugar

The new study in The Lancet Diabetes and Endocrinology journal was written by researchers from Karolinska Institute, who analysed the health records of 280,000 type 2 diabetes patients treated with SGLT2 inhibitors. The drugs are prescribed to help lower blood sugar levels, boost weight loss and protect against heart failure and kidney disease.

‌



The tablets are taken once a day. As well as low body weight, other risk factors include having had ketoacidosis before, having high blood sugar or suffering malnutrition.

Those with a history of dangerously low blood sugar are also at higher risk. Ketoacidosis can be triggered by an infection, and can in turn trigger kidney problems and stroke.

View 3 Images The pills have been linked to a serious condition

‌



"SGLT2 inhibitors provide medical benefits for many patients, "said Peter Ueda, assistant professor at the Department of Medicine in the Karolinska Institute. " Our findings are not primarily about avoiding treatment, but about improving our ability to identify high-risk patients and use these medicines more safely."

Last year, researchers from Imperial College London found ketoacidosis cases had risen by 81 per cent between 2015 and 2023. Symptoms can include feeling thirsty and needing to urinate more often than usual as well as stomach pain, nausea or vomiting, diarrhoea and blurry vision, unusually deep breathing, fruity-smelling breath and feeling extremely tired, sleepy or confused.

Article continues below

Ketoacidosis can trigger fatal multiple organ failure.

News.title: Chris Mason: Will Burnham find PMQs as 'nail biting' and 'nerve wracking' as Blair did?
News.content:
The weekly ritual that sits at the heart of Westminster's public image beckons, the half an hour or so of verbal jousting at Prime Minister's Questions (PMQs).

Prime ministerial memoirs tell the stories of how central a moment it is in the week of any occupant of 10 Downing Street.

Sir Tony Blair wrote that "PMQs was the most nerve wracking, discombobulating, nail biting, bowel moving, terror inspiring, courage draining experience in my prime ministerial life, without question".

Now, for the first time, it is Andy Burnham's turn to feel those nerves. And yet, curiously, the questions at lunchtime may well feel like a minor extension to the three and a half hours of questions he faced on Tuesday afternoon.

And this is because Parliament is playing catch-up: six weeks into the job, Burnham is encountering the moments that would typically arrive in the opening days, the routine moments of scrutiny in the House of Commons.

His arrival in office coincided with the departure of MPs from Westminster for the summer, and so the prime minister had a month or so that felt rather like a soft launch, heatwaves plentiful, Commons questions absent. Now plenty of them are coming, all at once.

I observed Andy Burnham's opening moments in the Commons as prime minister from the Press Gallery. He hovered by the Speaker's chair waiting his turn, flanked by Labour's Deputy Leader, Lucy Powell, who appeared to brush some fluff from the back of his jacket, and Louise Haigh, his first secretary of state.

News.title: Children as young as six going to A&E in mental health crisis
News.content:
There has been a sharp rise in children and young people - some as young as six - attending A&E units in England in a mental health crisis, NHS doctors are warning.

The number of six to 17-year-olds turning up in significant distress for things like self-harm and eating disorders, or in emotional crisis, rose by 36% between 2019 and 2025, according to the Royal College of Paediatrics and Child Health analysis.

Some faced waits of more than 12 hours once there. The college said A&Es were not the best place for them, but a lack of support in the community meant they often had nowhere else to turn.

The government said it was looking to improve services and would be setting out plans soon.

The analysis â based on figures provided under the Freedom of Information Act by NHS England â found there were 75,491 attendances at A&E by children and young people for a mental health concern in 2025.

That is up from 55,525 in 2019 with some of the biggest rises seen in very young children aged six to nine. The increases far outstrip the overall jump in attendances, which has risen by just over 8% over the period.

Doctors said the cases included children and young people brought in by families, carers and police â some of those in emotional crisis become aggressive or have challenging behaviour.

In total, more than 6,200, around 8%, waited over 12 hours in A&E.

News.title: Ariana Grande completes tour and steps back from public life
News.content:
Ariana Grande made an emotional exit on Tuesday night, as she wrapped up her Eternal Sunshine tour, and prepared to step back from public life.

The singer was occasionally close to tears - most notably during One Last Time, the song that took on extra meaning as an anthem for survivors of the 2017 Manchester terror attack.

"London, I'm going to need you to help me on this one," she said, kneeling down to be near the audience throughout the performance.

Last month, Grande announced a break from all future public-facing appearances following months of intense speculation about her health and appearance.

The step-back includes Grande's withdrawal from a production of Stephen Sondheim's Sunday in the Park with George at London's Barbican next summer.

She was due to appear alongside her Wicked co-star Jonathan Bailey. He also pulled out of the production on Tuesday.

On stage in London, Grande showed no signs of fragility or poor health - other than a foot injury that required her to swap her trademark stilettos for a succession of knee-high platform boots.

Nonetheless, she sprang across the stage in sync with her dancers, often on tip-toe to compensate for the lost height of her high heels.

But her voice faltered again during the song Nowhere, Nobody, as she sang the line: "Hard to believe in a perfect ending."

The blip was short-lived, though. Professional to the core, Grande regained her composure and was never less than magnetic on stage.

News.title: Watch: Astronauts set out on rare all-female spacewalk
News.content:
For the sixth time in history, a team of two women completed a spacewalk outside the International Space Station.

Nasa astronaut Jessica Meir and French astronaut Sophie Adenot suited up for a 6.5-hour spacewalk. Meir rode the stationâs Canadarm2 robotic arm to the worksites, while Adenot remained tethered to the station.

Meir previously made history in 2019 when she and Nasa astronaut Christina Koch completed the first ever all-female spacewalk.

This event marked the 284th spacewalk in support of space station assembly, maintenance and upgrades, and the seventh spacewalk of the year.

News.title: Fake 10 Downing Street listing exposes 'unfit' Booking.com, says consumer group
News.content:
Consumer group Which? says it was able to create a fake listing for 10 Downing Street on travel giant Booking.com.

The UK watchdog said its researchers were able to book a bogus stay at the prime minister's address - as well as leave a fake review noting "hanging out" with resident mouser Larry the cat as a highlight.

It said despite clear signs it was fake, Booking.com did not remove the listing until two months after it was uploaded.

"This limited test is not a true reflection of the experience of millions of listings or reviews published on our platform," a Booking.com spokesperson told the BBC.

They said because Which?'s listing was not "live" on its site across the two months it was present, "some of our automatic fraud controls were not triggered to completely remove the closed listing".

People could only see the listing and request to book the property during a 20-minute window opened by Which? so its researchers could try to book it.

Booking.com's spokesperson added "a range of checks and verification measures" help secure the site, and technologies such as AI "help us detect and remove the majority of fraudulent listings within 24 hours".

But Which? Travel editor Rory Boland said its checks had been shown to be "unfit for purpose".

"If Booking.com's so-called sophisticated AI systems can't spot that 10 Downing Street is not a holiday rental, then it's no wonder scammers can exploit the platform so easily," he said.

"It would be laughable that we were able to list the UK's most famous address for rent, if the consequences weren't so devastating for holidaymakers, who risk losing thousands of pounds to bogus listings and phishing links."

It is not the first time the site has faced criticism over its security efforts and customer service.

News.title: Apple Maps renames Lake Ontario as Lake America after Trump order
News.content:
Apple has renamed Lake Ontario as Lake America on its Maps app, after an order from US President Donald Trump as part of Washington's trade spat with Canada.

The change was made for US-based users, while those in Canada will continue to see Lake Ontario displayed. The BBC has contacted Apple for comment.

The iPhone maker's move follows Trump's executive order to change the lake's name after trade talks between the neighbouring countries collapsed late last month, with Washington imposing new 50% tariffs on $20bn (Â£14.8bn; C$28bn) worth of Canadian goods.

Rival technology giant Google made a similar switch for its users in the US in recent days, leading to backlash on social media.

Canada has responded to Washington's levies, saying it will implement "dollar for dollar" counter-tariffs.

Prime Minister Mark Carney's administration had walked away from the trade negotiations, due to what his office has called unacceptable demands.

Carney told the Trump administration to "start being serious" and stop trying to be tough before discussions between the sides can restart.

Trump's executive order gives the US Department of the Interior 30 days to update the change with the Geographic Names Information Service - the official database of what places are called in the country.

Apple was specifically urged by Trump to rename Lake Ontario on its Maps platform to comply with the executive order signed, according to US Interior Secretary Doug Burgum

The president has also posted several AI-generated videos on social media, including a clip of him kicking over a Lake Ontario sign and replacing it with another that says "Welcome to Lake America".

At the lake itself, Canada has installed a new sign with the words "Lake Ontario. Now and Always".

"Just in case President Trump or anyone else forgets, we've set up this sign to remind them, it's Lake Ontario, now and forever," Ontario Premier Doug Ford said.

News.title: Cup noodles made with cold water? BBC tries Japan's viral snack
News.content:
The BBC's Tokyo correspondent Kurumi Mori tries Japan's latest food trend, instant noodles made with cold water. The product has sold out in the country after going viral online.

Unlike regular cup noodles, this version is designed to be a cooling summer snack, but does it really do the job? The BBC puts them to the taste test.

News.title: Soft launches and late sittings - six ways to get cheaper meals out
News.content:
Restaurants often want to fill seats outside of peak lunch and dinner hours so opting for earlier or later sittings can be rewarded by a cheaper bill.

Apps such as First Table, which operates across 21 UK cities, as well as Ireland, New Zealand and Australia, give diners 50% off food when they book a participating restaurant's first or last dining slot. In exchange, diners pay a small booking fee.

EatClub is another, giving walk-ins up to 50% off the whole bill at thousands of venues when they redeem an offer within its app. The biggest discounts are at off-peak times.

Shokofeh Hejazi, director of foresight and innovation at global trends agency The Food People, says earlier dining appeals because it tends to be quieter and calmer, people drink less and it allows them to get home sooner.

Meeting up for breakfast also tends to be a bit more wallet-friendly as it's usually just one course and diners get the same catch-up time with friends and family, she adds.

News.title: UK long-term borrowing costs highest since 1998 ahead of October Budget
News.content:
Long-term government borrowing costs have risen to a 28-year high, putting further pressure on Prime Minister Andy Burnham ahead of his first Budget next month.

The yield on a 30-year gilt â a loan to the British government â rose to 5.89% on Tuesday, the highest since 1998.

Borrowing costs in the US, Japan and Europe have hit similar highs in recent days, reflecting investors' concerns about inflation, state borrowing levels and spending levels by large tech companies on AI.

Burnham told the House of Commons his government's "bedrock", as it seeks to tackle the cost-of-living crisis, would be "fiscal responsibility".

All of those factors will make the Budget process trickier for Burnham, who on Tuesday addressed MPs for the first time as prime minister, and his Chancellor, John Healey.

Burnham told the House of Commons the economy and the cost of living were "the biggest issues facing the country".

Higher borrowing costs will reduce the amount of headroom the government has against its self-imposed fiscal rules, limiting the amount Healey can spend on consumer-friendly measures to ease the cost of living.

Despite the squeezed public finances, Burnham said he would bring about "more substantial change" to ease living costs.

"Britain is not where any of us would wish it to be," he added.

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch accused Burnham of "living in the past".

"His diagnosis is completely wrong," she told the House of Commons. "His theory of growth is completely wrong. He thinks that if Government spends more money, we will all get richer.

"That is not how this works."

The chancellor has previously said he will stick to a set of fiscal rules imposed by his predecessor, Rachel Reeves, that restrict borrowing. These rules are designed to help markets have clarity about the path of borrowing.

The more that is forecast to be spent on interest payments, the more likely that there will be a squeeze on spending or some form of tax rise to meet these rules.

On top of that, higher government rates can feed through to higher business and household borrowing costs, and so weigh on the economy.

The prime minister was already facing a tough balancing act with taxing and spending, due to pressures on defence and the cost of living.

Burnham's ex-economic adviser Lord Jim O'Neill told BBC News that high government borrowing costs would force Labour to "get real" about "dealing with the triple lock" on the state pension, and "excessive" welfare spending.

Lord O'Neill, who recently turned down the offer of a formal position in the prime minister's team, said that current market pressure would force changes over "some of the things that no political figures ever seem to want to deal with".

As well as the rise to 30-year gilt yields, the yield on the benchmark 10-year gilt rose to 5.22% on Tuesday. This is its highest rate since June 2008, at the height of the global financial crisis.

Gilt yields move counter to the value of the bonds, meaning their prices fall when yields rise.

News.title: Israel warns it will retaliate if UK imposes sanctions
News.content:
Israel's Foreign Minister Gideon Saar has warned his country will retaliate if the UK imposes sanctions against it over the potential expansion of settlements in the West Bank.

Addressing Parliament for the first time as foreign secretary, Ed Miliband said he would introduce a "comprehensive reset" of policy on Israel "in the coming weeks".

He said the government would examine how to stop UK companies "financing, constructing or advertising new settlements" in the occupied West Bank.

Responding, Gideon Saar told Hebrew-language news website Ynet: "If Britain acts against Israel, Israel will act against Britain."

"If they act, I think they will be making a big mistake," he said.

Last month, Israel opened up tenders for the construction of some 1,200 settlement homes in the so-called E1 area - a strategically important area east of Jerusalem. The plans have drawn widespread international condemnation.

The development would in effect divide the West Bank in two and isolate East Jerusalem.

Miliband said the plans are "illegal under international law" and called them "the crossing of a red line, as it cuts through the heart of the West Bank and risks making a Palestinian state unviable".

UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham also warned that Israel's statement about the E1 area could "imperil or end" the two-state solution in the Middle East.

All settlements are illegal under international law and, under global pressure, Israel held off for decades on plans to build in the area.

News.title: Women pose as men to buy testosterone online after prescription difficulties
News.content:
Tomlinson said: "It's a postcode lottery and very dependent on the practice and the clinician, but you can hit barriers along the way.

"It's really difficult when you might know somebody else who's going through exactly the same thing and has sailed through the process and might not have gone into secondary care.

"There is no consistency across the board unfortunately."

Olver runs the menopause clinic at Aneurin Bevan's health board and said "we have definitely seen a very sharp increase in testosterone referrals from primary care - for women wanting to access it".

"It is difficult to meet demand and we have a testosterone clinic set up now for women who want to trial it."

She said each of the seven health boards in Wales used a traffic light system - some are red, meaning only specialists can prescribe the drug.

There are two amber options - one involves a GP requesting the support or agreement from a hospital specialist that testosterone is appropriate for a patient.

The second requires the hospital specialist to start and monitor the prescription with a "shared care agreement", with GP's continuing to prescribe it.

"One of the main reasons for this disparity is because we don't have a licenced product for woman on the NHS," Olver said.

A female testosterone product has been available in other countries for many years, and is available from private clinics across the UK.

Olver said it had now achieved a licence in the UK but still needed to be appraised by NICE, external to determine if it was cost-effective to use in the NHS, at which point discussions would also be required with the pharmaceutical industry about the cost to the NHS.

Currently the female product, Androfeme, costs the NHS around Â£100, but the male product, Testogel, is Â£30.

"Studies show about 60% of women will find benefit in improving their libido," said Olver.

"It's really important to manage expectations, because it's not this wonder drug that sometimes it's made out to be on social media.

"There's lots of reasons why women don't want to be intimate - some of those will be external factors, some will be anatomical.

"So it's really important to be fully counselled on what to expect when using testosterone, but also the limitations of its use."

The Welsh government said: "All health boards are expected to adhere to the NICE guidelines on identification and management of menopause including providing individualised care when prescribing HRT.

"We are aware this may include some practitioners prescribing testosterone for some women.

"We expect all health boards to conform to any recommendation made by NICE in relation to prescribing testosterone when its guidance is published."

News.title: Urine test can spot more than nine in 10 bladder cancers
News.content:
More than 300,000 cystoscopies are performed in the UK each year and there are significant waiting lists in some areas.

While the urine test is not a replacement for cystoscopies, it could help doctors identify patients at greater risk who should be prioritised for urgent ones rather than wait.

This NHS trial found that the Galeas urine test identified 92% of bladder cancer cases.

A negative result meant there was more than a 99% chance that the patient did not have bladder cancer.

It checks for any genetic material shed into the urine by bladder cancer and was originally developed by the University of Birmingham with funding from Cancer Research UK (CRUK).

It looks for more than 450 DNA mutations associated with bladder cancer across 23 genes.

Prof Richard Bryan, co-author of the study and from Birmingham University, said after spending years developing and evaluating the science, it was exciting to see "very promising early performance" in a large real-world patient population.

Under a licensing agreement, the test has been commercialised by Nonacus, which pays back part of the revenue to the University and CRUK.

Michelle Mitchell from CRUK said: "Too many people are waiting longer than they should for a bladder cancer diagnosis, and it's essential that we find ways to tackle this problem.

"It's early days for this test and further research is needed, but it's vital that we continue to find faster and less invasive ways to help diagnose or rule out cancer."

Bladder cancer is more common in men over the age of 60 and the main symptom is blood in your urine.

How serious bladder cancer is depends on how big the cancer is and whether it has spread elsewhere in the body.

Early detection and treatment of cancer saves lives.

News.title: Range Rover launches first fully electric model
News.content:
Range Rover has unveiled its first fully electric model, after a yearâlong delay to its planned launch.

The Range Rover Electric, to be built in Solihull, marks a major shift in its electrification programme, backed by largeâscale upgrades across its West Midlands sites.

Parent company JLR said it had up-skilled 10,500 workers for electric production as it pushes ahead with modernisation despite recent financial pressures and planned job cuts.

The launch comes as the Coventryâbased carmaker faces falling profits, supply chain disruption and restructuring following a cyber attack last year.

The company said the launch was being supported by new battery and electric drive unit production lines as well as training around 9,000 employees in Solihull for electrification and a further 1,500 trained across the region.

JLR's Electric Propulsion Manufacturing Centre in Wolverhampton is now producing battery packs and electric drive units alongside internal combustion engines.

Martin Limpert, managing director of Range Rover, called the new model the result of a decade of "considered engineering".

JLR's electric roll-out comes after a turbulent year with profits dropping to Â£66m in the first quarter after a fire at a key Norwegian supplier.

The business is also undergoing restructuring, confirming that fewer than 300 roles will go less than a year after a cyber attack halted production for more than a month.

At the time of the results, the firm said new product launches would leave "JLR in good shape whilst acknowledging the continuing geopolitical, inflationary and regulatory challenges the industry faces".

News.title: Families hit by long waits for dementia diagnosis
News.content:
Keith and Sue Andrews first met when they were 15, and they've been married for 57 years.

Sue's condition has deteriorated so much that she now lives in a home.

Keith says they had to wait almost a year for a diagnosis, which was difficult.

He says life became more maneagable, once they knew for sure.

"I won't say it's easy, but you know where you're going, and you know where you're heading and you feel a lot more confident in what you're doing.

"Because you know you're doing the right thing, but before that diagnosis, you don't know if you're doing the right thing or what to do even.

"And it's a horrible time, a horrible time."

Like Keith, 9 out of 10 families surveyed said that a formal diagnosis made at least one aspect of life easier.

That included understanding symptoms and behaviour, supporting the person living with dementia, accessing information or speaking to healthcare professionals.

A spokesperson for the Department of Health and Social Care said:

"This Government is determined to strengthen the support that is available both to individuals affected by dementia, and the family members who look after them.

"We are bringing forward the timetable for Baroness Casey's commission on reform of the social care system, and we are appointing a new dementia tsar to help lead our work in that area, as recommended by Baroness Casey."

"We are also implementing a new action plan for unpaid carers to ensure that they receive the support and recognition they deserve for the selfless work they do."

News.title: More than 110 rescued a week after Nepal deadly floods, army says
News.content:
One hundred and nineteen people have been rescued using air resources in Nepal following deadly floods, a spokesperson for the country's army said.

It comes nearly a week after the disaster that hit both Nepal and neighbouring Tibet, killing more than 1,000 people, with more than 3,900 still missing.

A Nepali army spokesperson earlier said a British male was among those rescued, along with 118 Nepalese people, of whom 44 were female and 74 male.

Later on Tuesday, the British man, Alastair Chambers, told the Telegraph and PA Media he was not rescued and had travelled to the region to help with aid efforts.

The BBC has contacted the UK Foreign Office for comment.

On Tuesday, Foreign Office minister Lord Wood of Anfield confirmed 36 British people remain unaccounted for - an increase from the 33 previously reported.

More than 600 are workers believed to be trapped in a vast network of mud-filled tunnels at hydropower sites along Trishuli River are among the thousands who are still missing.

Nepalese Prime Minister Balendra Shah said on Monday that 279 people had been rescued from the sites.

The rescue operation is being spearheaded by an international team made up of Chinese and Nepalese military personnel, while experts from India, Korea and Australia are also involved.

On Tuesday, the Nepalese Tourist Board said it had rescued 330 foreign nationals in total.

Saturday saw a rapid development team from the UK arrive in Nepal to provide support for Britons and their families.

News.title: Family mourn 'deeply loved' girl killed in Middlesbrough fire
News.content:
The family of a seven-year-old girl killed in a house fire said their lives had been changed forever by her "devastating loss".

Valentina Foster died alongside her aunt Natalie McDonald, 34, in the blaze at Grangetown, near Middlesbrough, in the early hours of 26 August. A man has been charged with their murders.

In a tribute, the youngster's parents said their daughter would "always be in our hearts, and her memory will live with us forever".

"She was deeply loved and will be missed beyond words by her family, friends, and everyone whose life she touched," they said.

"Our lives have changed forever, and we are struggling to come to terms with this devastating loss."

They added she would be "forever missed" by her brothers and sisters.

Sixteen people were killed and ⁠28 injured in a bus accident in eastern Egypt on Wednesday, local authorities said.

Egypt’s health ministry said the incident occurred on the Dahab-Nuweibaa ⁠road in South ⁠Sinai, on an area along the ‌Red Sea ‌coast that is popular ⁠with tourists.

According to the AFP news agency, 20 ambulances rushed to the scene of the accident on the country’s eastern coast.

The nationalities of those who died have not yet been released.

Last month, 15 people were killed and 32 injured in ‌a ​road accident in ‌Egypt's ⁠Ismailia governorate.

“Dr. Khaled Abdel Ghaffar, Minister of Health and Population, is following up on the health repercussions of a bus overturn incident that occurred this morning, Wednesday, on the (Dahab – Nuweiba) road, before the Al-Saada area heading towards the city of Nuweiba in South Sinai Governorate,” the ministry said in a statement.

A spokesperson for the ministry confirmed that Dr Ghaffar had directed health authorities to “provide the highest level of medical care to the injured, ensure the provision of all necessary supplies and medications, and maintain ongoing coordination with the relevant authorities in South Sinai Governorate”.

“The ministry affirms that all medical teams are operating at full capacity to handle the incident with utmost efficiency and speed, and the situation is being monitored moment by moment,” the statement said.

It added that it “extends its sincere condolences to the families of the victims and wishes a speedy recovery to all the injured”.

More to follow...

News.title: What happens next if the Lindsay Clancy jury can’t reach a verdict?
News.content:
The latest headlines from our reporters across the US sent straight to your inbox each weekday Your briefing on the latest headlines from across the US Your briefing on the latest headlines from across the US Email * SIGN UP I would like to be emailed about offers, events and updates from The Independent. Read our Privacy notice

Jurors in the murder trial of Lindsay Clancy are set to resume deliberations Wednesday, a day after telling the judge they couldn't agree on whether she was criminally responsible for killing her three children.

The jury, then in its fourth day of deliberations, sent Judge William Sullivan a note saying it had been unable to reach a unanimous decision, which is required by law for either a conviction or an acquittal.

Sullivan told the jurors to keep trying, a common instruction in criminal trials when juries indicate they are having trouble reaching a verdict.

After deliberating in private for the rest of the day, the jury asked at around 3:30 pm to go home and resume deliberations in the morning.

Clancy, a former labor and delivery nurse, doesn't deny strangling her children, but she says postpartum psychosis led to her actions. Prosecutors argue that she knew what she was doing.

The 36-year-old has pleaded not guilty by reason of lack of criminal responsibility.

open image in gallery Judge William Sullivan asks the jury to continue deliberations, on the day the jury in Lindsay Clancy's murder trial said to Judge Sullivan that they cannot reach a verdict, in Plymouth, Massachusetts, U.S ( Reuters )

Jurors heard testimony from relatives and doctors about how her mental health declined in the months before the killings and how her treatment included several medications and a short stay in a psychiatric hospital. Medical experts hired by the prosecution and the defense reached sharply different conclusions about her psychiatric state when she killed the children.

What happens if they can’t reach a verdict?

A mistrial will be declared and the case essentially goes back to the same status as before the trial, with the 36-year-old former labor and delivery nurse charged with murder and held at a psychiatric hospital awaiting resolution of the criminal case.

Clancy will likely go back on trial, but prosecutors have options

Prosecutors will decide whether to try again with a new jury. If they do, the jury selection process will begin again and a new trial will be scheduled.

Prosecutors could also offer a plea deal to Clancy, said Brad Bailey, a Boston defense attorney and former prosecutor who is not involved in the case.

“Any time the threat of a retrial with murder one hanging over the client is re-interjected, defense lawyers will, at the very least, explore whether or not there’s any interest in a resolution,” Bailey said.

Clancy doesn’t deny strangling her children at their home south of Boston, but says postpartum psychosis led to her actions. After the killings, her husband found her badly injured in the yard, where she landed after jumping from a second-story window. She was left paralyzed from the waist down.

open image in gallery Supporters of Lindsay Clancy gather outside the courthouse as the jury continues to deliberate during Clancy's murder trial at Plymouth Superior Court in Plymouth, Massachusetts on September 1, 2026 ( AFP/Getty )

Prosecutors argue she knew what she was doing.

Though less likely, the district attorney’s office could decide to not retry the case.

“Sometimes they decide not to, because of the sense that there may be the same result each time they try it, and because of the expenditures involved in trying the case to begin with, particularly when you have expert witnesses,” he said. “Those are going to be expensive cases.”

Clancy's defense will likely push to drop the charges

Bailey expects her defense attorney to aggressively lobby against another trial, making a case to the district attorney’s office along the lines of: “‘Why are you doing this to this poor woman? She’s still clearly obviously suffering. She’s been punished with her paralysis and, worse than that, the loss of her three children.’”

A conviction could mean life in prison for Clancy, while an acquittal might lead to confinement in a mental health facility.

Karen Read was another high-profile mistrial in Massachusetts

Karen Read was charged in the 2022 death of her Boston police officer boyfriend. Jurors in her 2024 trial deadlocked on the fifth day of deliberations, leading to a mistrial.

Prosecutors chose to retry the case, but a different jury last year found Read not guilty of second-degree murder and manslaughter charges.

Like Read's case, Clancy's has drawn a divided public reaction.

Clancy's livestreamed trial drew attention to maternal mental health after childbirth and was closely watched by a polarized public. Clancy’s sympathizers saw her as a loving mom who had realized something was badly wrong in the months ahead of the killings and sought help, including checking herself in to a psychiatric hospital. Her detractors said she deserved to be punished for an evil and selfish act.

Ariana Grande completed her 41-date Eternal Sunshine tour with an emotional final performance at London’s O2 Arena on Tuesday, before stepping back from public life for an extended break.

The 33-year-old singer became tearful during the sold-out show, which brought her 10-night London residency and the three-month tour to a close.

Speaking to the audience from the stage about halfway through the two-hour concert, Grande thanked fans for making the tour “one of the most beautiful, extraordinary experiences of my life”.

“I just want to express my gratitude without sobbing completely,” she told the crowd, according to Variety. “But really, thank you from the bottom of my heart, it’s been so special and I’ll cherish this experience always. I have the best fans in the entire world and I always have.”

“And I love your outfits, I love your faces, I love seeing you, I love connecting with you in this way. Thank you for all of your effort for making this so special,” she added. “All your messages and your costumes and your wardrobe and makeup is just so beautiful. I have loved every minute of this with you all and I just want to make sure I express how grateful I am. Thank you, and I love you so much.”

open image in gallery Ariana Grande completed her 41-date Eternal Sunshine tour with an emotional final performance at London’s O2 Arena ( Invision )

Grande began the tour with three shows in Oakland, California, in June and went on to perform a total of 41 shows across North America and London, with the final 10 taking place at the O2 Arena. Just like her penultimate show, she wore flat, above-the-knee boots, having announced earlier that she would need to wear “cosy footwear” on stage after suffering a “deep cut” to her foot.

The Wicked star also changed the lyrics to “thank you, next”. “Wrote some songs about Ricky/I’m tryna make him my last,” she said, referring to former boyfriend Ricky Alvarez. While the “Side to Side” singer didn’t confirm publicly that they were back, she made an Instagram post in August of the two together.

In a review of Grande’s show, The Independent’s Adam White wrote that the staging was “confined to the burnt-out husk of a house, which is first engulfed in flames, then weeds, then flowers, while police car sirens and helicopter spotlights suggest violent state surveillance”.

“The show’s ethereal closer – in which Grande, her body slack and floating, is absorbed into a great, white light in the rafters of the O2 – is beautiful yet strangely morbid. Is this a symbolic... death?” he wrote. “Whatever we’re meant to take from all of this, it undoubtedly feels like a goodbye.”

Grande’s decision to step back from the spotlight comes after months of intense public scrutiny of her appearance and health.

In a statement issued in August, the singer said she looked forward to “finishing the tour and ending it on a high note, both healthily and happily, and then taking a much-deserved break from public-facing work and appearances, which has led to endless, ongoing public scrutiny”.

At a show in Chicago soon after, the “we can’t be friends” singer read from a prepared note, telling her fans that the announcement wasn’t “a reactive or impulsive thing”. “It’s something that I had decided to plan,” she said.

open image in gallery Grande had been due to appear in the forthcoming London revival of Stephen Sondheim’s Sunday in the Park with George opposite Wicked co-star Jonathan Bailey, who announced on Tuesday that he too was withdrawing from the production ( Getty )

Her hiatus will take her out of the forthcoming London revival of Stephen Sondheim’s Sunday in the Park with George at the Barbican. Grande had been due to appear opposite her Wicked co-star Jonathan Bailey, who announced on Tuesday that he too was withdrawing from the production.

“Ari is one of my dearest friends, and my support for her is unwavering. Marianne is extraordinary and one of my longest collaborators and friends. After much consideration, I have decided to also step back from Sunday in the Park with George,” the 38-year-old said in a statement shared on social media.

Grande will be seen next in Focker-In-Law, the latest instalment in the Meet the Parents franchise, due to arrive in cinemas on 25 November. Directed by John Hamburg, who co-wrote the previous three films in the series, the comedy reunites Ben Stiller and Robert De Niro, with Grande playing Olivia Jones, a former FBI hostage negotiator who is dating Stiller’s character Greg Focker’s son, Henry.

Humanity has lost its chance to keep global warming within the safe limit set a decade ago, the United Nations has said, though it insists temperatures can still be brought back down if countries act with urgency now.

The world is set to cross the 1.5C warming threshold agreed under the 2015 Paris climate accord within the next few years, according to a first-of-its-kind report published on Wednesday by the UN Environment Programme.

Rather than abandoning the target, scientists and UN officials are now recommending a strategy of "overshoot," in which temperatures are allowed to rise above 1.5C for a period before being brought back down, through a combination of ending fossil fuel use and developing technology to remove carbon dioxide from the atmosphere.

However, the report warns of decades of worsening weather disasters, rising seas, species extinctions, and melting glaciers.

"Humanity is speeding past the limit to avoid climate catastrophe," said UN secretary-general António Guterres.

The 1.5C goal became the accepted global benchmark after UN scientists found the impacts of warming grew dramatically worse at 2C compared with 1.5C. The world is already around 1.4C above pre-industrial levels, based on a 20-year average.

The report's most optimistic scenario has warming peaking at 1.8C around the middle of the century if governments pursue the most ambitious climate goals available, though current policies are on course to push temperatures to 2.6C above pre-industrial levels by 2100.

open image in gallery Houses lie abandoned in the aftermath of flood caused by glacial lake outburst, at Thame village in Solukhumbu district ( AFP/Getty )

"Let's be very clear, 1.5 target is still the goal. But now we need to approach it differently from above," said Inger Andersen, executive director of the UN Environment Programme.

"It's a reality check. We have to live with this warmer world," said Richard Betts, a climate scientist at the University of Exeter and one of the report's authors. "But there's still a lot we can do to limit warming."

Andrew Weaver, a climate scientist at the University of Victoria who was not involved in the report, said the 1.5C limit was not "some magical climate cliff" beyond which the situation becomes hopeless.

"Every tenth of a degree we avoid still means less damage," he said, adding that the report was "among the bleakest UN climate reports I have read. It carries the unmistakable tone of desperation, frustration and urgency, but not resignation."

Every five years of delay in cutting emissions adds at least a tenth of a degree to the eventual peak temperature, said Joeri Rogelj, a climate scientist at Imperial College London and one of the report's authors.

Responding to the report, Katie White, the UK's minister for climate transition, said the summer's heatwaves and wildfires showed the climate crisis was already being felt at home.

"This summer of heatwaves and wildfires shows that we're living through the climate crisis, and every fraction of a degree that we limit global warming will count in our battle to protect our way of life," she said.

"The report reinforces why Britain is acting with urgency and ambition on climate change, both at home and with our partners around the world. We've more than halved our emissions since 1990, set world-leading carbon budgets, and we are accelerating clean homegrown power in a way that is bringing investment to our shores and creating jobs in regions up and down the country."

open image in gallery An aerial view shows an excavator clearing sludge next to damaged houses along the Trishuli riverline in the aftermath of flash floods at Trishuli Center in Nepal's Nuwakot district ( AFP/Getty )

David Waskow, director of the World Resources Institute's international climate initiative, said the report should be read as a warning rather than a reason to give up.

"Crossing 1.5C is no longer a distant possibility," he said. "Extreme heat, floods, fires and droughts are already giving us a glimpse of what a hotter world brings, homes under water, harvests wiped out and communities still rebuilding when the next disaster strikes.”

“With a developing Super El Niño, the worst may still be ahead. Every fraction of a degree raises the toll."

He said moving faster on clean energy and resilience was already proving that countries could protect both people and their economies, but warned that "carbon removal cannot substitute for deep emissions cuts, including rapid reductions in methane. We need both, and much faster."

Not every campaigner welcomed the report's emphasis on carbon removal technology. Lili Fuhr, fossil economy programme director at the Center for International Environmental Law, said overshooting 1.5C should be treated as a failure, not a strategy to manage.

"Exceeding 1.5C is not a strategy, it is a moral and political failure that locks us into irreversible harm, while those least responsible for the climate crisis are forced to bear its worst consequences," she said.

She warned that land and ocean-based carbon removal technologies, which remain under a UN moratorium because of the risks they pose to biodiversity and human rights, were being "rebranded as 'climate solutions' but more accurately understood as geoengineering."

Even the most optimistic large-scale use of such technology "would not deliver more than a few tenths of a degree this century, while locking us into decades of additional fossil fuel use, injustices, and harm," she said.

"The only way to minimize harm is to cut emissions now, starting with a rapid, just phase-out of all fossil fuels, not to delay action with speculative techno-fixes that shift the burden to future generations and vulnerable communities."

Fenton Lutunatabua, of the campaign group 350.org's Pacific office, said the report should harden, not soften, the resolve to cut emissions.

"We absolutely have to claw back every fraction of a degree possible," he said. "Just because overshoot is deemed inevitable, that doesn't mean we stop fighting to limit it to as short an overshoot as possible. Every day above 1.5C is another coastline swallowed, another plantation flooded, another coral reef lost."

Savio Carvalho, the group's head of campaigns and networks, linked the report directly to last week's disaster in the Himalaya. "We've just watched a glacier collapse bury Himalayan communities under mud and water, and we're watching Pacific nations lose land to the sea in real time," he said. "There is no version of 'limiting overshoot' that doesn't start with ending new coal, oil and gas expansion today."

The report warns that climate risks and the likelihood of triggering irreversible "tipping points" intensify with every additional fraction of a degree of warming and every year spent above the 1.5C threshold, including the destabilisation of the West Antarctic and Greenland ice sheets, the degradation of the Amazon rainforest, and the disruption of the Atlantic Ocean circulation system that keeps much of Europe temperate. "Some locations might become more or less uninsurable or even uninhabitable," the report said.

On the question of how to bring temperatures back down once they overshoot, the report said planting trees, the traditional approach to removing carbon from the atmosphere, could shave at most a tenth of a degree off global temperatures, meaning more novel carbon removal technology will be needed. Other scientists were sceptical that such technology could be relied upon.

"We were unable to stop the runaway train of global emissions to avoid 1.5C of warming," said Rob Jackson, a climate scientist at Stanford University who was not involved in the report.

"Now overshoot scenarios require us to stop the train quickly and to back it up. Is it our best hope? Absolutely. Is it likely? Absolutely not."

Bill Hare, chief executive of Climate Analytics, said the report did "a good job of describing the hole we've dug ourselves into" but "a poor job of showing us that there's a way out."

Additional reporting by agencies.

News.title: Transfer deadline day LIVE: Chelsea furious as Camara deal falls through, Balogun walks away from Everton, Man City sign Fernandez
News.content:
Transfer window: More money spent than ever, fewer clubs happy

A hectic summer transfer window has come to an end for the Premier League after a dramatic deadline day full of twists and turns.

Manchester City eventually completed a record-equalling transfer of Enzo Fernandez for £125m – but Chelsea’s deal for Monaco’s Lamine Camara dramatically fell through after the transfer deadline. Chelsea are said to be furious after Monaco pulled out of a £47m deal for the 22-year-old midfielder at the last moment.

Everton, too, were dealt a bitter blow after the deadline as striker Folarin Balogun walked away from his £40m move from Monaco, which came after they had sold Beto to Fiorentina and Iliman Ndiaye to Manchester City. The Toffees were left with Jack Grealish and Ainsley Maitland-Niles as their only deadline day replacements, while Tottenham have signed Mykhailo Mudryk on loan. Sunderland beat Crystal Palace to the signing of Malick Fofana after a dramatic tug-of-war for the £30m Lyon winger.

Manchester United did not sign a left back, despite being offered the chance to sign Rayan Ait-Nouri from rivals Manchester City. Liverpool’s business finished after signing Bradley Barcola for £120m and agreeing to sign 18-year-old Belgian goalkeeper Lucca Brughmans next summer.

Arsenal’s summer-long pursuit of Julian Alvarez finally concluded with the forward remaining at Atletico Madrid, who had refused to allow the Argentina international to join Barcelona. The Gunners have sold Gabriel Martinelli and Gabriel Jesus and even allowed Ethan Nwaneri to depart on loan – and the window closes without Mikel Arteta signing the marquee attacking signing he craved.
