World.title: They live by a shrine to a saint. Why are their homes being demolished?
World.content:
They live by a shrine to a saint. Why are their homes being demolished?

toggle caption Betsy Joles for NPR

ISLAMABAD, Pakistan –- For more than 300 years , people have settled around the soaring marble shrine of the Sufi saint known as Bari Imam, nestled at the foothills of the Himalayas. Some served the hundreds of pilgrims who visit each day, others to seek the saint's blessings. They include the ancestors of 30-year-old Wirasat Aly, who for generations lit evening lamps to honor the saint whose shrine now abuts upscale areas of Islamabad, the capital of Pakistan.

But on a recent day, Aly was salvaging bricks from his razed home, tossing the good ones in a pile to sell to construction companies. A truckful is worth the equivalent of $5.40, and it's how he's scraping together $70 monthly rent to shelter his family, including 8 children in his care.

Sponsor Message

They include the nieces and nephews of his disabled brother.

"We have to do something for the children," he says. "I'm going crazy. "Our stomachs are empty." Aly says he had to pull the children out of school because he couldn't afford the monthly bus fees, lunch money or books.

toggle caption Betsy Joles for NPR

In a roughly one-mile radius around Aly, there's rubble where there were once tightly-packed homes, as well as roadside stalls offering trinkets like meditation beads and prayer carpets. There were also tiny tent-like kitchens manned by cooks who, for a price, would prepare cauldrons of rice to serve at the free cafeteria adjacent to the Bari Imam shrine: a hall crowded with pilgrims and families of the working poor. Worshippers pay for those cauldrons as a way to seek the saint's blessings.

A neighborhood's demolition

But between December 2025 and April, local authorities razed much of the neighborhood, including hundreds of homes and shops.

toggle caption Betsy Joles for NPR

It was unprecedented, says leftist academic and housing rights activist Aasim Sajjad Akhtar : "I have never seen the intensity that I've seen," he said, referring to the demolitions, describing it as "something that is far more brazen than I've seen before." Akhtar and other activists estimated that 50,000 people lost their homes, or about a tenth of the estimated 500,000 residents of Islamabad's slums, or informal settlements.

toggle caption Betsy Joles for NPR

Residents say they believe this demolition drive took place because one of Pakistan's most powerful men indicated his interest in developing the area: the interior minister, Mohsen Naqvi. He's widely considered to be close to the chief of the army, which is Pakistan's most powerful institution. And in April, Naqvi said he had a vision of converting the area behind the prime minister's residence into a futuristic hybrid of Shanghai and Manhattan.

Sponsor Message

The area behind the prime minister's house is the Bari Imam shrine and its surrounding neighborhoods.

toggle caption Betsy Joles for NPR

"See how you can come and invest," Naqvi told businessmen in comments carried on local media outlet City21. He did not respond to NPR's request for comment about his involvement in these developments.

But an official at the Capital Development Authority, which governs Islamabad, said most razed homes belonged to an informal settlement known as Muslim Colony, and they had exhausted all legal avenues to stay.

The official, who requested anonymity because she wasn't allowed to speak to journalists, said residents who lived there before 2005 were compensated. But residents who stayed on or rented out their illegally-built homes, were expecting more compensation to move. "A perverse initiative was at play," she said.

Residents and activists told NPR that many of those people who came after 2005 were displaced because of conflict with militants near the Afghan border, an earthquake in Pakistan-held Kashmir, and by floods and droughts. Most worked to serve the city's elites as guards, cleaners, tailors and butchers. But the official said residents who could not afford Islamabad's expensive rents should go. "It's better to not move in a city if you cannot afford the price of living."

Local media reported that another 200 razed homes belonged to a neighborhood that was once a village, Nurpur Shahan . The official says authorities compensated residents for their land in 1957 after it was seized to build the capital city, Islamabad .

She said residents would not be compensated again. Some neighborhoods still stand for now, but a billboard planted near their homes warns: "All structure and activities on this land are unauthorized and illegal."

A local resident and lawyer representing families here, Tanvir Hussain, told NPR that the decades-old compensation was never properly carried out. He also noted other residents were promised relocation to other Islamabad neighborhoods, which never happened. The CDA official said the protesters were simply trying to extract more money because "this land is very valuable."

toggle caption Betsy Joles for NPR

Hussain said the argument was galling. His village existed before the state of Pakistan, and their lands were seized to build upscale areas, including "the prime minister house, foreign ministry, all this land," and yet, he says, they were treated like squatters.

Sponsor Message

Fearing the future

On a recent summer day, Atif Mehmood, 30, stood on the balcony of his home, threatened with demolition. He and his sister, and their children, watched worshippers squeeze through their alley as they marched toward the shrine of Bari Imam to commemorate Ashura, the slaying of the prophet Mohammad's grandson.

"This house is all we have," said Mehmood. He gestured to his niece Noor Fatima, 11, who has cerebral palsy and is confined to a wheelchair. Mahmood stroked her hair and asked, "if we lose this house, where will we go?"

The lawyer Tanvir Hussain contrasted how they were treated, and spoken of, to residents of a nearby luxury high-rise called One Constitution Avenue . It was built without proper authorization and media reported that developers failed to keep up with court-mandated payments to authorities.

toggle caption Betsy Joles for NPR

On May 1, police ordered its wealthy residents to evacuate. After an outcry that lasted a day, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif ordered authorities to halt operations and formed an investigation committee. A spokesman for Sharif referred questions regarding the high-rise to the interior ministry.

Amid the rubble around Bari Imam, Saida Tanvir, 50, was also given a reprieve of sorts, after her son Azeem Ahmed, 16, died while trying to block a bulldozer from crushing their roadside grocery store over the winter. Tanvir says police pushed her son hard and he hit his head on rocks. Days later, he died. Islamabad police did not respond to repeated requests for comment, but journalists at the time reported there were clashes between residents and security forces. They did not report any deaths.

Her home was visible, because the outer walls were cracked, but still standing. Tanvir managed to run a fan using an unwieldy connection of power cords.

toggle caption Betsy Joles for NPR

Tanvir says authorities let her stay a little longer in her home, despite the order.

Sponsor Message

Tanvir tells NPR that she used her last $180 to bury her son. Tanvir gestures toward the Bari Imam shrine and the cafeteria where volunteers serve free food. "That's where we eat now."

She said it hurt, because she'd worked hard her whole life, even as a widow with 8 children. "I never once begged. Now, we ask for the saint's charity."

With reporting by Zia Rehman in Islamabad.

World.title: Canada's top soldier expresses pride in 'who we are,' after Hegseth targets cadets in post
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The Canadian cadet and her instructor singled out by U.S. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth will be the ones to decide how — or even if — they will respond to a controversial social media post, says Canada's top military commander.

Gen. Jennie Carignan, speaking from a conference of chiefs of the defence staff currently underway in Victoria, B.C., said both members are receiving support from the Canadian military after the inflammatory post and suggested they'll be given agency to respond should they want to do so.

"We have personnel affected by various events. We are consulting with them on how they want to go about doing this," she said.

On Monday, Hegseth shared an image from the Cadet Training Centre in Vernon, B.C., depicting two young women in uniform with the caption "this is real" alongside a Canadian flag.

The online response to Hegseth's post was filled with remarks belittling the physical appearance of the people in the photo, but it also triggered massive backlash from Canadians.

Carignan says focus is on affected members

Top U.S. military officials, including the chairman of U.S. joint chiefs of staff, are present at the conference, and Carignan said she hasn't specifically addressed the matter with her counterparts, nor sought an apology.

"We are very much focused in supporting the affected members, and I have a lot of pride in what our Canadian Armed Forces do and who we are, what we are about," Carignan said in an interview with CBC News.

"We have professional competent personnel. And again, reinforcing this aspect, my U.S. counterparts are absolutely well versed in understanding how much of a contribution we are making."

She said the controversy is "a topic for later."

Some people posted that it was unfair for Hegseth to target the youth program in an attempt to disparage the Canadian Armed Forces and others criticized him for body-shaming women serving in the cadet program.

A screenshot of the post from U.S. War Secretary Pete Hegseth's X account. CBC News has blurred the faces in the image because cadets in Canada are 12 to 18 years old and are minors in British Columbia, where the age of majority is 19. (Pete Hegseth/X)

Asked about the backlash today, Pentagon deputy press secretary Jacob Bliss said "the X post speaks for itself."

Cadets blast Hegseth post

The Army Cadet League of Canada condemned the online harassment and mockery of cadets and their achievements.

"Directing derogatory commentary toward youth who are actively working to better themselves and serve their communities is unacceptable," the league said about Hegseth's remarks in a statement.

It said the league "stands firmly behind cadets, adult staff, volunteers, and officers who dedicate their time to building stronger communities and developing the next generation of Canadian leaders."

The national, community-based cadet program is for youth aged 12 to 18. A federal government website says the program provides "opportunities for youth to gain valuable knowledge and skills that build confidence and help pave the way in a transition to adulthood."

It's not clear how exactly the cadet training program's Instagram account — which had 1,821 followers as of Tuesday morning — came onto Hegseth's radar. Bliss, who works in the office of the assistant to the secretary of war for public affairs, did not respond to questions about how the defence secretary became aware of it.

When asked by reporters in Ottawa today about the post from Hegseth, Prime Minister Mark Carney said the message was "beneath their office."

"When the Americans stop doing memes, stop throwing shade, stop trying to be tough and start being serious about having the discussions, we can have those discussions," he said. "But it's not constructive, but that's their democracy."

B.C. Premier David Eby said Hegseth's post and the Pentagon's defence of it were an embarrassment.

"It tells you everything you need to know about the amateur-hour, distracted, bizarre leadership that Americans are being subjected to," Eby said.

He cited an ongoing military conference in Victoria, which includes U.S. representatives, as an example of the importance of co-operation during "unstable times."

Hegseth's post was also condemned by Arizona Democratic Sen. Ruben Gallego, a U.S. Marine Corps veteran, who called the comments "stupid" and "really deeply disrespectful to the men and women of Canada that have died fighting with us."

WATCH | U.S. Democratic senator calls Hegseth's comments 'deeply disrespectful': Hegseth's comments on Canadian military 'stupid,' says U.S. Democratic senator | Duration 1:37 Arizona Democratic Sen. Ruben Gallego says recent comments regarding Canada's military by U.S. cabinet secretaries are 'deeply disrespectful to the men and women of Canada that have died fighting with [the U.S.].'

Comments come amid trade tensions

The post comes as tensions between Canada and the United States increased after trade talks broke down last month.

The Trump administration hit Canada with 50 per cent tariffs on an array of goods in August, with both countries blaming the other for adding last-minute changes during negotiations.

Canada is set to implement its retaliatory duties next week.

Trump has spent the weeks since talks were frozen incessantly targeting Canada in his public remarks and social media posts. Last week, he signed an executive order to change the name of Lake Ontario to "Lake America" in his latest effort to agitate America's northern neighbour.

Many in Trump's team have turned their insults to Canada's military. U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Monday told CNBC the U.S. isn't at war with Canada.

"What are they going to do, take their two submarines from the Edmonton mall and sic them on us?" Bessent said.

WATCH | U.S. treasury secretary mocks Canada: Trump official mocks Canada, insists there's no trade war | Duration 1:56 U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent mocked Canada's ability to retaliate against the U.S. while insisting there is no trade war, comments that garnered pushback from several Canadian politicians.

The week prior, U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy claimed on Fox News that Canada "doesn't have a military."

Conservative MP Garnett Genuis responded to Hegseth's post on Monday saying "cadets do great work, and are not members of the military." He added that "158 members of the Canadian military gave their lives in Afghanistan after your country was attacked."

"Canada and the U.S. have a great history of fighting together for freedom and justice. It's history worth remembering," Genuis said.

Hegseth is facing immense pressure domestically from an unpopular and escalating war with Iran, the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, depleting stockpiles of munitions and the departure of top military figures during his tenure.

In the latest series of shakeups of military leadership, on Monday, Army Secretary Dan Driscoll resigned following widely reported tensions with Hegseth.

World.title: Alberta Premier Danielle Smith says Tennessee trip isn't sending wrong message amid trade war
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith denied suggestions Tuesday that her upcoming trip to Tennessee could be sending the wrong message amid a trade war between Canada and its southern neighbour.

"I hope no one's surprised to hear that I believe it's my job to continue reaching out at all levels to various influencers in the United States and get our message across that we have an incredible partnership," Smith told reporters at an unrelated news conference in Calgary.

"It's an incredible economic partnership, trade partnership, defence partnership, and we want it to continue."

The premier is set to travel to Nashville later this week on a personal trip, and her office said she'll be taking time out to meet with the head of the city's chamber of commerce, state tourism commissioner Mark Ezell and the chief executive of a Nashville tourism marketing agency.

While Smith positioned the meetings as examples of her diplomacy efforts during the trade dispute, she also said a priority would be learning more about how Calgary can position itself as "Nashville north" and boost investment in the music industry.

"It is a personal trip, but being down there I thought I'd take advantage of some of the expertise that's down there," she said.

Smith said the Tennessee capital made changes 25 years ago to make itself a music industry haven and economic powerhouse and she wants to find out how.

"I want to find out a little bit about what that is and see if we can develop some excellent partnerships with the music industry so that we can do a transfer of talent and transfer of expertise."

Smith also said Alberta wants to expand its tourism economy and that it's a good time to discuss leveraging Calgary's assets.

Nathan Cooper, Alberta's senior representative to the United States, is set to join the meetings.

Smith has said she wants to see Canadian officials double down on diplomacy efforts and get back to the negotiating table with the United States before Ottawa implements retaliatory tariffs next week.

Ottawa's tariffs, set to take effect Sept. 8, are in response to 50 per cent tariffs that U.S. President Donald Trump ordered on $27.6 billion worth of Canadian goods starting Aug. 22.

Trade talks broke down in the final hours before the U.S. duties kicked in, with Prime Minister Mark Carney saying the United States was asking for too much and offering too little.

World.title: 6 more byelections on horizon will test Liberal momentum, pressure other parties
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The Liberals are taking a victory lap after scoring a hat trick of byelection wins on Monday night — but there are still a batch of seats that need to be filled and will serve as another temperature check of the electorate in the months to come.

Prime Minister Mark Carney's party garnered over 50 per cent of the vote in each riding that was up for grabs on Monday, picking up seats in Ontario, B.C. and Quebec.

"The message from Canadians I think is clear. They've given their support … to the government's plan and I think that's because Canadians are united," Carney told reporters in Ottawa on Tuesday.

Lori Turnbull, a political science professor at Dalhousie University, said the Liberal wins in North Vancouver-Capilano and Beaches-East York aren't surprising given that they're considered safe Liberal seats. But she said she thinks Daniel Gobeil's win in Chicoutimi-Le Fjord was a vote of confidence in how Carney is handling the trade war with the U.S.

Turnbull said the Liberals picking Gobeil was a sign the Carney government wanted to make the byelection about the trade war.

"The fact that he chose a dairy farmer as a candidate, [signalled] a clear commitment to supply management," she said.

Three MPs resigned in the past week, which makes for five official vacancies at the moment. With Ontario Conservative Larry Brock set to step down later this month, that means six byelections will need to be held.

Conservative Cathay Wagantall officially resigned her Saskatchewan seat on Monday. Her resignation was preceded by former Liberal cabinet minister Steven Guilbeault — who officially resigned on Friday after giving notice that he was leaving back in May — and former NDP MP Alexandre Boulerice who stepped down last Tuesday to run in Quebec's provincial election.

The Bloc Québécois' Simon-Pierre Savard-Tremblay stepped down in June, also to run provincially. Liberal Shaun Chen resigned in mid-August.

Éric Grenier, author and analyst with The Writ, told CBC's Power & Politics that as things currently stand in the polls it's likely that the Liberals will keep the ridings they previously held and possibly pick up a few more.

WATCH | Grenier breaks down byelection results: What does the Liberal byelection sweep mean for the federal parties? | Duration 7:07 The Liberals managed to flip a Conservative seat in Quebec with Monday’s byelection while also keeping two seats in Ontario and B.C. Power & Politics breaks it all down with political analyst Éric Grenier from The Writ.ca.

"Still going to have lots of intrigue and interest in that next set of byelections and the Liberals will be looking to expand their majority," he told guest host John Paul Tasker.

Grenier said although Brock's riding of Brantford-Brant South-Six Nations has previously been considered a reliable Conservative seat, it will be one to watch when the campaign kicks off.

Brock won re-election in 2025 with just over 50 per cent of the vote, but the Liberals pulled in about 40 per cent. The Liberals picked up around 30 per cent in previous iterations of that riding.

"That will be a lot of pressure for [Conservative Leader] Pierre Poilievre," Grenier said.

WATCH | Liberals sweep 3 federal byelections: Liberals sweep 3 federal byelections in Ontario, Quebec and B.C. | Duration 6:58 The Liberal Party swept all three federal byelections held on Aug. 31, with wins in Ontario, Quebec and British Columbia. The victories ensure the Liberals maintain their majority government ahead of six other byelections expected in the coming months.

Turnbull expects the Liberals will make a push for Rosemont-La Petite-Patrie, Boulerice's former riding. The former NDP MP was the last ripple of the 2011 Orange Wave — the only New Democrat who remained in Quebec. Like in Chicoutimi-Le Fjord, Turnbull said the trade war might become a key issue in the Montreal riding.

"The Bloc and the NDP are in a really tough spot because if the question is, 'who do you want to run the country' — they are not in a position to form government," she said.

When Carney set Monday's three byelections in motion, he opted not to include Saint-Hyacinthe-Bagot-Acton.

That riding, east of Montreal, has been largely Bloc territory since the early 1990s. Turnbull said Carney avoiding that byelection in this round of votes "was no accident."

All parties have caps on how much they can spend promoting candidates during byelections. But the cap for a party increases if they're running candidates in multiple byelections and it's up to the party to decide how they want to distribute campaign funding amongst those ridings.

WATCH | 13 byelections expected in just 2 years: PM Carney to call 13 byelections in just 2 years | Duration 5:37 Prime Minister Mark Carney is set to be the first prime minister in 75 years to call more than 13 byelections in their first two years. So, what does this mean for the current state of Canadian politics? The founder of The Writ.ca, Éric Grenier, joins Power & Politics to discuss.

By calling two byelections in safe seats and one in a competitive Quebec riding, the Liberals had a spending advantage over the Bloc who only run candidates in that province. If Carney had included Saint-Hyacinthe-Bagot-Acton, it would have given the Bloc wiggle room to direct more campaign funding to Chicoutimi-Le Fjord.

"Clearly Carney has been very strategic in grouping the byelections in ways that will make sense for him," Turnbull said.

"I think that there will be machinations for sure to try to maintain a Liberal advantage in those [upcoming byelections], both financially and also in terms of just the overall ground game."

Grenier added that the Bloc might have concerns about how safe Saint-Hyacinthe-Bagot-Acton is after Monday.

WATCH | Win in Chicoutimi-Le Fjord 'means we can maintain Canadian unity,' MP-elect says: Win in Chicoutimi-Le Fjord 'means we can maintain Canadian unity,' Liberal candidate says | Duration 0:50 In his victory speech on Monday, Liberal candidate Daniel Gobeil said his win in the Chicoutimi-Le Fjord federal byelection means the voice of Saguenay 'will now be at the decision-making table.' He said Quebec MPs in the Liberal Party and Prime Minister Mark Carney 'will make a significant, positive change in Quebec's economy.'

"The Bloc is going to have to defend their seat … which, after the results in Chicoutimi, might make them sweat a bit," he said.

Of the six byelections coming, three will be in Quebec, two in Ontario (including in a safe Liberal Toronto seat, Scarborough North) and one in Saskatchewan.

In addition to the Bloc stronghold riding, Turnbull said she expects Carney will aim to use the timing of byelections to give his party some sort of advantage over the Conservatives in Brock's Ontario riding.

Once an MP officially resigns, the Speaker has to inform the chief electoral officer of the vacancy, at which point election rules state the prime minister has 11 to 180 days to call a byelection.

Because Savard-Tremblay stepped down in June, the last day that Carney can legally call the next byelection is Dec. 19.

World.title: Hannah Einbinder, Ilana Glazer and other Hollywood stars defend Mark Ruffalo against antisemitism accusations
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

More than 170 Jewish members of the entertainment industry, including Hannah Einbinder, Joel Coen and Canadian filmmaker Emma Seligman, have signed an open letter defending American actor Mark Ruffalo from what they called an "outrageous smear campaign."

"We are Jewish artists, writers, creative professionals, faith leaders and thinkers who have ... a simple message to share with the world," reads the letter, published Tuesday. "Enough!"

The letter says Ruffalo has been facing "the false and dangerous weaponization of charges of antisemitism" for speaking out against Paramount Skydance's proposed acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery and drawing connections between the deal and the war in Gaza.

Paramount Skydance is 47 per cent owned by CEO David Ellison and his father, Larry Ellison, who is also co-founder and chief technology officer of Oracle. The Austin-based technology company has been open about its support of Israel, with a top executive previously acknowledging that Oracle shared technology with the Israeli army.

CBC News has reached out to Ruffalo's representatives, as well as Paramount Skydance and Oracle, for comment.

In a statement to TheWrap and other outlets last month, Paramount said Ruffalo invoked antisemitic tropes when criticizing the deal.

"Words like 'genocide' and 'apartheid,' applied to a corporate transaction, aren't just wrong — they're a bridge too far, and they cheapen the very real suffering those words are meant to describe," the statement said.

An earlier letter signed by more than 1,000 Jewish members of the entertainment industry similarly condemned the actor's statements for "singling out Jewish executives" with "terms lifted from centuries-old antisemitic conspiracy theories."

Ruffalo has not publicly commented on Tuesday's letter, though he has since reshared a video on Instagram criticizing the proposed merger.

He has previously called the accusations of antisemitism against him "appalling and fundamentally dishonest" in a post on X, saying his criticisms were limited to "the actions of the Israeli prime minister, a military technology contract or the executives who supply it."

"My views ... should never be interpreted as hostility toward Jewish people, for whom I have deep love and respect."

Ruffalo attends the Oscar nominees luncheon in Beverly Hills, Calif., in February 2024 wearing an Artists4Ceasefire pin, calling for a ceasefire in Gaza. (Mario Anzuoni/Reuters)

The letter released Tuesday is the latest in an ongoing clash between Ruffalo and Paramount. Paramount Skydance's potential acquisition of Warner Bros., valued at $110 billion US, has been delayed until June 2027 after 12 U.S. state attorneys general sued to block it over anti-competition concerns.

A merged Paramount Skydance-Warner would create one of the largest studios in Hollywood, controlling massive properties such as Harry Potter, the DC superhero franchise and CNN.

Other signatories to the latest open letter defending Ruffalo include author Naomi Klein, retired rabbi David Mivasair and physician Gabor Maté, who are all Canadian, as well as American actor Ilana Glazer and filmmaker Jane Schoenbrun.

"We stand proudly with Mark Ruffalo," the letter reads, "and with all decent people who are bravely rising and speaking truth to power."

Broad City star Ilana Glazer was among the Hollywood celebrities who signed the letter defending Ruffalo from accusations of antisemitism. (Jack Plunkett/Invision/The Associated Press)

'A classic antitrust case'

On Aug. 21, Ruffalo criticized the merger in a series of Instagram stories, focusing in particular on Oracle for its dealings with the Israeli military. (Ruffalo is an outspoken critic of Israel's military actions in Gaza.)

He reposted a video of Oracle executive vice-chair Safra Catz speaking at the Israeli-American Council National Summit in Washington, D.C., in late 2024.

"There's a few things that we did that I really can't talk about ... to advance the agenda for the Israeli military," said Catz, who was then the company's CEO.

"We have some really profoundly scary technology at Oracle, and we wanted to make sure that it was available for the effort, let's just say that."

A spokesperson for Catz later told the Hollywood Reporter that the technology in question was meant for rescuing hostages taken during the Hamas attack on Israel on Oct. 7, 2023.

In his Aug. 21 post, Ruffalo said the Palestinian enclave is experiencing a genocide, "built on an apartheid system of oppression powered by Oracle."

"These [technologies] will most likely be merged into one of the largest media conglomerates in the world and one day used on you," he wrote, without going into further detail.

Israel has adamantly and repeatedly denied that its actions in Gaza constitute genocide, calling such accusations "wholly unfounded" and insisting it is targeting militants, not civilians, and aims to safeguard its security.

Ruffalo in his post also called the potential Skydance-Warner merger a "classic antitrust case," saying it would result in a loss of jobs, higher prices for consumers and reduced competition in the industry.

Paramount, which itself was bought by Skydance last year, has previously said the U.S. states' lawsuit pausing the merger "distorts settled antitrust law," maintaining that it would instead create a stronger competitor against other dominant streaming and tech platforms that have harmed the theatrical exhibition market.

WATCH | Israel rejects Trump's peace plan for Gaza: Israel rejects Trump's Gaza peace plan | Duration 1:57 Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu told his cabinet that 'Israel rejects the 15-point document' proposed by U.S. President Donald Trump's Board of Peace, and Israel's military will not withdraw from the territory until Hamas completely disarms first.

Oracle's support of Israel is well documented. Soon after the Oct. 7 attack, the company posted a message supporting the country, declaring its "solidarity with Israel in the fight against terror."

It also announced a donation of $1 million US to Magen David Adom, the country's national emergency service.

"We knew we might lose customers because of our support for Israel, but it didn't matter to us," said Shmulik Hauzer, who leads sales at Oracle Israel, in an interview with Ynet in 2025. "Supporting Israel is in our DNA — even if it costs us clients. That's our agenda."

The war in Gaza began after that Hamas-led attack on Israel, which by Israeli figures killed around 1,200 people and left 251 taken hostage into Gaza. More than 73,000 people in Gaza have been killed in the war since, according to Palestinian officials.

World.title: 'Where's Newfoundland?' ask shocked residents looking at Hilroy exercise books
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

As a new school year approaches, parents and students are out buying new school supplies — but one classroom staple has people in Newfoundland and Labrador demanding answers.

Hilroy Canada exercise books are known for the map of Canada on the cover. The design for a glossy version of the notebook also features the map but it's missing some of Canada's geographical features — namely Newfoundland and Cape Breton.

When handed a book by CBC News, Victor Aucoin, a teacher, initially adm ired the design but on closer inspection asked, "Where's Newfoundland?" before laughing.

"There's no Newfoundland. Oh, so we don't exist in Canada, OK! That's nice to see," he said.

"The most beautiful island on Earth and … we didn't make it to Canada," he added, shaking his head a little. "What a sin."

WATCH | 'It's totally unacceptable, I will be writing to Hilroy and tell them to take it off the shelf,' says teacher Victor Aucoin: ‘What a sin’: Missing Newfoundland, Cape Breton on Hilroy cover maps draws ire | Duration 2:43 A new line of classic Hilroy notebooks carries an image of a map of Canada on the cover, without any island of Newfoundland or Cape Breton Island. The CBC’s John Harris gets reaction on what’s missing.

Aucoin said given the province's economic importance to the country, it was shocking to see the island missing, adding he won't be buying these books.

"I know in my classroom if some children come in, I will ask them to tell their parents to contact Hilroy and file a complaint, as I will as well."

He added his mother is from Cape Breton.

"Wait till I call her and tell her Cape Breton is no longer part of Canada. She's going to be pleased. No Newfoundland. No Cape Breton," he said, again shaking his head.

Aucoin reiterated the situation is unacceptable and he would be contacting the company to tell them to take the new exercise books off the shelves.

"This is an uproar."

CBC News contacted ACCO Brands, which owns Hilroy, for an interview. In a statement, vice-president, culture and administrative services Lori Conley said the problem with the cover, which came out in 2025, is the result of a printing error.

"This was our error, we're sorry for it, and we're correcting it. We have stopped distribution of the affected cover and are working on the remaining inventory," she wrote.

Conley added people can reach out to the company for a replacement or refund.

" To everyone who spotted it: you're right and thank you for telling us," she wrote.

'It's bananas'

Johnathan Goodyear, also looking over the new design, said it was "kind of crazy" that Newfoundland is missing and wondered how it happened. He'd like to see the company recall the exercise books.

"It's bananas," he said.

Goodyear added Newfoundland and Labrador has contributed a lot to Canada, especially on a military front, so "knocking us off is pretty rough."

Some people worried the omission could have a detrimental impact on students learning about the country.

Goodyear is concerned it could leave students unaware of the country's geography.

"It's kind of a big deal."

Rose Wilkinson says Newfoundland should be included in the cover's map and worries people don’t know where Newfoundland is. (Danny Arsenault/CBC)

Rose Wilkinson said Newfoundland should be included in the cover and worries people don't know where Newfoundland is.

"I feel like most people don't think of it as a place [in] Canada because it's so small," she said.

Dace Gruchy, who initially admired the new design for its bright colours, was also unimpressed when he noticed Newfoundland was missing from the cover.

"That's mad disrespectful," said Gruchy. "We should be on this 'cause we're part of Canada."

World.title: Hong Kong pro-democracy activist Joshua Wong pleads guilty in 2nd national security case
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Prominent Hong Kong pro-democracy activist Joshua Wong pleaded guilty Wednesday to conspiracy to collude with foreign forces to endanger national security under a Beijing-imposed law that has effectively stifled the city's once-thriving pro-democracy movement.

It was the second prosecution of Wong, a former student leader in the pro-democracy movement and one of its most recognizable faces, under the national security law introduced in Hong Kong in 2020 to quell massive anti-government protests that rocked the city the year before.

Wong, who wore a blue shirt, appeared thinner as he entered his plea.

Before the hearing, a supporter shouted "hang in there" to Wong. His friend Louis Lee said Wong read books, studied, learned guitar and exercised in prison, exploring new hobbies and new things behind bars. He said he hoped to see Wong outside prison as soon as possible.

"I believe he and I, or friends outside, we will do our best in our own roles and continue to work hard in our fields," he said.

Pro-democracy activist Joshua Wong, seen here in March 2021 in police custody, pleaded guilty to a second national security charge in Hong Kong. (Tyrone Siu/Reuters)

Current sentence due to end in January

Wong is expected to be sentenced later. The offence is punishable by a prison term of three to 10 years, or up to life imprisonment if the offence is deemed to be "of a grave nature." Pleading guilty could typically result in a reduced sentence.

He was already serving a prison term of four years and eight months after entering a guilty plea in a separate national security case linked to an unofficial political primary.

Before the arrest for the collusion-related offense in June 2025, Wong had been expected to be freed next January.

Critics say Wong's case showed the authorities' determination to silence prominent dissidents, chilling civic activism. But to Beijing, Wong is an anti-China figure who supports Hong Kong independence, a red line for authorities.

Rose to prominence as student activist

Wong, 29, was accused of conspiring with fellow activist Nathan Law and others to ask foreign countries, or institutions, organizations, or individuals outside China to impose sanctions, blockades or engage in other hostile actions against Hong Kong or China from July 1-Nov. 23, 2020.

In 2012, Wong rose to prominence as a high school student leading protests against the introduction of national education in Hong Kong schools. His fame spread later as a student leader of the 2014 Occupy Movement.

Wong co-founded a political party, "Demosisto," in 2016 with fellow young activists, including Law, who became the city's youngest lawmaker that same year.

During the leaderless 2019 protests, Wong helped seek overseas support for the democracy movement, including from the U.S. But Beijing criticized his actions, saying he "begged for interference" by foreign countries.

Demosisto disbanded when Beijing imposed the security law in 2020, which authorities said was necessary for the city's stability.

Many other leading activists were also jailed under the same law, including former media tycoon Jimmy Lai. Some activists fled to other democratic countries, including the U.S. and the U.K.

Hong Kong authorities separately offered rewards of one million Hong Kong dollars ($176,000 Cdn) for information leading to the arrests of Law, who moved to Britain, and other overseas-based activists.

World.title: Day of attacks by U.S. and Iran marks most serious escalation of conflict in weeks
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The U.S. launched new air strikes on Iranian targets on ‌Tuesday, in a move that threatened to reignite the six-month-old conflict that has driven global energy prices higher and weighed heavily on U.S. President Donald Trump's popularity at home.

The strikes followed a weekend exchange of fire — the first since July — and took place after two tankers were hit on Monday while leaving the Strait of Hormuz, the global oil supply waterway that Iran has effectively closed to shipping. Global oil prices rose more than $4 US a barrel on Tuesday, settling at a five-week high.

Tehran struck back at U.S. assets in Jordan, Bahrain and Iraq and remained defiant, warning that it would prevent oil being exported from the Gulf, despite a threat by U.S. President Donald Trump to hit Iran "hard" in response to the renewed Iranian strikes, and a warning from U.S. ​Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent that Washington was about to impose new sanctions.

Five people were killed and 50 wounded at a wedding near Sirik, ​a coastal area on the Strait of Hormuz, the Iranian Red Crescent reported. The Mehr news agency said a four-year-old child was among those killed.

WATCH | Escalation of attacks from both sides: U.S., Iran trade new strikes, warnings as hostilities flare | Duration 3:08 The U.S. launched a fresh round of airstrikes against Iran on Tuesday, following a weekend exchange of fire that broke a month of relative calm in the conflict. Tehran said it responded with missiles and drones on U.S. targets in the region while warning that U.S. attacks would 'tighten the lock' on the Strait of Hormuz.

There was no immediate U.S. reaction to the reports.

The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said in a statement the U.S. attacks would "tighten the lock" on the Strait of Hormuz, which carried one of every five barrels ​of the world's oil before the war. Iranian threats against unauthorized shipping have shut most of the tanker traffic through the strait, driving up oil prices.

"If the enemy wants us ⁠not to export oil from the Persian Gulf, no one ⁠will be able to export oil," Iranian parliament speaker Mohammad Baqer Qalibaf was quoted as saying by Iranian media.

Strikes disrupt relative calm of past month

The second round of U.S. strikes in three days followed a month of relative calm in which the U.S. and Iran mostly held their fire while exchanging bellicose statements.

Trump called Tuesday's strikes retaliation for Iranian attempts to place sea mines in the Strait of Hormuz after the U.S. military announced last week it had cleared a strategic shipping lane of Iranian mines, and for Iranian missiles fired at a U.S. military ⁠base in Jordan.

Later, sirens sounded anew in Jordan, state television reported.

Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said it launched a heavy ballistic missile attack on the U.S. Marine Corps base in Jordan and "killed a large number of U.S. forces." Iran's Fars news agency called it a retaliatory operation that fired missiles and drones.

There were no casualties so far from the Iranian attack on facilities in Jordan, two U.S. officials told Reuters. This was based on initial information and could change ‌as Iranian attacks continued, the officials said.

Iranian media also reported the country's military targeted a U.S. base in Bahrain with a large-scale drone attack, and the Kuwaiti army reported ⁠its air defences were responding to a hostile drone attack. Since the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran on Feb. 28, Iran has responded with missile and drone strikes on U.S. allies in the region.

Jordan's armed forces said its air defence systems dealt with 13 ballistic missiles that entered the kingdom's airspace. The military said 10 missiles were intercepted and destroyed, while three fell in remote areas far from population centres.

The IRGC ⁠also said its ground forces carried out combined missile and drone attacks on ​U.S. bases in Erbil in northern Iraq, destroying a repair facility, warehouses for technical equipment and a system used to control a U.S. surveillance balloon. The IRGC also said fuel tanks were set ablaze and several U.S. ​personnel were killed.

Neither Iraq nor the U.S. had confirmed ⁠the attack.

Another ceasefire unlikely, Trump suggests

Trump had earlier warned if Iran retaliated for the attack, "they will be hit again at a much harder and higher level."

In an interview with Fox News, Trump played down the prospects of another ceasefire. The U.S. and Iran reached a deal in June that quickly fell apart, largely over interpretations of Iranian control of the Strait of Hormuz.

"I think ⁠an agreement with them isn't worth the paper it's written on. We gave them a lot of chances," Trump told Fox News.

The Fars news agency cited an IRGC spokesperson as saying the U.S. "will regret its new attacks."

The U.S. Embassy in Qatar urged Americans currently in the Middle East to exercise "heightened vigilance and be aware of potential flight cancellations, airspace closures, and travel disruptions."

WATCH | A look at sea mines: Can Iran really launch sea mines from rockets? | About That | Duration 2:56 U.S. Central Command says it carried out fresh strikes on Iran, claiming it was retaliation for Iran preparing to launch sea mines from rockets into the Strait of Hormuz. Andrew Chang digs deeper into what may be Iran's novel ability to deploy underwater mines with missiles. (Photo credits: The Canadian Press, CAT-UXO, Reuters, Adobe Stock and Getty Images)

Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian had said early Tuesday at a regional summit in Kyrgyzstan that Tehran would reciprocate immediately if Washington honoured its commitments under a June memorandum of understanding that was intended to halt the conflict.

The MOU declared an end to fighting that has now killed thousands in Iran and Lebanon since U.S. and Israeli strikes began on Feb. 28. But it also deferred many of the most difficult issues and paved the way for a broader 60-day negotiation period — which passed without further agreement.

Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil ⁠Baghaei told a news conference in Tehran that Washington was "addicted to making excessive demands and has mistaken negotiations for dictating terms."

Children swim as ships are seen anchored in the Strait of Hormuz on Aug. 10, off the coast of Bandar Abbas, Iran. (Ali Saeedi/Getty Images)

Energy exports curbed

Iranian and U.S. blockades ⁠of the Strait ⁠of Hormuz have sharply curbed energy exports ‌from the Gulf as both sides tried to assert their authority over the waterway.

Efforts by mediators, including Qatar and Oman, to broker a deal to reopen the strait, which carried about a fifth of ⁠global oil supplies before the U.S. and Israel launched strikes on Iran more than six months ago, have so far proven inconclusive.

U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on Tuesday that the United States is likely to announce sanctions on a bank this week as part of its economic campaign against Iran. Another may follow the week after, Bessent said, as well as new secondary sanctions meant to increase economic pressure on the country.

"We are speaking to our allies here, who have all come forward, and we have had a great show of support," he said at an event on the sidelines of the U.S.-hosted G20 finance leaders in Asheville, N.C.

U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced a new set of sanctions against Iran, describing them as 'an economic D-Day' on Aug. 24. (Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images)

He said the U.S. may also target airline leasing companies and others that did business with the IRGC.

"We have zero tolerance," Bessent said. "We are going to economically asphyxiate this regime."

Iran's central bank governor, Abdolnaser Hemmati, said earlier on Tuesday that Tehran had sufficient foreign currency reserves.

World.title: Apple Maps follows Google, changes name of Lake Ontario to 'Lake America'
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Apple changed the name of Lake Ontario to Lake America on the web version of its Apple Maps following U.S. President Donald ‌Trump's executive order renaming the lake.

The move by Apple on Tuesday followed a decision by Alphabet late on Saturday to change the name of the lake on its Google Maps for U.S. users.

Apple confirmed that ​U.S. users will see the label "Lake America" following a change to ​the body of water's name in the U.S. Geographic Names Information System. U.S. Secretary of the Interior Doug Burgum had told Fox Business on Monday that Trump "reached out to Apple directly" about the renaming.

Users in Canada will continue to see Lake Ontario, and ​users in the rest of the world will see both names, ⁠following the same approach ⁠Apple used after Trump renamed the ‌Gulf of Mexico as the Gulf of America.

Google's switch caused some confusion in Canada over the weekend, with some companies and government organizations briefly showing maps using the Lake America name on their websites.

WATCH | The name 'Lake America' showed up on Canadian maps on the weekend: Lake Ontario appears as 'Lake America' on some Canadian government sites | Duration 2:40 Lake Ontario now appears as 'Lake America' on Google Maps in the United States, but also on some Canadian federal and provincial government websites that use Google's API for their maps.

New York sides with Canada

The name changes illustrate how U.S. tech companies are being pulled into geopolitical disputes as the Trump administration pressures them to comply with executive orders that allies and international bodies ⁠have rejected.

Trump's executive order on Lake Ontario, one of the five Great Lakes of North America, applies to U.S. federal usage for the lake, and does not govern what ‌Canada, international bodies or other organizations call the lake.

A majority of Americans oppose Trump's moves last week to raise taxes on imported Canadian goods and his order to rename Lake Ontario as Lake America, a new Reuters/Ipsos poll ​found.

Within hours of Trump's executive order, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and New York Governor Kathy Hochul, ⁠a Democrat, said they would not be changing the name, which is more than ⁠400 years old. New York borders the lake on the U.S. side.

About 52 per cent ⁠of ⁠the surface area of Lake ​Ontario is in Canada, with the remainder in New York.

WATCH | Historian says Trump lacks authority to rename the lake: Trump renamed Lake Ontario to 'provoke Canada,' historian says | Hanomansing Tonight | Duration 8:34 Historian Tim Naftali says U.S. President Donald Trump's decision to rename the American side of Lake Ontario was intended to stir nationalist sentiment in the U.S. and provoke Canada.

Since early 2025, Trump has repeatedly ​taunted Canada about becoming ⁠the 51st U.S. state, an idea Canadian leaders have dismissed as ridiculous.

Trump also ordered the Gulf of Mexico renamed to Gulf of America in January 2025 and both Google and Apple revised their map apps to reflect the change for U.S. users.

World.title: Iran targets U.S. bases in Middle East in retaliation for earlier attacks
World.content: U.S. and Iran exchange attacks as Middle East hostilities reignite Trump told Fox News on Monday that the U.S. would respond to Iran's attacks on U.S. forces, without giving details Author of the article:Bloomberg News Bloomberg News Kevin Whitelaw, Wendy Benjaminson and Omar Tamo Published Aug 31, 2026 4 minute read 66 Comments Strait of Hormuz FILE: An Iranian woman enjoys a dip in the sea as vessels are seen in the Strait of Hormuz off the port city of Bandar Abbas, in southern Iran on August 10, 2026. Photo by ATTA KENARE /AFP via Getty Images Article content The US and Iran exchanged strikes for the first time in about a month as American forces hit an island in the Strait of Hormuz and the Islamic Republic responded by launching attacks on the United Arab Emirates and Jordan. Article content President Donald Trump told Fox News on Monday morning that the US would respond to Iran’s attacks on US forces, without giving details. Article content Article content Iranian media also said the country’s authorities seized a bulk carrier near the port of Bandar Abbas in the strait and claimed an oil supertanker trying to go through the waterway was hit by mines early on Monday. US Central Command said in a social media post on Monday that no ships had hit mines in Hormuz. Article content Article content Crude oil prices rose, with Brent climbing 2.4% to above $90 a barrel. European natural gas prices increased too. Article content Downtown Tehran Pedestrians walk past a wall mural along a street in downtown of Tehran on August 31, 2026. Photo by ATTA KENARE /AFP via Getty Images Article content opening envelope Channel Israel Columnist Jesse Kline keeps you up to date with what’s happening in Israel and the effects of antisemitism on life here in Canada. Friday mornings. youremail@email.com Sign Up By signing up you consent to receive the above newsletter from Postmedia Network Inc. Interested in more newsletters? Browse here. Article content The incidents underline the high tensions between Washington and Tehran, with the countries still at odds over the status of the Strait of Hormuz and neither willing to restart negotiations to end a war now more than six months old. Trump’s comments of further US attacks indicate they may be back in a cycle of military escalation that could bring further volatility to energy and stock markets. Article content Several current and former US and Iranian officials have said they expect the conflict to drag on for months, with the sides essentially deadlocked and bouts of fighting puncturing weeks-long lulls in hostilities. Article content “The state of neither war nor peace cannot be a sustainable solution,” Anwar Gargash, a senior foreign-policy adviser to the UAE’s leadership, said on X soon after the country fended off a drone attack. “What is needed today are realistic and sustainable political solutions that address the political and economic dimensions of the crisis, beginning with overcoming the escalation and returning navigation in the Strait of Hormuz to its normal state.” Article content Article content US Central Command, which oversees military operations in the Middle East, said it fired on Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps forces after spotting them preparing to deploy mines into the Strait of Hormuz. Article content Donald Trump U.S. President Donald Trump waves after stepping off Air Force One at Joint Base Andrews, Maryland on August 28, 2026. Photo by KENT NISHIMURA /AFP via Getty Images Article content Read More None Jamie Sarkonak: Provinces should hit gangs where it hurts — by going after window tint Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney speaks about the trade dispute with the United States at the Davie Shipyard in Levis, Quebec, Canada on August 24, 2026. Michael Higgins: Trade war was never about sovereignty  1 Article content It was a “limited, precise action,” Central Command said. “Iran created the threat and the US military eliminated it to protect civilian mariners, commercial shipping, and the free flow of global commerce.” Article content Iran said several people were killed in the US strikes, and that they targeted Larak Island overnight. The IRGC retaliated with a missile-and-drone attack on US air bases in Jordan early Monday. Jordan’s military intercepted eight missiles, destroying them before they caused any damage, the Jordan News Agency reported. Article content The UAE’s military dealt with a drone coming from Iran over the country’s territorial waters and said its forces remain on high alert. The Gulf Arab state denied an IRGC claim that the Al Minhad airbase just outside of Dubai was targeted with missiles. Article content Iranian media reported that a vessel carrying sugar was seized near the port of Bandar Abbas, which sits in the strait, because it was polluting the surrounding waters. The ship wasn’t identified.  2  Article content The US attack was the first against Iran since late July, as Trump has shifted toward an economic pressure campaign aimed at winning concessions from Tehran. Countries with ties to Tehran have so far shrugged off sanctions threats. Iran analysts and sanctions experts have largely been underwhelmed by early US actions, including proposing to cut off the UAE branches of Egypt’s Banque Misr from the American financial system. Article content Mourners pray for Iran's slain supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei Mourners pray for Iran’s slain supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei during the second day of funeral ceremonies at the Grand Mosalla in Tehran on July 5, 2026. Photo by ATTA KENARE /AFP via Getty Images Article content Any sustained return to hostilities risks driving up energy costs and stoking inflation, which would unnerve global investors and complicate Republicans’ efforts to retain control of the US Congress in November’s midterm elections. Polls show growing frustration among American voters with the war and Trump’s inability to bring it to an end. Article content Last week, the US military said it finished clearing mines from shipping routes in the strait, which previously carried one-fifth of the world’s oil and liquefied natural gas. US allies, however, have privately warned that the strait was still likely mined. Article content Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi has said Iran remains open to resuming diplomacy with the US, but argued that progress depends on Washington abandoning its pressure campaign. Article content Article content Iran, in particular, wants the US to lift a blockade of Iranian ports. That operation is preventing Iran from getting its oil onto international markets and importing many vital goods, causing inflation to rise. Still, the economic squeeze isn’t powerful enough yet to convince Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei and hardliners within the government to accept American demands and allow ships free passage through the Strait of Hormuz. Article content Following what he described as “creative discussions” last week with Qatar, a mediator in the conflict, Araghchi said progress “hinges on US understanding of one simple fact: Pressure doesn’t work.” Article content Scott Bessent Scott Bessent, US treasury secretary, speaks to members of the media outside the White House in Washington, DC, US, on Thursday, Aug. 20, 2026. Photo by Yuri Gripas /Bloomberg Article content US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent promised an “economic onslaught” against Iran and its trading partners. That includes China, which buys 90% of Iran’s oil. He said the White House would discuss with allies their plans to stop buying Iranian products, but so far there have been no agreements to do so. Article content Bessent told the Associated Press ahead of the Group of 20 finance ministers meeting in North Carolina that the US would penalise a second bank that does business with Iran this week. Article content “This is going to be financial violence if we have to,” Bessent said. World.title: 1 killed, 15 injured in northeast Colombia car bomb attack on police station
World.content:
At least one person was killed and another 15 injured in a car bomb attack on a police station on the outskirts of Cucuta, the capital of Norte de Santander.

According to the National Police, the bomb exploded on Monday evening outside of the police station in Los Patios, a municipality that is part of Cucuta’s metropolitan area.

Apart from the casualties, the blast also damaged buildings and vehicles that were parked near the police station, police told local media.

In an initial response, President Abelardo de la Espriella said on social media platform X that he had convened a security council meeting “with the entire top brass of the security forces.”

“Wherever the terrorists try to sow fear, that is where the State will be with all is might,” said De la Espriella.

We will pursue with an iron fist those who threaten Colombians, until we capture them, dismantle their networks, and restore peace to our communities. Abelardo de la Espriella

In the region around Cucuta, guerrilla organizations ELN and EMBF have been fighting each other. Organized crime groups operate mainly inside the urban area of the capital of the Norte de Santander province.

No group immediately claimed responsibility for the attack.

World.title: Vote to move Uribe’s massacre probe to Congress triggers infighting among Colombia’s left
World.content:
Internal fractures within Colombia’s leftist opposition burst into the open following a vote by five representatives of the Historic Pact (PH) party to transfer a criminal investigation against former President Alvaro Uribe to Congress’ Accusations Commission.

The controversy erupted after the five PH members of the committee backed a motion of Uribe’s Democratic Center (CD) party to assert legislative jurisdiction over long-standing criminal cases against Uribe, including investigations into the massacres of El Aro (1997) and La Granja (1996), and the 1998 assassination of human rights defender Jesus Maria Valle.

PH members

David Alejandro Toro

María del Mar Pizarro

Heráclito Landínez

Jorge Bastidas

Gabriel Becerra

As the former governor of Antioquia, Uribe would have been in on the massacres carried out by the Bloque Metro and AUC paramilitary groups, according to the Prosecutor General’s Office, which refused to turn over the investigations.

The commission claimed jurisdiction over the Uribe file because the paramilitaries didn’t demobilize until after 2002, when he became president.

Critics of the decision, including the prosecution and PH Senate chief Ivan Cepeda, argued that Uribe’s alleged involvement in the crimes happened years before he was granted presidential immunity.

Cepeda spent much of his career fighting Uribe in court over his alleged ties to the AUC.

Because of the committee vote, the Constitutional Court will have to rule on who gets to investigate Uribe’s alleged crimes against humanity, which could delay the investigation.

Journalists who reported on the PH support for the fabricated conflict suggested that this may be part of a political deal between congressmen political deal between Uribistas and Petristas, supporters of former President Gustavo Petro.

Becerra, who is close to Cepeda, said in a statement that there “existed nor will there exist any political deal that would compromise justice, truth or the rights of victims.

According to the house representative, the PH lawmakers “initially considered it reasonable and legally appropriate to clarify the jurisdiction of the authority responsible for conducting the investigation,” but changed their mind in response to the controversy and calls for their resignation.

Lawyer Miguel Angel del Rio, the victims representative in the Uribe case, told Tercer Canal that “the ethic committee of the Historic Pact should investigate these five congressman,” adding that “what we have here is solidarity with impunity and this cannot be allowed.”

The Historic Pact became Colombia’s largest political party after congressional elections in March, but has seen an increase in internal tensions after Cepeda’s failure to win the presidential election in June.

World.title: Finance minister presents Colombia’s $203B budget proposal
World.content:
Colombia’s Finance Minister Miguel Gomez presented a budget proposal of COP634.9 trillion ($203 billion) for the coming year, a 14% increase compared to last year.

Much of the increase is due to the government’s debt obligations, which went up 55% to 155.4 trillion ($49.8 billion), almost a quarter of the entire budget.

At a presentation, Gomez told press that an earthquake that left tens of thousands homeless in western Colombia earlier this month also forced the administration of Abelardo de la Espriella to increase spending.

In a video, the finance minister also said that the government “has taken deci

The budget bill, a revision of the one that was presented by the former government of former President Gustavo Petro, will have to be approved by Congress before October 20 or be issued as a decree.

The government will also present a Finance Bill, which determines how the government plans to pay for its spending, before December.

World.title: Colombia claims killing eight suspected EMBF guerrillas
World.content:
President Abelardo de la Espriella said Thursday that Colombia’s armed forces killed eight guerrillas of FARC dissident group EMBF in a joint operation.

In a post on social media platform X, De la Espriella said that the military offensive targeted “camps used by structures of the Jorge Suarez Briceño Block,” a unit of the EMBF, in a rural part of El Retorno in the Guaviare province.

In a precision airstrike followed by an operation carried out by our commandos, the preliminary tally shows that 8 terrorists have been killed so far, 11 rifles and 5 machine guns have been seized, along with a large amount of logistical supplies. President Abelardo de la Espriella

De la Espriella said that “Colombia must know we are going on the offensive” against organized crime and illegal armed groups that are all deemed “narco-terrorist” organizations by the government.

“Major ringleaders and their criminal organizations will find no hiding place or sanctuary anywhere in the country,” the president added.

De la Espriella took office earlier this month, vowing to end peace negotiations with illegal armed groups and go on a military offensive with the help of the US military instead.

One of the groups that was negotiating peace with the administration of former President Gustavo Petro was the EMBF, led by former FARC commander “Calarca.”

The group, together with FARC dissident group EMC, controls large swathe of territory in southern Colombia and along the border with Venezuela.

World.title: De la Espriella calls for “iron fist” against crime in Colombia
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella called on the security forces to impose the law “like a giant with an iron fist, the iron fist of the State.”

During a meeting with commanders of the security forces, De la Espriella stressed that security “is the cornerstone of our government and the most forceful government policy.”

The president urged the security forces to confront crime with an iron fist and stressed that “our soldiers and police officers have the full and unconditional support of this government. Never again will they be mistreated or forced to bow down to crime.”

Here we must act like a giant with an iron fist—the iron fist of the state. And that ability to convey a sense of unity is what has a psychological impact on crime and sends a clear message to citizens: we are here to protect you, to look out for you, but also to enforce the law. President Abelardo de la Espriella

De la Espriella called to erase the distinction between organized crime and illegal armed groups, and “treat them all under a single designation, which is that of terrorist groups,” claiming they are interconnected.

We have to stop treating these criminals differently. We must treat them all under a single designation, which is that of terrorist groups, because the criminal pyramid we have in Colombia—whose base is drug trafficking, followed by illegal mining, extortion, and smuggling—is all perfectly interconnected. The foundation of all crime and the primary source of all forms of violence is drug trafficking. President Abelardo de la Espriella

“When it comes to fighting crime, there are no differences—neither in the state’s actions nor in its response and certainly not in the categorization” that allowed peace talks with groups like the FARC and ELN, according to the president.

“That is over in this administration. They are all terrorists, and we are going to treat them as such, no matter what happens,” said De la Espriella.

World.title: De la Espriella claims 123,700 barrels stolen monthly from Colombia’s state oil company
World.content:
Oil thieves from north Colombia would be stealing at least 123,700 barrel of gasoline, diesel and naphtha, a month, claimed President Abelardo de la Espriella.

According to De la Espriella, the theft of the refined oil products that wee imported or produced by state-owned oil company Ecopetrol “is utterly alarming, and demands an immediate and forceful response from the State.”

Every month, approximately 123,700 barrels of refined products—gasoline, diesel, and naphtha—imported or produced by Ecopetrol would be stolen. This would occur solely on a 14-inch pipeline that connects Pozos Colorados, in Santa Marta, to the interior of the country, and the losses are concentrated mainly in Cesar and Magdalena. President Abelardo de la Espriella

“We would be talking about more than 1.5 million barrels a year, with losses exceeding $500,000 million for Ecopetrol and, therefore, for the nation,” the president said in a post on social media platform X.

De la Espriella added that “these fuels are used as raw materials in the illicit processing of cocaine” by illegal armed groups that operate in the country’s periphery.

If we confirm that a large portion of this fuel is being used to power cocaine production facilities, then we are not only dealing with a massive theft from Ecopetrol: we are dealing with a criminal network that may be linking the theft of hydrocarbons to drug trafficking and the financing of armed terrorist organizations. President Abelardo de la Espriella

The president ordered a “joint operation” of the military, police, prosecution and administrative authorities “to comprehensively combat this criminal economy” led by Defense Minister Jorge Eduardo Mora.

“I want results and periodic report on progress,” said De la Espriella.

Organized crime and illegal armed groups have been involved in fuel theft for decades.

World.title: Colombia expands disaster region in 2nd emergency decree
World.content:
Colombia’s government drastically expanded the region affected by the August 10 earthquake in a second decree declaring an economic emergency.

According to the decree, President Abelardo de la Espriella declared the emergency in 15 of the country’s 32 provinces “for a period of thirty (30) calendar days, in order to conjure the crisis and prevent the spread of the disaster’s effects.”

“The territorial scope includes all municipalities listed in UNGRD Situational Report No. 36 and any additional municipalities where direct damage from the August 10, 2026 earthquake is specifically demonstrated,” said the decree.

The emergency decree declared a State of Exception, which allows the government to “adopt, through legislative decrees, all additional necessary measures and budgetary/credit operations to address the crisis” in the emergency region.

According to the decree, the government is considering the following extraordinary measures to respond to the disaster that left more than $9.5 billion in damages.

Tax, credit, and budgetary flexibility to direct new resources to disaster recovery.

Expedited public credit operations bypassing lengthy CONPES/DNP approvals.

Use of the Royalty Savings and Stabilization Fund (FAE) resources as repayable loans.

Expanding the “Works for Taxes” (Obras por Impuestos) mechanism to affected municipalities.

Direct management and monetization of seized assets administered by SAE/FRISCO to fund emergency shelters and humanitarian relief.

Authorizing financial cooperatives to temporarily extend credit and savings services to non-members affected by the disaster.

Streamlining judicial operations, education delivery (remote/alternative spaces), school feeding programs (PAE), housing subsidies, telecommunications repairs, and labor support transfers.

Previously, De la Espriella announced a “Miracle Fund,” which would be used to channel donations from the private sector and international partners.

Since then, Colombia’s elite donated COP1.6 trillion ($526 million) of the $30 billion the government believes it needs for reconstruction.

World.title: Evacuations ordered in Chile as wildfires run amok
World.content:
Chile’s National Service for Disaster Prevention and Response (Senapred) Wednesday ordered the evacuation of 14 communes in the regions of Ñuble, Biobío, and La Araucanía, including Nacimiento, Purén, and Contulmo, which have all been particularly affected by the forest fires.

In messages broadcast through the Emergency Alert System (SAE), the authorities also called on residents to leave their homes to avoid further damage to their health.

It has already been a week since the first wildfires ran amok in south-central Chile despite efforts to contain them. High temperatures, dryness, and strong winds add to the plight of local people and some 5,600 firefighters deployed in the area while helping flocks in from abroad.

”We are entering this part of the week which is the most complex. Today, tomorrow, and the day after we have an alert for high temperatures in several regions of the country that has mobilized a very large effort (…) to prevent the fires from spreading,“ Interior Minister Carolina Tohá said regarding the 311 active fires, of which 89 are being fought. The Senapred also said 180 fires were under control, and 309,747 hectares have been affected.

”If the temperature rises and the wind increases we can indeed have more problems, and we already have many fires,” Spanish Lieutenant Colonel Carlos Javier Martín Traverso told AFP. Traverso’s Air Operations Section of the Military Emergency Unit (UME) arrived in Chile on Sunday to join the firefighting efforts.

Over 309,000 hectares have been consumed in the regions of Maule, Ñuble, Biobío, and La Araucanía with the death toll standing at 24, plus 2,180 people injured as 1,180 houses were destroyed, leaving 5,560 people homeless.

There seems to be a seamless scientific consensus that fires are the result of human actions, either by intentionality or carelessness, although the drought that has hit Chile for 13 years adds to the aggressiveness of the fires.

In this scenario, President Gabriel Boric Font has announced a curfew in the areas of Ñuble, Biobío, and La Araucanía where a state of catastrophe is in force, in order to guarantee the security and tranquility of

the families affected by the crisis. Defense authorities working on the sites will determine the restriction’s schedule.

“We have 24 people dead nationwide, three are from Santa Juana and we do not want there to be even one more,” Boric told reporters after visiting the area.

The number of fatalities was updated to 24 after two bodies were determined to belong to people who had died before the fires broke out.

Meanwhile, Biobío Governor Rodrigo Díaz said he was certain about “people criminally setting fires.”

“I have reports from police, firefighters, of people who have been setting fires. I do not have indications, but certainties, we need more patrols,” he insisted in a radio interview.

“We have fire outbreaks at the southern exit of Contulmo, different places where fires were set 300 meters away from each other, I could see it, nobody told me about it. The mayor of Mulchén told me how fires were lit in the four cardinal points, I have reports from the police, the Fire Department, from people who have been setting fires. I do not have indications, but certainties, we need more patrols in the area,” he explained.

President Boric’s Regional Delegate Daniela Dresdner said eight people had been arrested for “irresponsible and suspicious attitudes with respect to the setting of fires. This was due to citizen complaints and patrols by the Navy.”

“We are asking that all these conducts be denounced and we are filing a lawsuit for all these denunciations to [be] prosecute[d],” she added.

The Biobío Regional Prosecutor’s Office called on the citizenry to e-mail all data regarding criminal behavior to fiscaliaincendios@gmail.com, including pictures, videos, audios, or written information as to the probable causes of the fires, which will be handled confidentially. (Merco Press)

World.title: Chile’s wildfires death toll reaches 24
World.content:
Chilean authorities spoke Sunday of 24 fatalities, nearly 1,000 people injured, and some 800 houses destroyed in the past five days by wildfires spreading fast in amid a highly-irregular heat wave with strong winds and temperatures above 40°C in areas 500 km south of Santiago.

The death toll reached 24 after the death of one of the injured people who had been hospitalized in Angol, Undersecretary of the Interior Manuel Monsalve explained. “The risk situation in the country remains” in the regions of Ñuble, Biobío, and La Araucanía, and in certain localities of the central region of Maule, he said. A red alert was also decreed Sunday in communes of the southern regions of Los Ríos and Los Lagos due to the appearance of new fire outbreaks. He also pointed out that 26 of the 997 people injured were in serious condition.

“I came home from work and I was already without anything, without a house. I was left on the street, with my arms crossed, now with my son, and my wife, in a tent. I have no fodder for my animals,” a resident of the town of Purén, in the Araucanía region, told Televisión Nacional de Chile (TVN).

Meanwhile, President Gabriel Boric Font attended the wake of a firefighter in the town of Coronel. ”Chile is crying with you. I am here to tell you that you are not alone, that the family of Yesenia (Muñoz, the deceased firefighter) will not be alone,” he said.

According to Chile’s National Service for Disaster Prevention and Response (Senapred), the number of fires being fought went down from 87 to 51. “We are experiencing a small window of improving weather conditions during Sunday and Monday. That means that we are not with extremely high temperatures,” Monsalve said.

Undersecretary Monsalve also told reporters that 10 people have been arrested for their responsibility in starting some of the fires for which the red alert was still maintained. Of the total number of fires, 22 occurred Sunday for a total of 283 active fires, of which 151 were under control and 71 are being fought.

Given the magnitude of the fires in size and number, international help has been summoned. “We have just sent a plane to Chile with a contingent of the Military Emergency Unit to collaborate in extinguishing and controlling the fires that are raging in the country. All our support to the Chilean people,” tweeted Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez.

Chile’s Foreign Ministry also said assistance was being coordinated with Argentina, Brazil, Ecuador, the United States, and Mexico, while Boric’s administration has declared a constitutional state of catastrophe in the regions of Ñuble, Biobío and La Araucanía, to speed up additional resources while restricting free transit and involving military forces to contain the disaster.

In 2017, another chain of fires destroyed some 460,000 hectares, left 11 people dead, nearly 6,000 injured, and more than 1,500 homes burned.

Monsalve also warned that this week high temperatures will continue, as well as the risk of low humidity and strong gusts of wind, which will make it difficult to extinguish the flames. – MercoPress

World.title: Parts of Chile under red alert for major forest fires in central region
World.content:
