World.title: Congo's Ebola caseload tops 6,000 as concerns grow
World.content:
The Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo has surpassed 6,000 confirmed cases, with nearly 3,000 deaths. As the virus spreads, authorities are racing to contain one of the deadliest outbreaks in history.

The Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) continues to escalate, with confirmed infections now topping 6,000 and the death toll reaching 2,911, according to government figures.

The outbreak, caused by the Bundibugyo strain of the Ebola virus, has spread to around 60 zones in six provinces, raising fears that the virus is outpacing efforts to contain it.

"Around 60 health zones are now affected, every week more are added to the list. And the same pattern is repeated everywhere: initially, there is resistance and denial, followed by gradual acceptance," DW correspondent Jonas Gerding reported from Bunia, the capital of the Ituri province, the epicenter of the latest Ebola outbreak in Congo.

"Unfortunately, a lot more people will die until this Ebola outbreak gets under control," he added.

Health experts have said the situation is particularly worrying in eastern Congo, where conflict and insecurity are making it harder for response teams to reach affected communities.

Ebola outbreak in DR Congo outpaces efforts to contain it To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"This outbreak is the fastest-growing Ebola epidemic on record. It is growing faster and wider than the response to contain it, but it can be stopped," UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres told journalists last week.

The United Nations has appealed for more funding as humanitarian agencies struggle to keep pace with the increasing number of cases.

"International attention, political focus and resources are still lagging behind the reality unfolding on the ground," Guterres said, warning that the world "must also overcome another virus — the virus of indifference."

Vaccination campaign gathers momentum

As researchers continue trials aimed at developing a licensed vaccine for the Bundibugyo strain, Congolese authorities have rolled out a vaccination campaign focused on front-line health workers.

The vaccine was originally developed for a different Ebola variant, but officials hope it will provide some protection against the current outbreak.

Health Minister Samuel Roger Kamba said more than 50,000 doses had already arrived in the country.

"We will cover all the provinces that are around Ituri, moving in a ring towards the center of the outbreak, that is to say towards Ituri. But we have enough doses for all healthcare providers," he said on August 28.

Some health workers remain confident despite uncertainty over how effective the vaccine will be against the Bundibugyo strain.

"It is a vaccine that has already proven itself. We are talking about Ebola Bundibugyo, of Ugandan origin. But the vaccine that they want to administer to us was the vaccine that had succeeded for the Zaire type," said health worker Arnaud Batumbu.

"Since both cases involve a viral disease, I hope the vaccine will work for us now as well," he added.

Communities seek protection

Residents in hard-hit areas say they are ready to take the vaccine if it is properly explained to them.

"I will be ready to get vaccinated if only someone explains to me the importance of this vaccination," Clemency, a student in Tshopo province, told DW.

Health workers are worried about the spread of the virus Image: Xinhua/dpa/picture alliance

Others are calling for wider access. "Children need to be vaccinated too. They go back to school; there are many of them in class," said local resident Carine Lobwadji

Some community members also fear vaccine supplies may not be enough.

"I have learned that this is an insufficient quantity. I ask the authorities to add other doses for Tshopo and that we vaccinate everyone, especially those who will voluntarily agree, since some are afraid," said Onyeka Treasure, a photographer.

Violence hampers response

The latest outbreak is unfolding against a backdrop of violence and mass displacement in eastern DRC, complicating efforts to stop transmission.

Ebola response teams have reported attacks while carrying out their work, including during operations to safely handle Ebola-related deaths.

"We demand greater security so we can operate in the field and do our work without endangering our lives," Floribert Magene, a member of an Ebola response team, told The Associated Press on Monday after an attack in Ituri province.

Magene said his team was assaulted near Mambasa while responding to a call to secure a body.

Economic toll grows

Beyond the health emergency, the outbreak is worsening economic hardship for many families.

Schools have reopened in towns such as Bukavu and Bunia, but many parents are struggling to afford basic school supplies.

DR Congo launches Ebola trial for high-risk contacts To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Stationery shop owner Furaha Mpangu Esperance told DW that demand has collapsed as families prioritize food and other essentials.

"In any case, it doesn't work. The situation is serious because there are no customers. We have even lowered the prices but there is no one to buy. Before, we even sold 10 boxes, 20 boxes a day. Today not even three boxes, not even two! The situation is critical," he said.

To reduce disruption to education, the government has proposed radio-based learning for children unable to attend school.

"For us, it's a double objective: to ensure that children continue to go to school, despite the epidemic, and to ensure that distance learning is the device that will help them," Education Minister Raissa Malu told DW.

Schools have enforced protective measures, like hand-washing Image: DW

Teachers, however, say many areas lack the infrastructure needed for effective distance learning.

"We, the teachers, are ready, but we don't have the tools. In sensitive areas, even picking up frequencies is quite a problem," said Patrick Girinegi, president of the Ituri teachers' inter-union alliance. "The first-grade children can't read, nor do the parents. Several schools don't have printers or computers. How will it go?"

Many students and parents would rather see classrooms remain open with stronger health measures in place.

"It's easy for me to understand when it's my teacher himself who explains it to me. Saying that the child stays at home to listen to the radio, I don't think it's going to work. We [must] find ways to go to school without contaminating ourselves," said Viviane Tshipamba, vice-president of the Ituri children's committee.

Despite the challenges, health authorities point to a positive sign: more than 1,360 people have recovered from Ebola so far. For many Congolese, those recoveries offer hope that with stronger support, increased vaccination rates and improved security, the outbreak can still be brought under control.

Marcus Loika, Gaston Mukendi and Mitima Delachance contributed to this article.

World.title: Germany terminates lease for Berlin's Russian House
World.content:
Germany has announced the termination of the lease for the Russian House in the heart of Berlin. Critics have long said it is a hub for propaganda and espionage.

Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul has announced that the contract under which the Russian House is operated will be rescinded. This is one of several measures in retaliation for Russian involvement in the attempted airport drone attack at the Leipzig/Halle Airport on August 4.

The Russian House is centrally located on Friedrichstrasse in the heart of the German capital. As a throwback to a bygone era of friendly German-Russian relations, it has long been the subject of fierce disagreements and a bone of contention in Berlin.

The massive seven-story building covering an area of almost 30,000 square meters opened in 1984. At that time, back in the days of the East German state, its role was to celebrate friendship with the Soviet Union through concerts, film screenings and book readings. It even had its own small bookstore.

French authorities have previously linked the building to possible activities by Russian intelligence services.

"In light of the measures taken against German cultural institutions and organizations, the federal government is comprehensively and continuously reviewing the legal basis of the Russian House under international treaty law,” said German Foreign Ministry spokesperson Martin Giese at a press conference in Berlin at the beginning of August.

Back then, in response to a question from DW about the organization's future activities, Giese emphasized that the fate of the Russian House is linked to that of the Goethe Institut in Moscow, and that any action taken against one would also have direct consequences for the other.

German tax money for Russian propaganda?

The property on Friedrichstrasse belongs to Germany, yet the building is run by the Russian agency Rossotrudnichestvo, the Federal Agency for the Commonwealth of Independent States, Compatriots Living Abroad and International Humanitarian Cooperation.

Rossotrudnichestvo, whose primary purpose is to promote the Russian language abroad, currently has dozens of similar institutions worldwide. The German Foreign Office has repeatedly stated that the employees of the institute have diplomatic status in Germany.

Since 2022, following Russia's invasion of Ukraine, the agency has been on the EU sanctions list. At the time, the EU justified this by stating that the agency's goal was to consolidate "a wider public perception of the occupied Ukrainian territories as Russian."

Symbols of friendship remained on display in Berlin's Russian House in October 2023, more than year after the Russian invasion of Ukraine Image: Dmyrto Katkov/DW

Moscow still maintains that the Russian House is a place to celebrate the friendship between the two countries: "The Russian House is Russia's cultural embassy in the heart of Berlin," according to the Russian Embassy's website.

The events that take place there attract 200,000 visitors a year, according to Russian House organizers. Critics label them as propaganda.

Berlin media outlets have repeatedly reported on events at the in-house cinema where, for example, films were shown in which Ukrainian citizens were portrayed as Nazis.

Leipzig drone threat prompts security concerns in Germany To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Germany fears closure of Goethe-Institut in Moscow

The Russian House is owned by the Russian Federation, but the Federal Republic of Germany pays the property tax for the building on the basis of its legal obligation under the bilateral German-Russian agreement on property issues relating to cultural institutes.

Moscow and Berlin are also bound by the Intergovernmental Agreement on Cultural Cooperation, which was signed in December 1992 and entered into force in May 1993. It has a term of five years and is automatically extended for the same period unless one of the parties notifies the other at least six months before the expiration of the respective term.

Both agreements — regarding the property of the Russian House and the Goethe-Institut, as well as the cultural cooperation between Russia and Germany — remain in force even in the fifth year of Russia's war against Ukraine.

It is an open secret that the German government has been shying away from conflict over the Russian House because it fears the Russian government could respond by closing the Goethe-Institut in Moscow.

The institute was already forced to significantly scale back its operations in Russia in May 2023, when restrictions were imposed on the number of German officials in Russia.

A few weeks earlier, the Goethe-Institut's bank accounts in Russia were frozen in retaliation after the Berlin Public Prosecutor's Office opened a preliminary investigation against the Russian House for violating sanctions and ordered the freeze of its accounts.

So far, the Goethe-Institut continues to offer digital language courses in Russia. The libraries at its branches in Moscow and St. Petersburg continue to receive the latest German literature despite logistical difficulties, as representatives of the institute assured DW earlier this year.

Direct Russian-German contacts have become virtually impossible

In recent years, several German foundations in Russia have been classified as "undesirable organizations."

This includes the foundations run by Germany's established political parties.

Anyone who cooperates with "undesirable organizations" faces criminal prosecution in Russia. This makes all direct contact provided for in the cultural agreement virtually impossible.

This article was originally written in German and first published in August 2025. It was updated and republished in September 2026 to reflect news developments.

World.title: Marlaska exige al director de la Policía que aclare si el cuerpo tiene información de que Marruecos estuvo tras el asalto masivo a Ceuta
World.content:
El titular de Interior asegura en una carta a Pardo Piqueras que desconoce la información entregada a la Audiencia Nacional sobre la implicación de gendarmes marroquíes en los hechos del 30 de julio

El ministro de Interior de España, Fernando Grande-Marlaska, ha exigido en una carta en la madrugada de este miércoles al director general de la Policía, Francisco Pardo Piqueras, que, “de ser cierto”, ponga en su conocimiento desde cuándo disponía el cuerpo policial de información que apunta a que agentes marroquíes dirigieron la entrada masiva de personas a Ceuta con un objetivo distinto al migratorio. El titular de Interior da este paso después de que la unidad de inmigración de la Comisaría de Extranjería haya remitido un informe a la Audiencia Nacional comunicando que la entrada de unas 70.000 personas el pasado 30 y 31 de julio pudo estar planificada para colapsar el acceso fronterizo.

El contenido de dicho informe que se ha entregado ante la magistrada María Tardón, adelantado por El Español, expone que gendarmes marroquíes a las órdenes de agentes de paisano guiaron a los migrantes con el fin de colapsar el sistema fronterizo. Según confirman también fuentes policiales a este periódico, dicho documento analiza con detalle todas las imágenes y vídeos que se han visto sobre el terreno. Una información que el ministro Grande-Marlaska desconocía, de acuerdo con el oficio dirigido al director de la Policía.

En esta carta, a la que ha tenido acceso EL PAÍS, Grande-Marlaska insiste en que necesita “saber desde cuándo disponía la Policía Nacional de esa información, absolutamente esencial” para que, más allá de las actuaciones judiciales, él, como ministro del Interior, dice, “pueda ejercer mi responsabilidad y, en definitiva, el Gobierno pueda adoptar las decisiones oportunas en relación con la crisis migratoria de Ceuta”. El titular de la cartera recuerda que es a él a quien corresponde adoptar decisiones en materia de “defensa del Estado” y evidencia así que ignoraba lo redactado por el Centro Nacional de Inmigración y Fronteras (CENIF), remitido este lunes a la Audiencia Nacional.

El oficio añade que se trata de una información que, “habiéndose declarado la situación de interés para la seguridad del nacional prevista en la Ley 36/2015, de Seguridad Nacional, debe ponerse inmediatamente a disposición de los miembros del Consejo de Seguridad Nacional, de la autoridad funcional designada por real decreto del Presidente del Gobierno y de los demás órganos con competencias en este ámbito”. Todo ello, dice Marlaska, “al margen de las actuaciones judiciales que puedan realizarse, que, de momento, se encuentran en un estadio incipiente”, y que no puede ser obstáculo para que las Fuerzas y Cuerpos de Seguridad del Estado le detallen a él estas cuestiones. “Te agradeceré que me informes a la mayor brevedad sobre la veracidad de lo publicado”, remata.

La cuestión de si Marruecos estuvo o no tras lo ocurrido a finales de julio es nuclear en esta crisis, puesto que el presidente del Gobierno, Pedro Sánchez, ha defendido públicamente que no existe ningún indicio que haga sospechar que Rabat pudo organizar a los migrantes. Sánchez, en una entrevista en la Cadena SER este mismo lunes, señaló que el país vecino ofreció una “cooperación instantánea, inmediata” y aseguró que se estaba colaborando de forma estrecha para las devoluciones. El líder del PSOE insistió en que tras lo sucedido podían estar mafias, pero siguió la línea marcada antes por Marlaska, que aseguraba que nunca existió información suficiente de que un número tan elevado de personas fuera a cruzar la frontera.

Lo cierto es que María Tardón tiene en su mesa este documento policial que trasladó este martes a la Fiscalía para que se pronuncie. La magistrada decidió el pasado 3 de agosto dar un primer paso para iniciar una investigación después de que el partido Iustitia Europa denunciara la entrada masiva de personas a la ciudad autónoma. Antes de abrir una causa, la instructora pidió distintos informes policiales tanto a la Policía como a la Guardia Civil para aclarar si lo ocurrido se trató de “una acción concertada o dirigida” por algún “grupo criminal” o cualquier otro actor y si, en su caso, el Gobierno manejaba cualquier tipo de información previa.

Una vez la Unidad de Extranjería contestó, la jueza ha remitido la información a la Fiscalía para que esta aclare si el asunto es competencia de la Audiencia Nacional, según informan fuentes judiciales. Está previsto que, tras la contestación del ministerio público, la magistrada dicte un auto que decida si efectivamente hay material suficiente para iniciar una investigación y si esta debe quedarse en ese órgano judicial porque afecta a la seguridad del Estado o trasladarse a un juzgado ordinario de Ceuta.

En la denuncia de Iustitia Europa se planteaba que la “movilización” de personas migrantes de Marruecos a Ceuta no podía “ser calificada como un fenómeno migratorio ordinario o espontáneo” por la “dimensión temporal y la concentración de miles de individuos lanzándose simultáneamente al mar desde las costas marroquíes”. “Nos encontramos ante una instrumentalización de flujos migratorios que, por su volumen y forma de ejecución, supone un desbordamiento de las capacidades de las fuerzas y cuerpos de seguridad del Estado y de los servicios de acogida, comprometiendo la integridad territorial y la seguridad pública en una frontera exterior de la Unión Europea”, exponía.

World.title: Leucemia linfocítica crónica: cuando la investigación equivale a supervivencia
World.content:
Del total de personas a las que se diagnostica leucemia linfocítica crónica, un tercio no necesita tratamiento y la decisión de aplicarlo depende de que la enfermedad esté activa o no, según establecen las guías clínicas de esta patología. /GETTY IMAGES

La supervivencia a cinco años sitúa la leucemia más habitual en adultos entre los cánceres con mejor pronóstico. La incorporación de tratamientos de duración limitada ha permitido, además, reducir la toxicidad y facilitar una mejor calidad de vida a los pacientes

La historia de la oncología se ha escrito con avances paulatinos que han supuesto un aumento en la supervivencia del cáncer en general, y además con grandes saltos terapéuticos, como la medicina de precisión, que han marcado un antes y un después en el abordaje de algunos tipos de cáncer. Uno de ellos es la leucemia linfocítica crónica (LLC). Los datos de supervivencia a cinco años de los pacientes con LLC revelan ese impacto: ha pasado de un 59% en 2005 a un 85% en la actualidad, según datos recogidos por la Sociedad Española de Hematología y Hemoterapia en su informe Avance en los cánceres hematológicos.

Francesc Bosch, jefe del servicio de Hematología del hospital Vall d’Hebron de Barcelona, sitúa el punto de inflexión definitivo en la última década: “El conocimiento de la biología de la LLC se ha traducido en el desarrollo de medicamentos muy dirigidos que van a buscar las debilidades de la enfermedad”.

La combinación de mutaciones que se registran en un cáncer es única en cada persona y la medicina de precisión aplicada a la oncología se basa en buscar esas alteraciones genéticas tumorales para predecir la respuesta al tratamiento. En la LLC ha supuesto, en la práctica, pasar de la quimioterapia que se aplicaba a todos los pacientes a un tratamiento personalizado. Los avances terapéuticos han supuesto, además, menos efectos secundarios y, como consecuencia, mejor calidad de vida para los pacientes.

En qué consiste la leucemia linfocítica crónica Fuente: Instituto Nacional del Cáncer (NIH) de EE UU y elaboración propia a partir de las fuentes consultadas.

Las leucemias se clasifican según la rapidez con la que se desarrollan y la célula en la que se originan. Francesc Bosch explica que “la leucemia linfocítica crónica afecta a los linfocitos y a los órganos donde se ubican estas células y, a diferencia de la leucemia aguda, que se manifiesta de forma abrupta, la LLC aparece lentamente, por lo que muchos pacientes no van a necesitar tratamiento para su enfermedad”.

Cuando una persona escucha en la voz de su médico la palabra leucemia, no espera que la indicación sea una cita a los tres o a los seis meses. En la mente de esa persona se instala la idea del cáncer, un diagnóstico que todo el mundo asocia automáticamente con recibir tratamiento urgente. Pero, en el caso de la LLC, la espera activa forma parte del proceso. Jesús Pérez Viejo, psico-oncólogo y profesor de la Universidad Nacional de Educación a Distancia (UNED), ha comprobado esa perplejidad inicial en numerosos enfermos: “A veces es difícil integrar palabras como cáncer y enfermedad crónica porque el paciente no espera convivir con la leucemia de por vida; la idea generalizada que tenemos de un proceso oncológico es que, si no te curas, te mueres”.

“La leucemia linfocítica crónica es de los cánceres con mejor pronóstico y la incertidumbre del diagnóstico desaparece si sabes que estás en buenas manos y si hay información sobre el camino por el que vas a pasar” Julio González González, presidente de la Asociación de Pacientes con Leucemia Linfocítica Crónica (ASPALLC)

Cómo gestionar esa incertidumbre es, según los clínicos y las asociaciones de pacientes, uno de los retos en la LLC. Julio González, presidente de la Asociación de Pacientes con Leucemia Linfocítica Crónica (ASPALLC), convive con ella desde hace 12 años y pone especial énfasis en la importancia de que la persona diagnosticada conozca lo mejor posible la enfermedad para despejar las nubes oscuras que tienden a instalarse en la mente y hallar respuesta a las docenas de preguntas que le surgen: “La leucemia linfocítica crónica es de los cánceres con mejor pronóstico y la incertidumbre del diagnóstico desaparece si sabes que estás en buenas manos y si hay información sobre el camino por el que vas a pasar”.

Un paciente implicado y una responsabilidad compartida

Los propios equipos sanitarios, cada vez más multidisciplinares, propician la implicación del paciente. Les corresponde ese protagonismo y asumirlo repercute, entre otras cosas, en la adherencia terapéutica. “Cuanto más formado e implicado esté el paciente, mayor es la adherencia”, señala el doctor Bosch. Jesús Pérez Viejo, por su parte, incide en que los beneficios alcanzan a todos los implicados en la LLC: “La participación de los pacientes, sobre todo en la toma de decisiones, mejora su capacidad de afrontamiento de la enfermedad y ayuda al personal sanitario a que su responsabilidad sea compartida”.

“Con los tratamientos que tenemos, basados en las características genéticas de la enfermedad en cada paciente, la respuesta es muy rápida: al cabo de un mes o dos desaparecen los síntomas y el paciente nota que mejora mucho” Francesc Bosch, jefe del servicio de Hematología del hospital Vall d’Hebron de Barcelona

Del total de personas a las que se diagnostica LLC, un tercio no necesita tratamiento y la decisión de aplicarlo depende de que la enfermedad esté activa o no, según establecen las guías clínicas; es decir, que el paciente presente síntomas asociados a la leucemia, como crecimiento de los ganglios, anemia o descenso de las plaquetas. Si se ha iniciado el tratamiento, la adherencia es muy importante porque hay un grupo de enfermos en los que la terapia será de por vida, igual que ocurre en enfermedades como la diabetes o la hipertensión.

Aunque los efectos adversos de estas terapias están lejos de los que producía la quimioterapia, siguen existiendo, como en cualquier tratamiento crónico. De ahí que los especialistas ponderen el valor de uno de los cambios que se ha registrado en los últimos años: la incorporación de tratamientos limitados en el tiempo a partir de la combinación de diferentes terapias ya existentes. “Con un terapia de duración fija se ahorra toxicidad para el paciente y se evita la posibilidad de que genere resistencias al tratamiento”, apunta Bosch.

La leucemia linfocítica crónica (LLC), en datos Fuente: Fuente: Elaboración propia a partir de las fuentes consultadas.

De la mano de los avances terapéuticos en los últimos años ha llegado también una atención cada vez más integral a los pacientes. Jesús Pérez Viejo precisa: “El cáncer afecta a todas las áreas de la vida, desde la familiar a la laboral y hay momentos en que los tratamientos o el avance de la enfermedad requiere un soporte emocional especializado”.

Los profesionales de la psico-oncología tienen cada vez mayor protagonismo en ese acompañamiento. Se trata de vivir y hacerlo con calidad de vida, y en el logro de ese objetivo el bienestar emocional es fundamental. Pérez Viejo comenta que el psico-oncólogo puede resolver muchos de los temores que viven el enfermo y su entorno: “La LLC conlleva síntomas que generan retos psicológicos, pues hay inmunosupresión y se deben cuidar las infecciones. A veces, esto genera inseguridad en muchos pacientes porque tienen miedo a contagiarse y eso les hace evitar determinados lugares y el consiguiente aislamiento”.

“La participación de los pacientes, sobre todo en la toma de decisiones, mejora su capacidad de afrontar la enfermedad y ayuda al personal sanitario a que su responsabilidad sea compartida” Jesús Pérez Viejo, psico-oncólogo y profesor de la Universidad Nacional de Educación a Distancia (UNED)

Con la experiencia de 12 años conviviendo con la LLC, Julio González recomienda disponer de “una caja de herramientas propia” para afrontar una relación no querida pero inevitable, como es la de la leucemia. Esa caja le sirve para afrontar las repercusiones de la enfermedad en todos los ámbitos en los que se desenvuelve. Así, para las personas que todavía están trabajando recomienda tener claro que “el diagnóstico forma parte de la información médica privada y es el paciente quien decide qué compartir, con quién y cuándo hacerlo”. Si se necesita flexibilidad para revisiones o pruebas, señala que lo mejor es ser práctico: “Necesito tal día o tal franja horaria. Hay que proponer soluciones. Menos drama, más claridad”.

Los pacientes, las asociaciones como ASPALLC y los profesionales que atienden a las personas con LLC consideran que todavía quedan necesidades no cubiertas, que tienen que ver, sobre todo, con la falta de equidad en el acceso a un soporte integral. “Hay sitios donde la posibilidad de recurrir a un psico-oncólogo simplemente no existe y la información para los pacientes se limita a una consulta cada cuatro meses aprisa y corriendo”, apunta Julio González. Las otras necesidades por cubrir alcanzan a otros ámbitos muchas veces ignorados, pero importantes, que precisa Jesús Pérez Viejo: “Tienen que ver con el trabajo, el gasto económico que supone una enfermedad oncológica o incluso con problemas sexológicos que pueden aparecer y que en un primer momento no son prioritarios, pero afectan a la calidad de vida”.

Todo suma en el abordaje integral de una enfermedad, la LLC, cuyo horizonte se tiñe cada vez más de verde. La investigación y los profesionales implicados en el proceso oncológico han conseguido prolongar drásticamente la supervivencia y mejorar la calidad de vida de los pacientes, pero no se han olvidado del objetivo final, que apunta Francesc Bosch como médico: “Se investiga mucho la LLC porque no deja de ser la leucemia más frecuente en adultos, pero nuestro fin último es curarla”.

World.title: Residimos en Madrid y tenemos una segunda vivienda en Tenerife que queremos dejar a nuestro hijo. ¿Es mejor la donación o la herencia?
World.content:
Los lectores envían sus preguntas al consultorio de vivienda de EL PAÍS en colaboración con Legálitas

Pregunta. Somos un matrimonio residente en Madrid y propietario en gananciales de una segunda vivienda en Tenerife. No sabemos si es más favorable dejársela en herencia a mi hijo, donársela o donarle el importe de la venta de la casa. ¿Qué opción nos interesa fiscalmente y que impuestos deben pagarse en cada caso? M. Gallego.

Respuesta. Las distintas opciones planteadas tienen diferentes implicaciones fiscales. Los impuestos que podrían resultar de aplicación son:

Impuesto sobre Sucesiones, en caso de herencia.

Impuesto sobre Donaciones.

Impuesto sobre la Renta de las Personas Físicas (IRPF).

Impuesto sobre el Incremento de Valor de los Terrenos de Naturaleza Urbana (Plusvalía Municipal).

En relación con el Impuesto sobre Sucesiones y Donaciones, en caso de herencia se aplica la normativa de la comunidad autónoma en la que residía la persona fallecida. En este caso, si no se produjera un cambio de residencia, sería de aplicación la normativa de la Comunidad de Madrid, que establece una bonificación del 99% sobre la cuota del impuesto.

Sin embargo, en el caso de las donaciones se aplican reglas distintas en función del bien donado:

Si se trata de un inmueble, se aplica la normativa de la comunidad autónoma donde esté situado. En este caso, Canarias, que establece una bonificación del 99,9% sobre la cuota del impuesto.

Si se trata de un bien mueble, como dinero, se aplica la normativa de la comunidad autónoma donde reside el donatario. En este caso, Madrid, que establece una bonificación del 99% sobre la cuota del impuesto.

En relación con el IRPF, la transmisión del inmueble ya sea por donación o por venta, genera para el matrimonio una ganancia o pérdida patrimonial equivalente a la diferencia entre el valor de transmisión y el valor de adquisición. Dicha ganancia o pérdida tributa en la base imponible del ahorro conforme a los siguientes tipos:

Hasta 6.000 euros: 19%.

De 6.000,01 a 50.000 euros: 21%.

De 50.000,01 a 200.000 euros: 23%.

De 200.000,01 a 300.000 euros: 27%.

Más de 300.000 euros: 30%.

En caso de herencia, esta ganancia o pérdida patrimonial no se genera.

Por último, en relación con la Plusvalía Municipal, tanto en los supuestos de herencia como de donación o compraventa, se devengará este impuesto. El importe a pagar será el mismo en todos los casos, siempre que el precio de venta o el valor de la donación o de la herencia sea superior al precio de compra, sin tener en cuenta ningún tipo de gasto.

Por lo tanto, la opción más interesante desde un punto de vista fiscal dependerá de si el inmueble tiene actualmente un valor superior a su valor de adquisición. Si es así, probablemente resulte más conveniente transmitirlo por herencia, evitando de este modo la ganancia patrimonial en el IRPF, especialmente si esta es elevada.

Si, por el contrario, el inmueble no tiene actualmente un valor superior al de adquisición, resultará más interesante realizar una donación del inmueble, ya que se aplicaría el Impuesto sobre Donaciones de Canarias, que es más bajo.

En cualquier caso, para realizar una valoración correcta será necesario conocer la fecha de compra, el precio de compra y los gastos asociados a la adquisición; el valor de referencia catastral; el precio de una posible venta, y el valor catastral actual y el valor catastral del suelo.

Si tiene dudas, sugerencias o simplemente quiere contarnos su caso, puede enviarnos un email a vivienda@elpais.es .

World.title: Calpe, renovarse a la sombra del Peñón
World.content:
Además de por su paquidérmica y famosa formación rocosa, la ciudad alicantina merece una visita por las Salinas, el conjunto arqueológico Baños de la Reina y una gastronomía en la que destaca la gamba blanca

Siempre que vuelvo a Calpe (cosa que pasa menos veces de las que querría) me sorprende y me exalta la colosalidad irredenta del peñón de Ifach. Esta paquidérmica protuberancia, ocasionalmente envuelta de nubes como la aureola de un santo, parece siempre a punto de saltar sobre el mar, que le es refugio y no abismo. Y, en efecto, ese tosco poliedro es una prolongación de la cordillera Bética, que se sumerge audazmente bajo las olas para dirigirse a Mallorca. Un tótem prodigioso, una ofrenda desmesurada y, quizás, en su priapismo cósmico, un tabú.

El parecido de esta gran roca con la de Gibraltar ha propiciado teorías diversas, normalmente descabelladas pero siempre amenas. Que Gibraltar e Ifach estuvieron unidos físicamente antes de abrirse el Estrecho es una de esas leyendas. Sí que es cierto que, en la antigüedad, el nombre Calpe designaba al peñón de Gibraltar. En un tiempo tan dado a las supercherías y otros golpes en el pecho de la ignorancia suprema me extraña que nadie haya propuesto que este titánico pedrusco pueda ser una ofrenda a algún dios. O quizás un monumento obra de los extraterrestres, como algunos partidarios desaforados del delirium tremens dicen que son las pirámides de El Cairo. Ajeno a todas nuestras elucubraciones, el Peñón sigue aquí, como el dinosaurio de Monterroso: una erección ciclópea, una insurgencia calcárea insolente y retadora, un desorbitado capricho morfológico.

Con este atractivo paisajístico, la ciudad alicantina necesita poco más para atraer visitantes. Y, sin embargo, las calidades de su oferta no dejan de aumentar. Ya se sabe que desde hace décadas recibe un elevado número de turistas extranjeros (muchos, hoy, residentes permanentes), principalmente procedentes del Reino Unido, Alemania, Bélgica y los Países Bajos. Este carácter cosmopolita no le ha hecho perder personalidad. Su casco antiguo con restos de los muros medievales resulta muy evocador, con sus calles estrechas, sus plazas tradicionales y edificios históricos como la iglesia Antigua (del siglo XV) y el Torreó de la Peça (baluarte defensivo de la antigua muralla). A esto une una variada oferta de restauración y comercio, amén de las actividades náuticas de su puerto deportivo o el senderismo que puede practicarse en el Peñón.

Torreó de la Peça, baluarte defensivo de la antigua muralla, en Calpe. TONO BALAGUER (GETTY IMAGES )

Entre sus atractivos naturales están las Salinas y el conjunto arqueológico Baños de la Reina. Las Salinas son parte de una antigua bahía cerrada por una barrera de dunas que unía el Peñón con el continente. La explotación de sal se cerró en 1988, así que, clausurada la industria, ha florecido la biodiversidad: allí viven 173 especies diferentes de aves. En cuanto a Baños de la Reina, es un yacimiento arqueológico, anexo a las Salinas, donde debió vivir un noble romano. Además de su lujosa villa, incluye una piscifactoría (donde se llevaba a cabo la salazón del pescado), unas termas, una noria y cuatro aljibes.

Esta antigua actividad pesquera ha llegado hasta la actualidad. A diferencia de otros destinos muy orientados exclusivamente al turismo, Calpe ha mantenido una flota de arrastre significativa. Su puerto alberga una de las lonjas más importantes de la zona, donde se realiza la ancestral e imprescindible subasta del pescado y el marisco locales.

Vista de Las Salinas, parte de una antigua bahía cerrada por una barrera de dunas que unía el Peñón con el continente. Jacek Krysciak ( GETTY IMAGES )

Su gran tesoro marino es la gamba blanca. Aunque la gamba roja de su vecina Dénia tiene una fama más consolidada, las propiedades de la blanca (su dulzura natural, su carne firme y sedosa, el suave aroma a yodo acabada de pescar) no son precisamente despreciables. Desde 2025, este fruto del mar goza de marca de calidad propia. Según el Portal Agrari de la Generalitat, ese año se capturaron y comercializaron más de 1.600 toneladas de gamba blanca en la Comunidad Valenciana (casi toda en la costa de Alicante). Es la tercera especie local en número de capturas (después del boquerón y de la sardina): genera 13,5 millones de euros, superando a la gamba roja y al boquerón, que hace años lideraban el ránking marino. Y ahora ese tesoro, que era cuantitativo, ha empezado a volverse cualitativo.

Parte de los Baños de la Reina, un yacimiento arqueológico anexo a Las Salinas. Teo Moreno ( Alamy / CORDON PRESS )

Es precisamente en la gastronomía donde Calpe ha afinado más su renovación en los últimos tiempos. La versatilidad culinaria de ese prodigioso crustáceo ha llamado la atención de los chefs más reputados de la zona. Dos ejemplos: los restaurantes Onami y Beat.

Marisco fresco expuesto en el puerto pesquero de Calpe, Alicante. Manoli Perez ( Alamy / CORDON PRESS )

Onami abrió este pasado mes de junio en el hotel A.R. Diamante Beach. Este imponente establecimiento ya disponía de otros dos locales de restauración, el Audrey’s (el primer local con estrella Michelin de Calpe) y el Amas. Onami comparte chef con Amas: Diego Laso. La diferencia entre los dos —inspirados ambos en la cocina japonesa— es que en Onami no hay carta y se come en la barra. El servicio está concebido como un menú degustación al estilo kaiseki-ryori: la forma más refinada y tradicional de la alta gastronomía japonesa. Onami es un juego de palabras entre ona (ola, en valenciano/catalán) y umami. Esto da la medida de su filosofía: ofrecer un diálogo entre la cocina valenciana y la nipona. De aquí la receta de gamba blanca en Amas (curada con sake y servida con crema inglesa y algas de Galicia), o el nigiri de este mismo crustáceo en Onami, simplemente pelado y servido sobre arroz.

Segundo ejemplo: el restaurante Beat (una estrella Michelin), ubicado en The Cookbook. Este hotel acaba de renovarse en profundidad. En Beat reina desde hace diez años José Manuel Miguel, el único cocinero valenciano que ha obtenido estrellas Michelin en Francia y en España. Si en Onami dialogaban la cocina local con la nipona, aquí la fusión está protagonizada por lo valenciano y lo francés. El gran referente de José Manuel Miguel es Paul Bocuse, emblema de la nouvelle cuisine gala. El bogavante lo cocina a la manera de la Salade de homard à la française de Bocuse, pero la gamba blanca no requiere mayor transformación: su hechizo radica en la ausencia de cocción.

Con todo esto ya se puede volver a visitar Calpe y saborear algo más que la siempre imponente vista de su Peñón. Tradición y modernidad, lo llaman.

World.title: Cabinet to scrap welfare cuts in revised budget deal – RTL
World.content:
The Dutch government has scrapped most of its planned cuts to social security as it tries to attract opposition support for next year’s budget, RTL Nieuws has reported.

The cabinet will also delay raising the excess charge for health insurance by a year and invest €1.5 billion in mitigating the impact of inflation, particularly rising energy prices, on spending power.

The deal was the outcome of protracted negotiations between the three coalition partners, D66, VVD, and CDA, which ran through the weekend and most of Monday as the party leaders stretched the deadline to send the draft budget to the Council of State.

RTL Nieuws said it had seen leaked details of the budget proposals, which will not be formally announced for another two weeks when finance minister Eelco Heinen presents it to parliament.

The U-turn on welfare spending is a blow for the right-wing VVD, which had earlier said it would not compromise on the €6.5 billion worth of cuts to incapacity benefit, unemployment payments and substitute pay for new mothers on maternity leave.

Another plan in the coalition agreement to save €2.8 billion by increasing the retirement age in step with life expectancy, rather than by eight months for every extra year, has also been cancelled, as announced earlier by social security minister Hans Vijlbrief.

Heinen and prime minister Rob Jetten had spent the last two weeks trying to do a deal with opposition parties in advance to get their support for the budget, as the coalition is 10 seats short of a majority in the lower house and 16 seats short in the Senate.

But those talks ended without agreement as the three coalition parties struggled to agree among themselves about what concessions they should make to opposition groups on the left and right. Ministers will now have to find the votes when the budget plans go through parliament during the autumn.

Jetten’s D66 party and the Christian Democrats (CDA) reportedly wanted to scale back welfare cuts to appeal to the largest opposition party, the left-wing Progressief Nederland (Pro), while the VVD preferred a package that addressed the demands of right-wing parties such as JA21, with more tax cuts and less welfare spending.

World.title: Far-right TV show editor Niemöller leaves after Hitler remarks
World.content:
Joost Niemöller is stepping down as editor-in-chief of far-right broadcaster Ongehoord Nederland (ON), weeks after he said on air that Adolf Hitler had put certain things “very well”.

The broadcaster said the immediate reason was a “difference of view about the editorial direction and recent programming”, according to director-general Peter Vlemmix. Its statement, reported by NOS, runs to two sentences and does not mention the item that set off weeks of criticism.

In the late-July broadcast, Niemöller said there were “certain things of Hitler’s” he agreed with, aside from the Nazi leader’s antisemitism.

Co-presenter Raisa Blommestijn also backed a statement, put to the pair after a clip of a Hitler speech referring to Jewish people, that a cosmopolitan elite was inherently hostile to ordinary people. Both said they did not share all of Hitler’s ideology.

Media minister Rianne Letschert called the broadcast “terrible, distasteful, hurtful and unnecessary”, and the ombudsman for the public broadcasters logged dozens of complaints. The cabinet is examining whether ON can be forced out of the public broadcasting system, and Letschert has said a decision will come “very soon”.

Ongehoord Nederland joined the public broadcasting system in 2022 and has been reprimanded and sanctioned several times for breaching journalistic rules. Niemöller became editor-in-chief about 18 months ago.

World.title: Three Dutch nationals remain missing after deadly Nepal floods
World.content:
Rescue workers in Nepal are still trying to trace three Dutch nationals among more than 4,000 people reported missing since the devastating floods that swept through the border region with Tibet last week.

They include two tourists, 29-year-old Christiaan Berghuis from Nijkerk and 51-year-old Maaike Moolhuijsen from Haarlem, who were on a pilgrimage to Mount Kailash, a sacred Tibetan mountain, when the disaster struck.

Their names were confirmed by the family support organisation Names de Familie. The third missing person is a Dutch woman who emigrated to Nepal, the foreign affairs ministry said.

The two visitors were part of a group of 80 people who were travelling from Kathmandu to Mount Kailash when a glacier in the Himalaya collapsed on Wednesday morning, causing the Bhote Koshi river to burst its banks and flood a large area with water and mud.

A spokesman for the Isha Foundation, which organised the trip, told RTL Nieuws the immigration office where the travellers were waiting at the time appeared to have been inundated.

Death toll passes 1,000

“At the moment nothing is known about the conditions of the people who were in the immigration office,” the spokesman said. “We are in constant contact with their families and are supporting them in every way possible.

“The last contact we had with our volunteer who was in charge of the group was around nine minutes before the flood happened.”

The Isha foundation was set up in 1992 by Jaggi Vasudev, an Indian yoga teacher better known by the name of Sandhguru.

A spokesman for the foreign affairs ministry said: “Their families in the Netherlands have been unable to contact them. The fear is that they were in the affected area at the moment of the flood.”

The death toll from the floods passed 1,000 on Tuesday as rescue workers continued to pull bodies from the water further downstream.

Altogether nearly 4,000 people are still unaccounted for in Nepal, as well as 546 in Tibet. They include around 900 hydropower workers who have been trapped in flooded tunnels for nearly a week.

World.title: Amsterdam taxi drivers launch app to rival Uber
World.content:
A group of Amsterdam taxi drivers has launched a rival booking app to try and loosen Uber’s grip on the city’s cab market, amid long-running disputes over employee status, wages and workers’ rights. The founders claim nearly 1,300 drivers have already signed up.

The app, NLCabs, was set up by driver Mostapha Ahidar and co-founder Ivo van Leeuwen, who told Het Parool they were tired of watching a US monopoly control the terms of their trade. It works the same as Uber: passengers order a ride through the app and nearby drivers pick them up.

The difference, the founders say, is the cut. NLCabs takes a 3% commission from drivers, which Ahidar said was only what the platform needs to keep running. Uber’s commission is variable and can rise beyond half the fare, according to the drivers, though the company does not publish its rates.

“We are treated like children by Uber,” one driver told the paper. “We have absolutely no room for negotiation.”

Years of friction

The launch comes after years of conflict between Uber and Dutch drivers, much of which has gone through courts and regulators.

In August, the data protection authority (AP) fined Uber €825 million for deactivating drivers’ accounts through automated systems, without proper human review or explanation – the second-largest penalty ever issued under EU privacy law. Uber is appealing and has called the fine disproportionate.

That followed a €290 million fine in 2024 for sending drivers’ data to the US, a record at the time. Both cases originally stemmed from complaints by French drivers.

Employee or entrepreneur

In January, an Amsterdam appeal court ruled that Uber drivers cannot all be treated as employees, overturning a 2021 judgment that had put them on the payroll. The FNV trade union, which launched the case, said it was weighing a Supreme Court appeal.

Many drivers work almost exclusively through Uber and have little way of finding fares without it.

NLCabs is live but has only a few hundred downloads on Google Play, and the founders said they know shifting a habit as ingrained as opening Uber will be hard. They plan to expand across the Netherlands.

World.title: Groningen University launches Frisian language degree
World.content:
Groningen University has launched a bachelor’s degree programme in the Frisian language, the first standalone course in the country’s second official language for 15 years.

Three students began the course this week, which covers linguistics, history and Frisian culture. Frisian was taught as a degree in its own right until 2012, when it was absorbed into a broader programme on Europe’s minority languages, Minorities & Multilingualism.

That programme drew too few students to survive and the university said it would phase it out from the 2025/26 academic year, leaving the academic study of Frisian at risk of vanishing altogether.

A rescue from The Hague

The course was saved after the Royal Netherlands Academy of Arts and Sciences (KNAW) recommended, in a report on the future of Frisian studies, that the state pay for a dedicated bachelor. The government agreed to put in €340,000 a year, with further provincial money.

For legal reasons the new degree sits as a Frisian track within the university’s Dutch Languages and Cultures programme, though the focus is now entirely on Frisian.

Professor of Frisian Arjen Versloot said he was happy with the intake, even though a course usually needs around 20 students to break even. “There are often only five students in French and German too, so as a small language we can’t complain,” he told regional broadcaster Omrop Fryslân.

Teachers in demand

The degree is also meant to supply qualified teachers. Since August, schools in Friesland have been required to use more Frisian in the classroom under new curriculum rules, and Versloot expects strong demand for teachers able to deliver it at the highest level.

Frisian is spoken by around 470,000 people in Friesland and is the closest living relative of English.

Reading and writing proficiency in Frisian has risen sharply over the past two decades, despite fewer people speaking the language at home, according to a recent survey.

Around 58% of residents in Friesland now say they can read Frisian well or very well, up from 46% in 2007. Self-reported writing proficiency nearly doubled over the same period, from 9.6% to 18.9%.

World.title: Man cleared of plotting to kidnap princesses Amalia and Alexia
World.content:
A man has been cleared of plotting to kidnap princesses Amalia and Alexia, the eldest daughters of king Willem-Alexander and queen Máxima, after a court ruled he was suffering from a psychosis at the time.

Anne Romke van der H., 33, believed he was in a relationship with Amalia, 22, and fantasised about marrying her before living in the wilds in Poland with her and her 21-year-old sister.

He bought items from a hardware store designed to use as a survival kit, including knives, cooking equipment and two hatchets, one of which he inscribed with Alexia’s name.

The prosecution service said he intended to abduct or attack the two princesses if they were unwilling to go along with his plans.

But a court in The Hague ruled there was no evidence that van der H., from Groningen, was preparing an actual attack on Amalia and Alexia or intended to threaten them.

A psychiatric assessment found he was schizophrenic and had become obsessed with the royal family, particularly the two princesses.

He was found guilty of insulting six police officers and smashing a window, but the court did not impose a fine or punishment because he was in psychosis at the time.

The court said the offences were not severe enough to justify a compulsory treatment regime (tbs), but Van der H. told the judges at an earlier hearing that he was willing to undergo voluntary treatment.

World.title: Housing minister announces sites for 30,000 new homes by 2035
World.content:
Housing minister Eleanor Boekholt-O’Sullivan has identified five new sites around the country to build 30,000 new homes by 2035.

The five urban locations in Friesland, Noord-Holland, Zuid-Holland and Limburg have been designated National Large-Scale Housing Locations (NGWs) as part of the cabinet’s plans to build 400,000 houses in the next 10 years.

Between 5,000 and 6,000 homes are planned at four of the sites in Haarlem, Deventer, Weert and Leeuwarden, while 8,000 houses are due to be built in Maastricht. All the sites apart from Haarlem are close to main railway stations.

The sites are the first to be identified by the current government under the NGW scheme, a €5 billion fund first announced in 2023 to speed up development in urban areas and relieve the pressure on housing.

It takes the total number of NGW areas to 26. However, last month plans to develop four sites nominated by the previous housing minister, Mona Keijzer, had to be put on hold because there was no money to build road and railway connections.

Boekholt-O’Sullivan said in a letter to parliament that the locations had been chosen because they could be easily connected to services such as water and electricity, allowing the areas to be developed quickly.

“In choosing these five new NGW locations we explicitly looked at locations where no extra measures are needed for availability to realise these homes,” she said. “That means we can use our joint efforts to realise new neighbourhoods at speed.”

World.title: VVD MP quits lobby group board over conflict of interest claims
World.content:
VVD MP Renate den Hollander has resigned from the management board of a vets’ lobby group after facing questions about her role as the party’s spokesman on animal welfare.

NOS reported that some of Den Hollander’s comments in parliament were almost identical to statements made by the BPW, an organisation representing owners of veterinary practices.

Den Hollander, 49, spent 22 as a vet and ran her own practice in Drenthe before being elected to parliament for the first time last November. She was a member of the BPW before becoming an MP, but only joined the board this year.

NOS reported that her response to a report by the consumer markets watchdog ACM that criticised high vets’ bills and unnecessary procedures was strikingly similar to the BPW’s official line.

Den Hollander said the VVD did not share all the ACM’s criticisms, stressed the need for veterinary staff to be paid properly and suggested alternative solutions to deal with rising costs such as encouraging people to take out more insurance.

Identical language

Although she was not a member of the board at the time, Den Hollander used almost identical language to the BPW in its response, such as comparing vets to other business owners such as bakers and garage owners.

A month later she was taken on as a member of the management board with an allowance of €1,000 a year.

In a written reply to NOS, she said she was stepping down from the board with immediate effect after the national broadcaster compared her speech with the BPW’s statement.

“The similarities to a contribution I later made as an MP, which you have rightly asked questions about. have made me realise that my membership of the management board of the BPW could lead in future to (the appearance of) a conflict of interests,” she said.

World.title: Poles eating more meat but drinking less alcohol

We cannot do what we do without your support. Poles are eating more meat but drinking less alcohol, continuing a long-term trend, the latest data from Statistics Poland (GUS) show. The average person in Poland ate 82 kilograms of meat in 2025, which was 7.5% more than a year earlier. It also marks an increase of 15.7% since 2015 and 22.7% since 2005. Likewise, consumption of eggs rose 8.5% in 2025 to an average of 218 per person. The increases have come amid rapidly rising incomes, which make such products more affordable. A separate GUS study earlier this year showed that the proportion of Poles who cannot afford to eat meat at least every other day fell from 8.2% in 2015 to 3% in 2025. By contrast, vegetable consumption has changed little, with the average Pole eating 108 kg in 2025, compared with 107 kg a year earlier and 110 kg in 2005. However, consumption of potatoes, a starchy staple of the Polish diet presented by GUS separately from other vegetables, has fallen sharply over the longer term, despite a slight increase last year. The average Pole ate 96.5 kg of potatoes in 2025, down 23.4% since 2005. Meanwhile, alcohol consumption last year continued its recent decline. In 2025, the average Pole drank 81.7 litres of beer, down 4.9% from the previous year and 18.7% from the peak of 100.5 litres per person in 2018. Likewise, consumption of spirits and liqueurs fell 5.9% year-on-year in 2025 to 3.2 litres per person. That was 13.5% down from a peak of 3.7 litres in 2019. In 2025, the amount of wine drunk per person, at 4.9 litres, fell even more, by 9.3% year-on-year. However, alcohol consumption is still higher than it was two decades ago, with the average Pole drinking 28% more spirits and 1.2% more beer in 2025 than in 2005. A 2023 study by ProVeg, an NGO, conducted in partnership with the University of Copenhagen and Ghent University, found that Poles were the most carnivorous among ten European countries surveyed. Three quarters of Poles (74%) said they ate meat frequently, compared to an average of 62% across all countries. Italians and Spaniards (both 69%) were the next biggest meat eaters, while Germans (45%), Austrians (48%) and the Dutch (53%) were the least likely to eat meat frequently. Meanwhile, 7% of people in Poland said they were either vegan (2%), meaning consuming no animal products at all, or vegetarian (5%), meaning they do not eat meat or fish. That was just below the European average of 8%. In terms of what kinds of meat are favoured by Poles, GUS’s most recent such breakdown, from 2017, showed that pork was most popular, with the average Pole consuming 39.8 kg that year, followed by poultry (26.kg) and beef (2.3 kg). Poland's first company to produce cultured meat – which is grown in a lab from animal cells without the need to raise and kill livestock – has received a state grant to support its work. A fundraiser for an eight-month-old baby who survived an accident in the Polish city of Kraków in which his parents were killed by a speeding driver has reached more than 1 million zloty (€231,000). The tragedy has prompted widespread anger, with calls from residents and local politicians for the authorities to take action to deal with dangerous driving in the city. To będzie jedna z najtrudniejszych zbiórek, jakie wspólnie przeprowadzimy.💔Proszę o RT🙏 Kilka dni temu rozpędzony kierowca w Krakowie wjechał w młode małżeństwo. Mateusz i Klaudia zginęli. Ich kilkumiesięczny synek, Oliwier, trafił do szpitala. Mam dla Was dobrą wiadomość.… pic.twitter.com/R8L1xgEBPn — Damian Żurawski (@damian_zurawski) August 26, 2026 On 22 August, a married couple, Mateusz and Klaudia, both 32, were walking with their baby on Solna Street, close to the southern bank of the Vistula river, when a car driven by 26-year-old Hubert B., whose surname is masked under Polish privacy law, mounted the pavement, killing both parents. The child, eight-month-old Oliwier, survived the accident but was hospitalised. His condition is continuing to improve, reports broadcaster TVP Kraków. According to prosecutors, the car was travelling around 40 km/h (25mph) faster than the speed limit in the area. Hubert B. has been charged with unintentionally causing a fatal accident, for which he could face up to eight years in prison. “The suspect pleaded not guilty to the offence he was charged with, explaining, among other things, that the car skidded due to the uneven road surface,” prosecutors said, adding that the suspect has been placed in pretrial detention. An online fundraiser set up last week to provide Oliwier “with financial security for years to come” shared the news that the baby’s condition is now stable, although “his arm and leg are in plaster”. “We can’t give Oliwier back his mum and dad,” reads the fundraiser’s description. “However, we can do everything we can to ensure he has the resources for his education and a peaceful start to adult life.” At the time of writing, the fundraiser has reached more than 1.05 million zloty, over double its initial target. There have been more than 23,300 donations so far. Meanwhile, Oliwier’s grandfather, Andrzej, told newspaper Fakt that the family had given its consent for the fundraiser and was very grateful for those who had donated. A court in Kraków has granted Mateusz’s brother custody of the child. As well as sympathy for the victims, the accident aroused anger from residents. Several hundred people attended a protest at the site, holding signs reading “How many more people must die for something to change?” and “Stop road killers”. They installed their own mock-up pedestrian crossing and speed bumps. “Such tragedies are not isolated incidents,” said the organisers, quoted by news website Interia. They cited police figures showing that Kraków had the most road accidents of all Poland’s provincial capitals in 2025. Its figure of 941 was over 100 more than in Łódź and over 250 more than in Warsaw. Local councillor Rafał Zawiślak told news website Onet that he was filing a complaint with the prosecutor’s office, saying the city authorities had been negligent, failing to respond to warnings from 2024 that the site of the accident was dangerous. Godzina ciszy w Krakowie. Mieszkańcy upamiętniają parę, która zginęła w sobotniej tragedii przy ulicy Solnej. He added, however, that the city would be installing a speed bump. “I believe that this is simply what we should do…as a kind of expression of solidarity with the victims of this tragedy,” he said, quoted by broadcaster TVN. City police said they had been monitoring and taking action about road safety issues in the district for years, but that the street in question had not previously been reported as a particularly dangerous place, with just one incident causing one injury in the five years before the fatal accident. MPs from The Left have called for tougher rules on illegal street racing, saying police currently do not have sufficient legal tools. We cannot do what we do without your support. A Polish student is to stand trial accused of planning a terrorist attack on a Christmas market in Poland as an act of support for Islamic State. On Monday, prosecutors announced that they have filed an indictment against the 20-year-old suspect, a student at the Catholic University of Lublin (KUL) who can be named only as Mateusz W. under Polish privacy law. Jacek Dobrzyński, spokesman for Poland’s security services, confirmed that Mateusz W. had been “preparing a mass attack at a Christmas market, which he planned to carry out using explosive materials”. Wracamy do sprawy 20-letniego Mateusza W. – studenta Katolickiego Uniwersytetu Lubelskiego podejrzewanego o przygotowywanie masowego zamachu na jednym z jarmarków świątecznych, którego planował dokonać z wykorzystaniem materiałów wybuchowych. Do Sądu Okręgowego w Koszalinie… https://t.co/6vGPcjiDnc pic.twitter.com/seFGV8nHMz — Jacek Dobrzyński (@JacekDobrzynski) August 31, 2026 The suspect was detained late last year, when details of his alleged plot and plans to establish contact with Islamic State were first revealed. He has remained in custody since then. Though the authorities have confirmed that Mateusz W. was a first-year student at KUL, a leading Catholic university that counts the late Pope John Paul II among its former students and lecturers, and that they have also searched premises in the province of Łódź, they have not revealed where his alleged attack was planned. However, prosecutors reported today that the suspect had established contacts through which he could gain access to explosive materials and devices, had looked for bomb-making instructions, and had tried to recruit others to his terrorist cause. “Mateusz W.’s actions were intended to further the policies of the terrorist organisation known as Islamic State and to seriously intimidate people with views contrary to the ideology espoused by the suspect,” wrote Katarzyna Calów-Jaszewska, a spokeswoman for the National Prosecutor’s Office. In a separate statement, the Internal Security Agency (ABW) revealed that the suspect had “intended to join a terrorist organisation affiliated with the so-called Islamic State and sought people who could help him carry out this plan”. Neither the security services nor prosecutors have indicated whether Mateusz W. denied or admitted to his alleged crimes or has offered any explanation for his actions. If convicted of preparing a mass attack, he could face up to ten years in prison. Last year, after Mateusz W. was detained, Dobrzyński said that he came from a devoutly Catholic family but had become “deeply infatuated with Islam” and had “fallen in love with terrorism”. In an appeal to parents, Dobrzyński said that, “if you see your children interested in Islam, communism, or fascism, and collecting all sorts of information and items on the subject, that’s the first sign. Take care of your own children, because things can only get worse from there”. Poland has detained a man who was allegedly planning a terrorist attack on a Christmas market as an act of support for Islamic State. The suspect, a 19-year-old Pole, had become "infatuated with Islam", say the security services https://t.co/N4WDVZdlai — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) December 16, 2025 After news of Mateusz W.’s detention emerged, KUL suspended his student status. The university’s spokesman, Wojciech Andrusiewicz, said that neither fellow students nor lecturers had noticed any unusual behaviour by the suspect. World.title: Polish WWII massacre victims reburied in Ukraine at ceremony attended by officials from both countries
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. The remains of 55 Poles – around half of them children – massacred by Ukrainian nationalists in World War Two have been reburied at a ceremony in Ukraine attended by political and religious figures from both countries. The victims, many of whose bones show signs of brutal deaths, were exhumed this summer after Ukraine recently ended a moratorium on searches for tens of thousands of victims of the so-called Volhynia massacres who are believed to remain buried in unmarked mass graves. “This is an important moment for [the victims’] families, but also the Polish state, because this funeral follows decades of waiting,” said Polish culture minister Marta Cienkowska at the ceremony in Ostrówki (Ostrovky in Ukrainian), a depopulated former village that, before the war, was part of Poland and now lies in Ukraine. “Poland has the right and obligation to speak about the crimes committed against its citizens. It has the obligation to commemorate the victims, search for their remains, and provide them with a dignified burial…We will continue this work…everywhere that the graves of the victims of the Volhynian crimes still remain.” Pogrzeb ofiar Zbrodni Wołyńskiej w Ostrówkach i Woli Ostrowieckiej Na cmentarzu w Ostrówkach na terytorium Ukrainy odbyła się uroczystość pogrzebowa 55 ofiar zbrodni dokonanej 30 sierpnia 1943 roku. W uroczystości, zorganizowanej w 83. rocznicę tragicznych wydarzeń,… pic.twitter.com/4dXPOj4m7y — Ministerstwo Kultury i Dziedzictwa Narodowego (@kultura_gov_pl) August 30, 2026 Others to attend the reburial included deputy Ukrainian culture minister Ivan Verbytskyi; Vitaly Skomarovsky, the bishop of Lutsk and president of Ukraine’s Roman Catholic episcopate; Piotr Zgorzelski, the deputy speaker of the Sejm, Poland’s lower house of parliament; and former Polish Prime Minister Mateusz Morawiecki. Karol Polejowski, the deputy head of Poland’s state Institute of National Remembrance (IPN), which led the exhumation work, said that the presence of Ukrainian representatives “fills me with optimism for the future”. While Polish President Karol Nawrocki did not attend, one of his advisors, Jakub Banaszek, read a letter on his behalf, quoted by the Polish Press Agency (PAP). “We will never forget those who died in agony simply because they were Poles,” wrote Nawrocki. “We will not cease our efforts to ensure that all our compatriots murdered by members of the OUN-UPA are properly buried and commemorated.” ✝️ W 8⃣3⃣. rocznicę zbrodni dokonanej przez ukraińskich szowinistów, na cmentarzu w Ostrówkach pochowaliśmy ofiary ludobójstwa na Wołyniu. 🔻🔻🔻 pic.twitter.com/5oh3uiCKX4 — Instytut Pamięci Narodowej (@ipngovpl) August 30, 2026 The Volhynia massacres, in which around 100,000 Poles were killed, were led by the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA), which was a partisan group founded by a faction of the Organisation of Ukrainian Nationalists (OUN) faithful to nationalist leader Stepan Bandera. They sought to ethnically cleanse areas that they saw as Ukrainian territory by wiping out other ethnic groups, in particular the large Polish population. Massacres took place in dozens of villages, including Ostrówki and the neighbouring Wola Ostrowiecka (Volya Ostrovetska in Ukrainian), where on 30 August 1943 the UPA killed over 1,000 Poles and razed the villages to the ground. Exhumations previously took place on the site of the two villages in the 1990s, and again in 2011 and 2015, uncovering the remains of hundreds of victims. However, hundreds more are believed to remain buried. In 2017, Ukraine imposed a ban on searches for victims on its territory in response to the dismantling of a monument to the UPA in Poland. However, in a diplomatic breakthrough last year, it allowed them to resume, including granting permission in December for work in Ostrówki and Wola Ostrowiecka. In April this year, mass graves were discovered there, with exhumations then beginning in July. Earlier this month, the IPN announced the results of that work. They uncovered the remains of 55 victims, 26 of them children (mostly under 12 years of age, with the youngest a few months old) and 20 women. In the Volhynia massacres as a whole, the majority of victims were women and children. The remains of a further 55 victims of massacres by Ukrainian nationalists during WWII have been exhumed in Ukraine. Around half were children, and most show signs of brutal deaths, including skulls pierced with farming tools https://t.co/LbLPzJcG1b — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 8, 2026 The locations and conditions of the remains reveal much about the manner of their death. Most were buried “at random” without coffins, which is consistent with contemporary accounts that they were killed in a barn and then thrown into a mass burial pit. Most of the remains, in particular skulls, show signs of injuries that are also consistent with contemporary accounts, which said that victims were ordered to lie on the ground before being killed with farm tools, including hammers for slaughtering cattle. Material from the bones has been secured for genetic testing, which was recently used for the first time to identify massacre victims exhumed at another location in Ukraine last year. Poland has for the first time used DNA testing to identify the remains of Poles massacred by Ukrainian nationalists in WWII. “After more than 80 years, families are receiving the answer they have awaited for generations,” says the culture minister https://t.co/c1gM3kQ83s — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 14, 2026 The Volhynia massacres have long been a point of tension between Poland, which recognises them as a genocide, and Ukraine, which rejects that label. The decision by Kyiv to allow exhumations to resume last year was regarded as a major step towards reconciliation. However, that process was undermined in May this year, when Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky decided to name a military unit after the “heroes of the UPA”. That prompted an angry response from Warsaw, where Zelensky’s counterpart Karol Nawrocki stripped him of Poland’s highest honour. In his letter read at Sunday’s ceremony, Nawrocki warned those who “continue the tradition of Banderite ideology” that they “place themselves outside the community of citizens of the free, civilised world” and are sending “a clear sign of hostility towards Poland and Poles”. President Zelensky has signed a law establishing a national pantheon to commemorate Ukrainian heroes, prompting Poland to again warn that Ukraine "will have a huge problem" integrating into the EU if it honours figures associated with massacres of Poles https://t.co/fN7Zgbovvu — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 24, 2026 Since the crisis broke out in May, there have been efforts to reach a diplomatic solution. Last month, Zelensky pointed specifically to the exhumation work in Ostrówki and Wola Ostrowiecka as evidence that “Ukraine is doing its part to fairly establish the facts about those who were killed in those years”. Subsequently, he announced a five-point plan to alleviate the crisis, including allowing more exhumations and opening up historical archives. Poland welcomed the move but said that it would wait to see how it was implemented in practice. Earlier this month, Zelensky signed a law establishing a new national pantheon of Ukrainian heroes. Poland has warned that the inclusion of figures associated with the massacres could have consequences for Ukraine’s ambitions to join the European Union. A survey conducted this month by Rating Group, a Ukrainian research agency, which asked Ukrainians to name their country’s greatest hero found that Bandera was the fourth most popular choice, having been chosen by 11% of respondents.
