World.title: Poland is terrible at promoting itself – but has never had better press
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. By Daniel Tilles Two incidents this month have highlighted how state-led efforts to promote Poland abroad often disappoint. Yet, at the same time, the country has never had better international press. Politicians should let Poland’s successes speak for themselves, and support those already telling its story. Poles care a lot about what the world thinks of their country. Major Polish media outlets regularly devote entire articles to what Western journalists, commentators and influencers are saying about Poland. “A German showed what he saw on the streets of Poland,” read one typical recent headline by Onet, Poland’s biggest news website, which devoted an entire report to one video by a German-speaking TikToker with around 7,000 followers. One rarely sees such reports in more self-confident Western countries. Given Poland’s history, such sensitivity regarding the country’s status is not surprising. Poland was, up until the 18th century, a major European country. But, for most of the last 250 years, it has been under foreign subjugation. Only since 1989 has it been able to develop independently, and Poles are understandably keen for the world to take note of their return to the top table. Poland has emerged as Europe’s undisputed growth champion over the past 35 years. In the first part of a new series of articles and podcasts, @AlicjaPtak4 explores the reasons behind Poland's rapid economic development, and the dangers that may lie ahead https://t.co/bW3bnV7Ozn — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 7, 2025 Polish politicians are also inevitably eager to capitalise on such sentiment by showing voters that they are making an effort to promote Poland abroad. The problem is that such efforts are often poorly conceived and executed – as two examples this month have shown. In mid-August, the sport and tourism ministry launched a new advertising campaign intended to attract visitors from western Europe and the United States. However, the first advert – featuring Polish football star Robert Lewandowski, supermodel Anja Rubik, Hollywood filmmaker Jesse Eisenberg, and actor Nikodem Rozbicki playing Fryderyk Chopin – was widely panned in Poland. Res Futura, an organisation that monitors social media sentiment, found that 85% of comments about the advert were negative. The campaign’s slogan – “Poland. More than you expected” – is negative and lacking confidence. The Polish Tourism Organisation says it is based on research showing that visitors to Poland are often positively surprised by how nice it is. Yet, while that is undoubtedly true, it does not mean it is a good idea to try to attract potential tourists by focusing on their low expectations. Poland has launched a new advertising campaign to attract tourists from Europe and the US. The first video, under the slogan "Poland. More than you expected", features footballer Robert Lewandowski, Hollywood star Jesse Eisenberg and supermodel Anja Rubik https://t.co/3jtqyUWQyy — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 19, 2026 The video also has no narrative, with the creators seeming to think that showing famous faces will be enough. Rubik does not speak a single word, while Eisenberg says only “Poland” and Lewandowski “More than you expected”. The film itself does nothing to show that Poland is more than anyone expects. In fact, its depressingly colourless palette and focus on Warsaw’s Stalinist Palace of Science and Culture actually reinforce (false) stereotypes of Poland as grey, dull and post-communist. The country has so many interesting and colourful places that could have been showcased instead. The advert is also a wasted opportunity to tell a story about the film’s stars, especially Eisenberg, who has reconnected with his family’s Polish roots, produced a critically acclaimed movie set in Poland, and last year obtained citizenship. Instead, Chopin dominates the film, but his dialogue is incoherent. When he says, “Warsaw is where my heart is”, almost no potential visitors would understand that this is a reference to the real Chopin’s heart being transported from Paris, where he died, to Warsaw, where it is now entombed in a church. Not long after that advert launched, another controversy emerged around a state official, Barbara Mróz-Gorgoń, who had been appointed only weeks earlier by the government to lead the promotion of Poland. It quickly transpired that a report she had authored last year on creating a national brand – and which appeared to have played a big part in her getting the new job – contained significant errors, questionable methodology, and bizarre language. Many parts showed signs of being AI-generated. Mróz-Gorgoń, who has now resigned, insists that the report was the genuine product of work by her and her team at Marka Polska (Brand Poland), a think tank she leads. However, that is not particularly reassuring given the report’s content. Many parts are simply obvious: at the end of the 26-page text, the three recommendations for the government are to “develop a coherent, long-term national branding strategy”, “invest in promotional campaigns in key markets”, and “coordinate between ministries and other entities”. Other sections are very strange, such as noting that “Germany does not build its brand on the Holocaust”. But perhaps the most telling aspect is that, although the introduction claims it is “a comprehensive report on building…a coherent, long-term branding strategy in the international arena”, the document focuses entirely on how Poles themselves view their own country (its title is even A Self-Portrait of the Poles). It includes no research into what foreigners know or think about Poland and what could interest or attract them. While any national branding exercise should of course take account of the views of the native population, it is clearly incomplete without research into the target of such a campaign, the outside world. Yet that is sadly typical of many state-led efforts to promote Poland, which focus more on pleasing a domestic audience – the voters that politicians want to keep happy – than on being truly outward looking. A government official appointed last month to promote Poland's brand abroad has been hit by a wave of criticism after it emerged that she authored a report containing major errors, bizarre language, and signs of being generated by AI https://t.co/9fpfzFCFuI — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 21, 2026 It should be noted that such failings are nothing new. Successive governments have been responsible for botched efforts to promote Poland. The uninspiring slogan “Poland. More than you expected” has been used since 2021. A previous one, “Polska. Spring Into”, launched in 2014, was simply bizarre and quickly disappeared. In 2016, the former Law and Justice (PiS) government established the Polish National Foundation (PFN), which was pumped full of money from state-owned companies and tasked with promoting Poland abroad. Instead, it focused much of its efforts on domestic activity, often intended to support PiS’s political agenda. The work it did do internationally was often of questionable efficacy, such as spending millions on buying a yacht, naming it “I Love Poland”, then attempting to sail it around the world (before it ended up breaking down and getting stuck in port). A senior official under the former PiS government has been charged over alleged misspending of funds. The case relates to a campaign in 2017 that used money meant for promoting Poland abroad to instead advertise PiS's judicial reforms domestically https://t.co/tH64Bekhec — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 15, 2026 Yet, despite woeful state-led efforts to promote Poland abroad, the country has in recent times been enjoying a soaring international reputation. Western media have been full of articles about the country’s economic success; about how not only are Polish emigrants returning from the UK, but many Brits are moving to Poland too; about how Poles are becoming major buyers of property in Spain; about how companies with roots in Poland, such as InPost and ElevenLabs, are pioneering their industries. Social media feeds are full of influencers extolling Polish cities, with their safe, clean streets; the beauty of Polish nature, with its mountains, lakes and beaches; and the sense of dynamic development that you can feel as soon as you set foot in the country. Last weekend,@thetimes reported on how Brits are moving to Poland. This weekend, on how Poles are replacing Brits as property owners in Spain. pic.twitter.com/IDDdDlluTE — Daniel Tilles (@danieltilles1) June 21, 2026 This positive publicity is largely organic – it is the product of Poland’s own actual successes, not of artificial efforts to create an image of success. It is generated from the bottom up, not from the top down. While the state can play a role – for example, by arranging visits for foreign journalists and influencers and supporting media and institutions that are already telling Poland’s story – it would be better for politicians to focus on creating the conditions for those successes, rather than concocting cockeyed schemes to promote them. World.title: Polish government sets out draft 2027 budget with deficit remaining at 7.1% of GDP
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland’s government has approved a draft budget for 2027 that keeps defence, healthcare and the energy transition among its spending priorities, while projecting another year of heavy borrowing. The deficit is forecast at 7.1% of GDP, unchanged from 2026 but well above the level of 3.7% the government had committed to reach by 2027 after Poland was placed under the European Union’s excessive deficit procedure in 2024. Rada Ministrów przyjęła projekt ustawy budżetowej na 2027 rok. Projekt odpowiedzialnie łączy finansowanie bieżących potrzeb państwa i przedsięwzięć wzmacniających jego bezpieczeństwo oraz potencjał rozwojowy.#BudżetPolaków 🔗 https://t.co/SjWyBUwi8U pic.twitter.com/X9ue6cw5ns — Ministerstwo Finansów (@MF_GOV_PL) August 28, 2026 The budget – which must still be consulted with business and trade union representatives before being approved by parliament and then signed by opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki – sets total expenditure at 977.6 billion zloty (€225.4 billion), 58 billion zloty more than this year. Revenues are projected to rise by 68.4 billion zloty to 695 billion zloty, leaving a nominal budget deficit of 282.6 billion zloty, the highest on record and 10 billion zloty more than this year. Defence spending will remain high, at 198.1 billion zloty, equivalent to 4.5% of GDP, one of the highest levels in NATO. The healthcare budget will reach 274.1 billion zloty, up 26.3 billion zloty from 2026. Spending on energy security and transformation will rise 8.3% year-on-year to reach 19.7 billion zloty. The government expects GDP growth to remain strong, at 3% in 2027, while average inflation is forecast at 2.8%, within the central bank’s target of 2.5%, plus or minus one percentage point. Average wages are expected to rise by 5.9% next year in nominal terms, slightly slower than the 6.4% forecast for this year. The government expects that unemployment, measured according to the national methodology, will stand at 6% at the end of 2027, broadly unchanged from its current level. Poland’s gross borrowing needs are projected at 565 billion zloty in 2027, below the 688 billion zloty budgeted for this year. Debt-servicing costs, however, are expected to rise to 107 billion zloty, up 17 billion zloty from this year. Finance minister Andrzej Domański said that the rise in debt-servicing costs is driven by an increase in the overall volume of debt and the need to refinance bonds issued in 2020 and 2021 at very low interest rates. Poland's debt has been growing at the second-fastest rate in the EU this year, and is set to continue rising. What is behind this trend – and should we be worried – asks Alicja Ptak in the latest of her series of articles and podcasts on Poland’s economy https://t.co/1pvnb2ZxoY — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 30, 2025 The projected deficit leaves Poland under continued pressure to bring its public finances into line with EU fiscal rules. In 2024, the country was placed under the EU’s excessive deficit procedure after its deficit exceeded the bloc’s limit of 3%. Warsaw pledged at the time to bring the deficit below 3% by 2028. However, last year the deficit actually rose, from 6.4% of GDP in 2024 to 7.3% in 2025, which was the second-highest level among all EU member states. This year, Poland’s public debt passed the EU’s limit of 60% of GDP for the first time on record. “The 2027 budget represents a continuation of expansionary fiscal policy, and Poland is making no progress in correcting its excessive deficit and is taking no action to bring it below 3% of GDP,” wrote analysts at ING Bank Śląski today. “The result is a further increase in public debt.” Poland’s public debt has passed 60% of GDP for the first time, thereby exceeding the limit enshrined in EU law. The country is already under the EU's excessive deficit procedure, requiring it to take steps to bring public finances under greater control https://t.co/LNJ0YrP2Ge — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 12, 2026 Efforts to reduce the deficit have also been complicated by political stalemate between the government and opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki, who has vetoed several fiscal measures, including tax increases. Nawrocki did, however, approve a new levy on banks that came into force this year. The situation has led two of the big three rating agencies, Fitch and Moody’s, to shift Poland’s credit outlook to negative. This year, Fitch warned that the political gridlock between Nawrocki and the government was making tackling the deficit and debt more difficult. However, speaking today, Prime Minister Donald Tusk said that the 2027 budget reflects Poland’s position at a time when war is being waged across its eastern border and other conflicts are weighing on the country’s finances. Meanwhile, 2027 will also see pivotal parliamentary elections, at which Tusk’s ruling coalition, which ranges from left to centre right, will seek a second term while the right-wing opposition, supported by Nawrocki, will attempt to win power. Ratings agency Fitch has again warned that the "political gridlock" between Poland's government president – such as the current clash over EU defence loans – is hindering efforts to tackle "large fiscal deficits and rapidly rising debt" https://t.co/JSqwwayTdm — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 18, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Polish “vampire” burial sheds light on 17th-century efforts to keep the dead in their graves
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Researchers investigating an unusual 17th-century burial in northern Poland, in which the remains of a teenage girl were found with a padlock fastened to her toe and a sickle placed across her neck, believe the measures may have been intended to stop her returning from the dead. The burial, discovered in 2022 at an unmarked cemetery in the village of Pień, is an example of what archaeologists describe as “anti-vampiric” or “anti-demonic” burial, in which precautions were taken to protect the living from a deceased person believed to pose a danger. In a newly published academic paper, a team of researchers led by Dariusz Poliński, an archaeologist at Nicolaus Copernicus University in Toruń, say that the girl, whom they have named “Zosia”, may have been blamed by her contemporaries for misfortunes such as disease and famine. The unusual combination of objects that Zosia was buried with – a triangular padlock attached to her left big toe and an iron sickle laid across her throat, with the blade facing towards her neck – immediately attracted archaeologists’ attention when they were discovered. Poliński and his colleagues have used radiocarbon dating, DNA sequencing, isotope analysis and X-ray and microscopic imaging to investigate the burial. Their findings have now been published in the Journal of Archaeological Science: Reports. The researchers have established that Zosia, who was aged between 17 and 19, died around the mid-17th century, most likely between 1620 and 1674. Her grave appears to have been secured in two stages, with analysis of soil layers showing that it was reopened after the initial burial and the sickle added later. “It was unusual that there were two precautions, two methods of showing that this skeleton should be kept in the grave – so the fear of the body coming back to life was greater,” Poliński told CNN. The researchers say the padlock had several possible meanings in funerary symbolism. It could mark the end of earthly life and the transition to the world of the dead, prevent contact between the living and the dead, break a run of bad luck, or protect the community from the deceased returning. “In some interpretations, it was also believed to help halt the spread of epidemics,” Poliński told the Polish Press Agency (PAP). The sickle had a more direct purpose: if the deceased tried to rise from the grave, it was positioned to sever the head or slit the throat, preventing her from returning to the world of the living. However, the latest findings suggest there may have been a third protective element. Researchers found “a distinct green discolouration” in the oral cavity, suggesting that an object containing a high proportion of copper had been placed in the girl’s mouth. Given the extent of the discolouration, they have largely ruled out the possibility that it was simply a coin. “The protective measures taken at the time of the original burial and subsequently after the grave was opened clearly demonstrate the immense fear of Zosia,” said Poliński, quoted by news website Wirtualna Polska. The grave of a "vampire child" – who was turned face down and secured with a padlock to ensure he could not rise from the grave – has been discovered in Poland Researchers believe the site was a cemetery for those excluded or feared by the local community https://t.co/Ez2QgvMnuX — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 11, 2023 Poliński believes that the woman may have been ill or had a physical or mental disability, leading her neighbours to treat her badly while she was alive and fear that she would haunt them after her death. However, the researchers found no skeletal evidence of trauma, violence or disease that might explain her treatment, and her cause of death remains unknown. The Pień cemetery, which has not been marked on maps, contains several other unusual burials, including a child buried face down with a padlock beneath the foot and skeletons weighed down with rocks. This has led researchers to suggest that the cemetery may have been located on unconsecrated ground, away from a church or chapel, and used for people who were poor, disgraced, feared, or otherwise excluded from the community. Zosia’s burial, however, appears to have been unusual in another respect. Analysis suggests she was of relatively high social status. Traces of silk and gold-and-silver thread near her skull suggest she wore an expensive cap, a luxury item generally associated with nobility or wealth. Two years ago, sculptor and artist Oscar D. Nilsson unveiled a 3D facial reconstruction of Zosia, based on measurements of her skull and skeletal clues about her age, weight and health. The reconstruction shows a young woman with blue eyes, light brown hair and a broad nose. “It’s really ironic, in a way,” Nilsson told Reuters at the time. “These people burying her, they did everything they could in order to prevent her from coming back from the dead…We have done everything we can in order to bring her back to life.” A team of scientists has reconstructed the face of a 400-year-old woman, once believed by her neighbors to be a vampire, revealing the human story buried by supernatural beliefs https://t.co/Q6sipo7h4O pic.twitter.com/0gLVIEfaZi — Reuters (@Reuters) October 30, 2024 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: New Pharmacy Partnership Makes Prescription Drugs Easier for Foreigners in Czechia
World.content:
Foreigners from outside the EU insured with Maxima pojišťovna can now collect prescription medicines at selected pharmacies without paying upfront.

The Czech insurer has expanded its network of partner pharmacies through a new agreement with LÉKÁRNA U MUZEA in Prague 1.

Under the arrangement, the pharmacy and insurer handle the reimbursement directly, bringing the process closer to the system used by patients covered by Czech public health insurance.



The change is aimed at simplifying access to medicines for foreigners, who can face difficulties navigating the Czech healthcare system and understanding the costs associated with medical treatment.

According to figures cited by the insurer, nearly 900,000 people from non-EU countries have been living in the Czech Republic on a long-term basis. They account for about 8.2 percent of the country’s population.

How the new system works

Previously, foreign clients with commercial health insurance could be required to pay for prescribed medicines at the pharmacy and then submit the receipts to their insurer for reimbursement.

Under the new arrangement, this step is eliminated. Eligible Maxima clients can collect their prescribed medicines through the partner pharmacy, while the financial settlement takes place directly between the pharmacy and the insurance company.

The model has already been operating for more than a year at the pharmacy operated by Maxima’s healthcare partner Innova Healthcare at the Hůrka Polyclinic in Prague.

The data also highlights some of the most common medical needs among patients visiting the participating clinics. More than 63 percent of patients seen by general practitioners, pediatricians and gynecologists were prescribed antibiotics.

More than 37 percent required treatment for sideropenic anemia, or iron deficiency, while 20 percent received prescriptions for blood-thinning medication following injuries.

The pharmacy in Prague 1 will also stock medical equipment and rehabilitation aids. Its range includes orthoses, crutches, wheelchairs and products for convalescence, rehabilitation and everyday healthcare.

Maxima says it intends to expand the direct-settlement model to additional partner pharmacies in the future.

World.title: Dozens of Hot Air Balloons to Fill Czech Skies During September Festival
World.content:
Dozens of hot air balloons are expected to take to the skies over eastern Bohemia this week as the Balonové Nebe festival returns to Hradec Králové, Jaroměř and nearby areas.

The five-day event will run from Wednesday, September 2, through Sunday, September 6, with a program combining competitive balloon flights, mass launches and evening shows. All public events are free to attend.

Weather will play a major role in the festival schedule. Balloon flights can only take place under suitable conditions, meaning launch sites and departure times may change at short notice.



Organizers say the exact location of each flight will depend mainly on wind direction and other weather conditions. Planned flights may also be postponed or cancelled if conditions are unsuitable.

The festival has established itself as one of the country’s major hot air balloon gatherings. Last year’s event set a Czech record when 81 balloons flew into the sky at the same time.

The 2026 edition will once again feature morning competitions, during which pilots will complete a series of tasks while large groups of balloons rise over the region.

Evening programs will offer a different spectacle, with balloon shows planned for spectators. The precise locations of these events will be announced according to the weather forecast and flying conditions.

Visitors planning to attend are advised to check the festival’s official website before setting out. The organizers will publish the latest information about launch locations, times and any changes to the schedule there.

World.title: VIDEO: Golden STARLUX Lands in Prague for the First Time
World.content:
A golden Airbus A350-1000 operated by Taiwan’s STARLUX Airlines landed at Václav Havel Airport Prague for the first time on Tuesday, September 1.

The aircraft, registered as B-58554, carries the special AIRSORAYAMA Gold livery created in collaboration with Japanese artist Hajime Sorayama.

Prague is one of only three destinations where STARLUX plans to operate the specially designed aircraft on a regular basis, alongside Tokyo and Phoenix.



The arrival marks another step in the expansion of STARLUX’s new direct connection between Prague and Taipei.

The airline launched the route on August 1, initially using the smaller Airbus A350-900. From September, the carrier has switched to the larger A350-1000, which can carry up to 350 passengers in four travel classes.

STARLUX, Airbus and paint manufacturer Mankiewicz developed a multilayer coating using mica particles to create the metallic effect while meeting aviation safety requirements.

Increasing capacity on Prague route

STARLUX launched Prague as its first European destination on August 1, connecting the Czech capital directly with Taipei three times a week. The service currently operates on Tuesdays, Thursdays and Saturdays.

Flight JX101 leaves Taipei at 12:10 a.m. and arrives in Prague at 8:35 a.m. The return flight, JX102, departs Prague at 10:35 a.m. and arrives in Taipei at 7:55 a.m. the following day.

The switch to the A350-1000 increases the available capacity on the route. The aircraft has four travel classes, including First Class, Business Class, Premium Economy and Economy.

An additional Monday flight is scheduled to operate from October through November, bringing the route to four flights per week during that period.

World.title: September 19: Celebrate South Africa’s Heritage Braai Day in Prague
World.content:
On Saturday, 19 September, Prague’s Rohan Beer Garden will host Heritage Braai Day, bringing the flavors and traditions of South Africa to the city.

The event is organized by Saffa Maso.



From noon, visitors can enjoy a relaxed day of grilling, music and socializing outdoors.

Heritage Day in South Africa is a public holiday celebrating the country’s cultural diversity. It has also become closely associated with the tradition of braai, or South African-style barbecuing, with friends and family gathering around the grill to share food.

In Prague, the event is open to everyone and will feature multiple grills, allowing visitors to prepare their own food. Those who prefer to leave the cooking to someone else can use the on-site grill master service, available for an additional fee.

Standard tickets include grills, coals and all braai equipment. Visitors can also choose a braai package, which includes 500g of traditional boerewors sausage and 150g of biltong.

On-site, guests will also be able to purchase Nando’s sauces, chutney, braai spices and other South African products.

Visitors should not bring their own drinks, as a selection of alcoholic and non-alcoholic beverages will be available at the venue. Guests should bring their own plates and cutlery, although disposable options are also allowed.

Tickets are available via SMSTicket at this link. Children under 12 enter free.

World.title: Prague Philharmonic Could Begin Construction in 2028. New Visuals Reveal Design
World.content:
Prague has taken another step toward building the long-planned Vltava Philharmonic.

The Prague Development Company (PDS) submitting an application for planning permission and new visualizations revealing the project in greater detail.

The application covers not only the Philharmonic building but also the surrounding public spaces, transport infrastructure and connections to the existing metro, tram, road, cycling and pedestrian networks.



If the permitting process stays on schedule, the city expects to receive the necessary approval in the first quarter of 2027. A tender for the construction company would then follow, with building work potentially starting in the first quarter of 2028.

The project is planned for the Bubny-Zátory district, near the existing Vltavská metro station. The new cultural complex is expected to be completed in 2033, when trial operations could begin.

The building was designed by Danish architecture studio BIG – Bjarke Ingels Group, which won an international competition in May 2022. Preparation of the detailed permit documentation began in 2025.

The complex will have three underground levels and six floors above ground. It will contain five music halls, creative spaces, restaurants and other facilities.

The project is also intended to provide new premises for the Prague Symphony Orchestra FOK and music collections belonging to the Municipal Library of Prague. The Czech Philharmonic is also expected to gain additional facilities, addressing the limitations of its current premises.

Construction could start in early 2028

The current estimated cost of the Philharmonic building is around CZK 12.33 billion, including equipment but excluding VAT. The surrounding infrastructure and public spaces are expected to cost an additional CZK 5 billion, also excluding VAT.

World.title: Tiny Steps, Big Milestones: What Really Matters When Toddlers Start Preschool
World.content:
For a one-year-old, starting preschool is not about learning letters or sitting through lessons.

It is about feeling safe without Mum or Dad nearby, discovering the joy of playing alongside other children, and slowly gaining the confidence to explore the world independently. At Tiny Tots in Prague, these small everyday moments are at the heart of the programme.

A favourite toy clutched tightly in one hand. A cautious look back at Mum or Dad from the classroom door. Perhaps a few tears (from either side).

For families with children aged one or two, the first experience of leaving a little one in someone else’s care can feel like a very big step.

And for the child, it is one too.



At this age, development happens through moments that can look almost insignificant to adults: reaching for a spoon without help, joining another child in play, recognising a familiar song, saying a new word, or feeling comfortable enough to wander a little further away from a trusted adult.

These are precisely the moments that Tiny Tots, a programme for children aged 1–2 at Nessie English Preschool, part of Park Lane International School, is designed to encourage.

Before learning comes feeling safe

For very young children, a good first preschool experience begins with something much more fundamental than an academic curriculum: trust.

“Parents often want to know how their child will cope with separation, whether we can follow the rhythm they are used to at home and, above all, whether their child will really be seen as an individual,” says Catalina Gonzalez-Got, who leads the Tiny Tots programme.

Catalina knows the feeling from both sides. An early-years educator with international experience, she is also a mother herself. Becoming a parent, she says, gave her a much deeper understanding of how emotional it can be to entrust a young child to somebody else for the first time.

That is why settling in is treated as a process rather than a test that a toddler is expected to pass on day one.

Some children may quickly become curious about their new surroundings. Others need more time, reassurance and proximity to a familiar adult before they are ready to explore.

Both are perfectly normal. The goal is to allow each child to find that confidence at their own pace.

For toddlers, play is serious business

Adults sometimes separate “playing” and “learning”. Toddlers do not.

When a child squishes playdough between their fingers, listens to a story, sings along to a familiar song, explores the garden or watches another toddler build something, they are constantly learning.

They are practising movement and coordination. They are discovering cause and effect. They are learning how to communicate, negotiate space with other children, manage emotions and make choices.

Tiny Tots therefore follows a play-based approach inspired by the English Early Years Foundation Stage framework, with activities designed around the developmental needs of one- and two-year-olds.

There are no miniature school desks or pressure to perform.

Instead, children encounter language, movement, music, creative activities, sensory experiences, stories and outdoor play as a natural part of their day.

The programme keeps the class to a maximum of eight children, allowing teachers to pay close attention to individual personalities, routines and developmental stages.

English without the flashcards

The same philosophy applies to language.

At one or two years old, learning English does not mean memorising vocabulary lists. Children absorb language through relationships and repetition: hearing the same words during snack time, listening to songs, following simple instructions, sharing a picture book or hearing an adult describe what is happening during play.

Tiny Tots provides an English-language environment, giving children regular, natural exposure to the language throughout their day.

Catalina, who raises her own child in a multilingual family, sees communication as something that should grow out of connection rather than performance.

Toddlers often understand far more than they can say, she explains. What matters is creating a positive environment in which language is associated with people, experiences and emotions that make sense to the child.

Learning to do things “all by myself”

Anyone who lives with a toddler knows how powerful those words can be.

Between one and two, children increasingly want to try things independently — even when the result is a spoon on the floor, mismatched shoes or a task that takes considerably longer than if an adult simply did it for them.

Tiny Tots gives children safe opportunities to practise that emerging independence while knowing that an adult is close by when they need help.

The milestone may be eating more independently, choosing an activity, joining a group song, approaching another child or simply becoming comfortable enough to explore a new corner of the room.

For a toddler, these are significant achievements.

And independence does not mean pushing children away from adults. In fact, the opposite is often true: children are more willing to explore when they know they have a trusted person to return to.

A small community for Prague’s smallest residents

For international families in particular, early-years programmes can provide something else that is easy to overlook: a sense of community.

Many parents raising children in Prague live far from grandparents, siblings and the wider family network that might otherwise form part of everyday life.

A nurturing preschool environment can therefore become more than somewhere a child spends part of the day. Familiar teachers, other children and their families can gradually become part of the support network that makes a new city feel more like home.

Tiny Tots is based at Nessie English Preschool in Prague 5, in a quiet residential setting with its own garden. The programme combines experienced early-years teachers, personalised attention and structured routines with plenty of room for children simply to play, discover and be little.

Because at one or two years old, success does not need to look impressive.

Sometimes it is a child who cried at the door last week walking in happily today.

Sometimes it is making a first little friend.

Sometimes it is a new word, a messy painting, a favourite song or the confidence to let go of a teacher’s hand and go exploring alone.

Those tiny steps are exactly where the big journey begins.

Tiny Tots at Nessie English Preschool is designed for children aged 1–2 years. Families interested in the programme can arrange a visit to the Prague 5 campus to see the environment and meet the team.

Enrolment for the 2026/27 school year is now open.

World.title: Wine Harvest Festivals in Prague in September: The Full Guide
World.content:
Every September, Prague celebrates vinobraní, the traditional wine harvest festival marking the end of the grape season.

Visitors can look forward to concerts, dance and theatre performances, food stalls, and tastings of young wine and the seasonal favorite burčák (partially fermented grape juice). The festivals are family-friendly, offering children’s theatre, horse rides, folk craft demonstrations, competitions, and workshops.



Here is an overview of the main wine festivals in Prague in 2026:

Vinohrady Wine Harvest Festival

September 11–12, 2026, 10:00–21:00

náměstí Jiřího z Poděbrad

Facebook

Winemakers from across Europe — Austria, Slovakia, Hungary, Italy, Slovenia, Croatia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Romania, Serbia, Ukraine, and Poland — will join Czech and Moravian producers.

Alongside wine, expect a wide range of food: sausages, cheeses, potato spirals, langoše (fried dough with toppings), and traditional Wallachian cakes (frgály). The festival also offers live music and a children’s zone with a playground, carousel, and creative workshops. Admission is free.

Wine Harvest at Prague Castle

September 5–6, 2026, 11:00–18:00

Royal Garden & Ball Game Hall, Prague Castle, Hradčany

hrad.cz

Set in the historic Royal Garden of Prague Castle, this festival features tastings of Czech and Moravian wines, sparkling wines, fresh grape juice, burčák, and high-quality local produce. The program includes folk ensembles, historical fencing, and family activities.

Entry to the garden is free; a tasting glass costs 120 CZK.

Grébovka Wine Festival

September 18, 2026 (14:00–20:00) at náměstí Míru

September 19, 2026 (13:00–20:00) at Havlíčkovy sady (Grébovka Park)

Facebook

Organized by Prague 2, the Grébovka Festival is one of the city’s largest and most popular wine events. Set in Havlíčkovy sady (often described as a hidden gem of Vinohrady), the festival offers wine tastings, culinary specialties, live music, dance performances, and a cultural program celebrating wine traditions. Families can enjoy workshops, theatre, competitions, and children’s activities.

St. Clare’s Vineyard Harvest Festival

September 12–13, 2026

Prague Botanical Garden, Fata Morgana greenhouse, Troja

botanicka.cz

Hosted at the St. Clare’s Vineyard in the Prague Botanical Garden, this festival is renowned for its carefully made burčák, produced from handpicked grapes. Guests can sample varietal wines, cuvées, and brandies from this rare Prague vineyard, along with wines from leading Czech and Moravian producers. Guided cellar tours, food stalls, live music, and terrace dancing complete the program.

Troja Wine Harvest Festival

September 13, 2026, 11:00–20:00

Gardens of Troja Chateau, Prague 7

Facebook

Held in the baroque Troja Chateau, this festival combines wine tastings from Czech, Moravian, and international producers with burčák, traditional food, and live music. Children’s activities include games, workshops, and a kids’ zone. Admission is free.

St. Wenceslas Wine Festival

September 28, 2026, 12:00–18:00

Villa Richter & St. Wenceslas Vineyard, Prague Castle

Facebook

Taking place in the historic St. Wenceslas Vineyard, the oldest in Bohemia, this festival is steeped in legend — St. Wenceslas is said to have planted and harvested vines here for sacramental wine. Visitors can enjoy wines from leading Czech and Moravian wineries, sample burčák, and take in panoramic views of Prague’s Old Town.

17th Malá Strana Wine Festival

September 19, 2026, 13:00–22:00

Kampa Park, Malá Strana

Set along the Vltava River in Kampa Park, this festival celebrates the traditions of the Horňácko region in South Moravia. Expect cimbalom music, folk dancing, local wines, burčák, homemade sausages, and slivovice (plum brandy). Craft stalls and lively performances bring a taste of Moravian countryside to the heart of Prague. Free entry.

Vinobraní na Náplavce

Tents selling wine and burčák from Czech producers will be located on the Rašínovo nábřeží embankment (between the railway bridge and the Vyšehrad rock). The festival will also offer snacks that pair perfectly with wine. Organizers have prepared live music and several different wine competitions for guests, including a corkscrew competition, blind tasting, flavor identification, and more.

September 25 and 26, 2026, from 1:00 PM to 9:30 PM;

Price: 100 CZK (includes a glass tasting glass)

World.title: Czechia Spent CZK 19 Billion on COVID Vaccines and Used Less Than Half
World.content:
The Czech Republic has spent roughly CZK 19 billion on COVID-19 vaccines since 2020, but fewer than half of the 41 million doses supplied under its pandemic-era procurement agreement were ultimately used in the country.

More than 18 million doses expired and had to be destroyed, representing a value of about CZK 8 billion.

A further four million doses were donated to other countries, according to information provided by the Czech Ministry of Health in response to a request from the Czech Technical Committee.



For the 2026-27 vaccination season, around 900,000 doses will be available in the country. By comparison, fewer than one-third of that number was administered during the previous season. The vaccination season runs from September through the end of August the following year.

Demand for COVID-19 vaccination has fallen sharply since the initial rollout. More than 15 million doses were administered during the first year vaccines were widely available. A year later, demand had fallen to roughly one-fifth of that level. Between 2022 and 2023, interest dropped by more than 80 percent, followed by further declines of about one-third in subsequent years.

Only about 1,500 doses had been administered by July 26 this year. Most vaccinations, however, take place during the autumn months.

The low demand has contributed to substantial vaccine waste. When the original purchases were made, authorities faced considerable uncertainty over how the pandemic would develop, how many booster doses would be required and how many people would seek vaccination.

Maintaining sufficient supplies was considered necessary in case the epidemiological situation deteriorated.

The Czech Republic is now considering a different approach to future procurement. The Ministry of Health is negotiating with vaccine manufacturers, health insurance companies and medical organisations over supplies and financing for the 2027-28 season. The talks are taking into account both the expected demand and the cost-effectiveness of vaccination.

World.title: Hungary has plenty of people working. So why is its business environment lagging?
World.content:
Hungary has one of the highest employment rates in Europe, matching Germany at 81.1%, but its relatively weak performance in innovation and digitalisation has dragged it down to 22nd place overall in a new business environment ranking.

The 2026 Doing Business in Europe study by Leadfeeder ranks 29 European countries based on nine indicators covering labour productivity, employment, investment, innovation, knowledge-intensive employment and the adoption of technologies such as cloud computing, artificial intelligence and e-commerce.

Hungary ranks 22nd overall, despite recording the joint sixth-highest employment rate among the countries included in the study. Its 81.1% employment rate for people aged 20–64 puts it level with Germany and ahead of Austria, Ireland and Denmark.

The figures suggest that Hungary’s challenge is not primarily getting people into work, but making the economy more productive, innovative and digitally advanced.

Hungary’s strong employment rate

The Netherlands records the highest employment rate in the ranking, at 83.4%, followed by Czechia at 82.9%, Sweden at 81.8%, Estonia at 81.7% and Cyprus at 81.3%. Hungary and Germany share sixth place, both recording an employment rate of 81.1%. At the other end of the table, Türkiye has the lowest employment rate at 58.1%, followed by Bosnia and Herzegovina at 59.5%.

Leadfeeder’s analysis points to a clear distinction between employment and productivity. A large proportion of the working-age population may be employed without the economy necessarily generating correspondingly high output from that labour.

Norway, for example, has the highest labour productivity in the ranking, with a score of 123.0, but finishes sixth overall. Its employment rate is therefore not the only factor behind its strong performance.

If you missed it: Would you work in Hungary for this median salary? Half of the Hungarians earn even less

Investment offers little relief

Hungary performs somewhat better on gross fixed capital formation, ranking joint 16th, alongside Finland, with investment equivalent to 21.9% of GDP. However, the country’s weaker results in several other areas prevent this from translating into a strong overall ranking.

Hungary ranks 24th for innovation, while enterprise adoption of artificial intelligence stands at just 10.4%, placing the country 22nd. Its share of e-commerce orders is 21.3%, corresponding to 21st place.

Knowledge-intensive employment also remains relatively modest. Hungary and Slovenia are joint 14th, with 36.5% of employment classified as knowledge-intensive. Together, these figures point to a gap between the number of people working and the sophistication of the activities they perform.

Digitalisation closely linked to overall performance

The Leadfeeder study also found a strong relationship between digitalisation and countries’ overall positions in the ranking. Digitalisation rank has a correlation of 0.89 with the overall ranking, while investment rank has a much weaker correlation of just 0.14.

This suggests that simply investing more is not necessarily enough to create a stronger business environment. The ability of companies and economies to turn investment into productivity, innovation and digital capabilities appears to matter considerably more.

The contrast is visible elsewhere in the rankings. Germany, Europe’s largest economy, ranks fifth overall and records the highest number of patents per million people. Norway has the most productive workforce but finishes sixth, while Türkiye has the highest investment relative to GDP but ranks only 19th overall.

Sweden tops Europe’s business environment ranking

Sweden takes first place in Leadfeeder’s 2026 ranking, with an overall score of 74.8. Denmark comes second with 69.2, followed by the Netherlands with 64.6. Germany ranks fifth despite being the largest economy covered by the study.

According to Leadfeeder, Sweden’s success comes not from dominating the individual indicators but from maintaining consistently strong performance across them. It leads only one of the nine metrics, yet has the largest gap between itself and the next country in the top nine.

The study covers 29 European countries with complete data across all nine indicators. Eleven other countries — including Switzerland, Iceland, Luxembourg, Malta, Montenegro, North Macedonia, Albania, Ukraine and Kosovo — were excluded from the overall ranking because of missing data for one or more indicators.

Leadfeeder says differences of less than 0.1 points in the overall score should not be interpreted as meaningful separations. Several individual indicators also contain exact ties, including Hungary’s joint sixth-place position with Germany for employment and its joint 16th-place position with Finland for investment.

The full Doing Business in Europe: Where the Action Is in 2026 study is available from Leadfeeder.

World.title: Croatian restaurant sends Hungarian tourists away for ordering only pancakes
World.content:
A holiday dining experience on Croatia’s Krk Island has sparked a heated online debate after four Hungarian visitors were reportedly asked to leave a busy restaurant because they wanted to order only pancakes during dinner time.

Hungarian tourists ordered pancakes in Croatia, then they were told to leave

According to an account shared by the mother of one of the young men, the four friends waited around 10–15 minutes for a table at a popular, crowded restaurant. When the waiter arrived, each ordered a portion of pancakes costing EUR 7, meaning the group would have spent EUR 28 in total.

The waiter reportedly reacted angrily, questioning why they wanted only dessert during the dinner rush. With other customers waiting outside, he allegedly asked the group to give up their table and leave. The story quickly divided social media users.

Was the restaurant right to refuse them?

Some commenters condemned the waiter’s behaviour, arguing that EUR 28 for four portions of pancakes was hardly an insignificant amount and that customers should be free to decide what they want to order. Others defended the restaurant, pointing to the economics of a busy dinner service. A table for four occupied during peak hours could potentially generate considerably more revenue if the guests ordered full meals rather than dessert.

Several commenters also noted that similar situations can occur in other popular tourist destinations, including Hungary, Italy and Spain, where restaurants may discourage customers from occupying larger tables during peak periods if they intend to order only drinks, coffee or dessert. But does a restaurant in Croatia have the legal right to require customers to spend a minimum amount?

Stay up-to-date with our Hungary Weekly Briefing: subscribe on Substack!

No general minimum-spending rule in Croatia

To clarify the legal position, the Hungarian representation of the Croatian National Tourist Board was contacted about the incident. Mira Horváth, a senior member of the organisation, explained that there is no general Croatian rule or code requiring every restaurant customer to spend a minimum amount, writes Blikk.

Restaurants must, however, clearly display their prices and terms of sale and comply with them. The Croatian National Tourist Board also stressed that it is primarily responsible for promoting and developing tourism rather than investigating individual complaints.

Customers who believe a restaurant has breached the rules can contact the Croatian State Inspectorate, which supervises hospitality and other establishments. They can also submit a complaint directly to the service provider, which is required to respond within the legally prescribed timeframe. The organisation expressed regret that the Hungarian visitors had such an experience and said it hoped the incident was an isolated case.

In case you missed it: Budapest taxi fares rise from today – airport pickups also become more expensive

Wider complaints about Croatian dining

The Krk incident comes amid wider online discussions among tourists about prices, food quality and service on Croatia’s Adriatic coast. Some travellers have complained about high-season prices in destinations such as Split, Dubrovnik and Hvar, while others have criticised inconsistent food quality and service.

Such individual experiences should not, however, be taken as representative of Croatian hospitality as a whole. Croatian tourism authorities have stressed their efforts to improve service standards, while the country has seen a growing number of Michelin-recognised restaurants.

For the four Hungarian visitors on Krk, the immediate issue was considerably simpler: they wanted four portions of pancakes during a busy dinner service. While the restaurant may have had commercial reasons for preferring customers ordering full meals, Croatian law does not impose a general minimum-spending requirement on restaurant guests.

Whether the restaurant handled the situation appropriately remains a matter of opinion — and one that has clearly divided diners online.

World.title: Uzbekistan Independence Day at 35: a country looking proudly back – and confidently ahead
World.content:
Uzbekistan Independence Day is being celebrated on 1 September with particular significance this year: the Central Asian country is marking 35 years of independence. I had the opportunity to experience part of the celebrations first-hand in Tashkent, where an extraordinary state ceremony offered not only a spectacular show, but also a revealing glimpse of how Uzbekistan sees its past, present and future.

There are national holidays that are primarily dates in the calendar, and there are others where the meaning of the occasion is impossible to miss once you are actually there. In Uzbekistan, Independence Day clearly belongs to the latter category.

The Uzbek capital was already in a festive mood when I attended the main state ceremony on 28 August. Yet beyond the flags, music, dancers and monumental setting, what stayed with me most was the sense that Uzbekistan’s 35th anniversary is not being presented simply as a celebration of an event that happened in 1991. It is also being used as an opportunity to demonstrate how much the country has changed – particularly during the past decade.

What does Uzbekistan celebrate on Independence Day?

Uzbekistan declared its state independence on 31 August 1991, in the final months of the Soviet Union. The following day, 1 September, was designated Independence Day and subsequently became the country’s main national holiday.

At an extraordinary session of the Supreme Soviet of the Uzbek SSR, lawmakers adopted both the resolution proclaiming the independence of the Republic of Uzbekistan and legislation establishing the foundations of the new sovereign state. The Uzbek SSR was renamed the Republic of Uzbekistan.

Thirty-five years later, the anniversary is therefore much more than a ceremonial event. For Uzbeks, it represents the restoration of national sovereignty and the ability of the country to determine its own political, economic and cultural direction.

This year’s official celebrations are being held under the theme “One Homeland, One People – Together We Create a New Life and Future!”, a slogan that also says a great deal about the government’s emphasis on development and national renewal.

More than a thousand performers in New Tashkent

I experienced the scale of Uzbekistan Independence Day personally on 28 August, when I attended the major state celebration in New Tashkent.

President Shavkat Mirziyoyev addressed the audience before a huge cultural programme began, involving more than a thousand dancers, performers and extras. The sheer scale of the production was striking: carefully choreographed scenes, traditional elements and modern staging combined to tell the story of the country and its people.

The choice of New Tashkent as the venue also carried a clear message. The enormous new urban development is intended to become a centre of education, culture and science and, in Mirziyoyev’s words, a symbol of the strength of the “New Uzbekistan”. The President also highlighted newly completed educational and cultural institutions in the area.

President Shavkat Mirziyoyev addressed the audience before a huge cultural programme began.

Several messages from his speech stood out.

Mirziyoyev stressed that although modern independence was achieved in 1991, Uzbekistan’s statehood and civilisation extend back thousands of years. He also described human dignity and the ability to live freely as fundamental achievements of independence, while pointing to the sweeping reforms launched during recent years.

Speaking shortly before the main celebration, the president summed up the scale of the transformation in unusually ambitious terms: “Thirty-five years is a short period by historical standards,” he said, while arguing that the scale of the country’s achievements made the period feel considerably longer.

The ceremony itself reinforced that message. This was a celebration of history, but very deliberately also a presentation of what the authorities believe Uzbekistan could become next.

Uzbekistan Independence Day at 35: a country looking proudly back – and confidently ahead Uzbekistan Independence Day at 35: a country looking proudly back – and confidently ahead Uzbekistan Independence Day at 35: a country looking proudly back – and confidently ahead Uzbekistan Independence Day at 35: a country looking proudly back – and confidently ahead Uzbekistan Independence Day at 35: a country looking proudly back – and confidently ahead

Thirty-five years of transformation – and an extraordinary last decade

This is where my own impressions of Uzbekistan become difficult to separate from the anniversary itself.

From what I have seen, the country has undergone enormous development during the 35 years since independence, both economically and politically. But the transformation over roughly the last decade is particularly visible.

You can see it physically in Tashkent: new roads, major construction projects, public spaces, hotels, business districts and ambitious cultural institutions. You can also sense a country that has become considerably more outward-looking and interested in attracting tourists, businesses, investors and international partners.

Economic statistics support at least part of that impression. World Bank figures show that Uzbekistan’s real GDP grew by 7.7 percent in 2025, following growth of 6.7 percent a year earlier. The country’s current-dollar GDP reached around USD 147 billion in 2025. The World Bank has also described the broad reform programme launched from 2017 onwards as an important factor supporting the country’s economic expansion.

This does not mean every problem has disappeared or that a 35-year transformation can be reduced to new buildings and GDP statistics. But for a visitor, the pace and ambition are difficult to overlook.

Perhaps that is one reason why the concept of “New Uzbekistan” appears so frequently in official speeches. After travelling around the country, the phrase begins to make more sense: Uzbekistan is consciously trying to build a new international image while preserving – and increasingly showcasing – its extraordinary historical inheritance.

Why Uzbekistan is worth the journey from Hungary

And that historical inheritance alone is a compelling reason to visit.

For Hungarian travellers, Uzbekistan may still seem distant. Yet few destinations offer such a concentration of spectacular architecture and Silk Road history.

Samarkand is the obvious starting point. Its Registan Square, with three monumental madrasas surrounding one of the most recognisable public spaces in Central Asia, is even more impressive in person than in photographs. UNESCO describes Samarkand as a crossroads and melting pot of world cultures, with more than two and a half millennia of history.

Registan Square, Samarkand, Uzbekistan. Photo: Daily News Hungary

Then there is Bukhara, a Silk Road city more than 2,000 years old whose historic centre remains one of the best-preserved examples of a medieval Central Asian city.

And Khiva offers yet another experience: entering its old walled city can feel less like visiting an individual monument and more like walking directly into another historical period.

Tashkent itself now has a major new attraction that deserves to be placed alongside these famous Silk Road cities.

If you missed it – Uzbekistan at 35: tourism becomes a powerful symbol of independence, openness and national growth

Tashkent’s extraordinary Center for Islamic Civilization

The Center for Islamic Civilization in Uzbekistan, officially opened in Tashkent in March 2026, is one of the country’s most ambitious cultural projects.

The vast complex combines a museum, library, research facilities and exhibitions tracing the intellectual and scientific history of Islamic civilisation in Central Asia. Its collections include manuscripts, historical objects and material relating to some of the scholars whose work influenced mathematics, astronomy, medicine and philosophy far beyond the region.

Its scale is remarkable. By the beginning of June – less than three months after opening – the centre had already received around half a million domestic and international visitors, according to Uzbek government figures.

For anyone interested in history, religion, science or architecture, it is worth allowing several hours rather than treating it as a quick stop on a Tashkent sightseeing tour.

Hospitality may be Uzbekistan’s greatest attraction

Buildings, monuments and economic transformation explain only part of why Uzbekistan leaves such a strong impression.

The other part is the people.

One thing I repeatedly experienced was the genuine hospitality of Uzbeks. Visitors are welcomed warmly, conversations start easily and food has a habit of appearing in quantities that make refusing another plate nearly impossible.

And that brings us to Uzbek gastronomy.

The country’s best-known dish is, of course, plov – rice cooked with meat, carrots, onions and spices, with regional variations across Uzbekistan. But reducing Uzbek cuisine to plov would be unfair. Samsa baked in a traditional oven, shashlik, lagman noodles, soups, fresh fruit, vegetables and the ubiquitous round Uzbek non bread make eating here an attraction in its own right.

Plov Center, Tashkent, Uzbekistan. Photo: Daily News Hungary Plov Center, Tashkent, Uzbekistan. Photo: Daily News Hungary Plov Center, Tashkent, Uzbekistan. Photo: Daily News Hungary

Food also has a social role. Meals are long, communal and generous. Tea arrives constantly. The table is not simply somewhere to eat; it is where guests become part of the occasion.

For travellers, this may ultimately be as memorable as Registan Square or the ancient walls of Khiva.

Uzbekistan Independence Day is about more than the past

Standing in New Tashkent as more than a thousand performers filled the enormous stage on 28 August, it was easy to understand why the 35th anniversary carries such weight here.

Uzbekistan Independence Day commemorates a decisive moment in 1991, but today’s Uzbekistan is clearly using the anniversary to look forward as much as backwards.

There is enormous pride in the Silk Road cities, ancient scholars and traditions that shaped this part of the world. At the same time, there is an equally visible determination to build new universities, businesses, transport links, museums, residential districts and an economy far more connected to the outside world.

After seeing both sides of the country – its historical treasures and the extraordinary amount of construction and development taking place today – my strongest impression is that Uzbekistan does not see its first 35 years of independence as the conclusion of a story.

It sees them as the beginning of one.

As we wrote earlier, Tashkent International Media Forum brought global journalists together in 2026

World.title: Cash refund for recycling bottles could soon disappear in Budapest
World.content:
Hungary’s bottle-recycling system could be facing a major change, with cash payments for returned bottles and cans potentially abolished at REpont collection points.

Cash could soon disappear from Hungary’s bottle recycling scheme

MOHU, the company responsible for Hungary’s deposit-return system (DRS), is proposing that the government remove the option of receiving the 50-forint deposit in cash. Instead, consumers would be able to use a voucher for shopping or have the money transferred to their bank account through the REpont app. Donations to charity would also remain available.

The proposal comes amid growing concerns in Budapest about people collecting returnable bottles from bins and the associated problems of litter, damaged rubbish bins and public safety. Also, several claims have arised that many of those spend the money from collecting and recycling these bottles on drugs.

MOHU proposes ending cash payments

Csaba Bozóki, MOHU’s director responsible for the deposit-return system, announced the proposal in a Facebook video, arguing that cash is not necessary for the system. Under the current rules, a voucher issued by a reverse vending machine can be redeemed for cash at the relevant shop. Changing this would require an amendment to the government regulation governing the scheme.

According to reports, MOHU has already discussed the proposal with representatives of Budapest and its districts. A joint proposal from MOHU, the capital and district municipalities could eventually be submitted to the government.

Bottle collecting and recycling has become a problem in Budapest

Since the HUF 50 deposit was introduced in 2024, the system has dramatically increased the collection and recycling of drinks packaging. However, it has also created a new phenomenon in Budapest, where people search through rubbish bins for returnable bottles and cans. Several district mayors say this has contributed to litter being left around bins, containers being damaged or overturned, and additional pressure on local cleaning services.

Terézváros (District VI of Budapest) Mayor Tamás Soproni previously called for the recycling system to be temporarily suspended until the problems could be addressed. The government rejected that idea, while MOHU has stressed that the deposit-return system is required by EU rules and cannot simply be abolished, as HVG.hu reported.

Stay up-to-date with our Hungary Weekly Briefing: subscribe on Substack!

MOHU: The system did not create the underlying problems

Bozóki has argued that homelessness, drug addiction and deep poverty in central Budapest are not new problems caused by bottle returns.

“These are very important social problems that we need to talk about,” he said, while stressing that a solution should involve local authorities, social organisations and the authorities. Supporters of removing cash payments nevertheless believe the measure could reduce the incentive to collect bottles from bins for immediate cash.

In case you missed it: Another Budapest city centre district may ban Airbnb – referendum on the horizon

Who could be affected?

Critics warn that eliminating cash would make the system less accessible for some people. Those without a bank account or smartphone, or those who simply want their HUF 50 deposit returned in cash, could face additional difficulties. The proposal would therefore change how people receive their own deposits without addressing the wider issues of homelessness, poverty or drug use.

The government now faces a choice over whether to amend the rules. If the proposal goes ahead, cash could soon disappear from Hungary’s REpont system, leaving shoppers with vouchers, bank transfers or charitable donations as the main alternatives.
