World.title: AI jobs war erupts at Sydney university as staff walk out
World.content:
NationalNSWEducation AI jobs war erupts at Sydney university as staff walk out David Barwell September 2, 2026 — 4:12pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Classrooms at the University of Sydney’s Camperdown campus fell unusually quiet on Wednesday as hundreds of staff walked off the job amid a growing dispute over artificial intelligence, workloads and job security. Up to 600 staff members established picket lines across campus entrances as part of a 24-hour strike, forcing most classes online and shutting laboratories. The action, led by the National Tertiary Education Union (NTEU), highlights mounting tensions across higher education as universities increasingly integrate AI into teaching. Academics at the University of Sydney walked off the job on Wednesday. Dominic Lorrimer Alongside claims for a 20 per cent pay rise and 17 per cent superannuation for casual staff, the union is seeking legally binding protections governing artificial intelligence, including guarantees AI will not be used to cut jobs or replace human interaction in teaching. NTEU NSW secretary Vince Caughley said academics were already seeing AI avatars and chatbots used in course delivery.



“For us, it’s not simply about our jobs. It’s about the nature of what a university is,” Caughley said. The University of Sydney has positioned itself as one of Australia’s most enthusiastic adopters of AI, with academics using its custom-built platform Cogniti to create chatbots and interactive learning tools. NTEU USYD branch president Peter Chen and NTEU NSW state secretary Vince Caughley speak during the rally. Dominic Lorrimer Tensions escalated after the university released a discussion paper last month outlining a future in which AI could provide personalised learning support to students while reducing staff-student contact hours. The proposal intensified concerns among academics that automated systems could eventually lead to job cuts and fewer staff teaching larger student cohorts.



Computer science lecturer Alan Fekete, who has taught at the university for 38 years, said staff were already managing heavier workloads. “The fact that they keep putting up the work we have to do, and having fewer people to do it, increases the stress and increases the risks of losing one’s job,” Fekete said. The strike resulted in most classes taught online on Wednesday. Sitthixay Ditthavong As part of enterprise bargaining negotiations, the union is also seeking consultation over AI deployment, transparency around algorithms and the right for staff to challenge automated decisions. The university, in a statement, described the strike action as “premature” and said it was committed to engaging at the bargaining table.



“Human judgment, accountability and relationships are essential to everything we do, and can never be replaced by technology,” the spokeswoman said. Staff at the University of Sydney set up picket lines on Wednesday, Sitthixay Ditthavong The strike comes as universities grapple with broader financial pressures. Despite generating $1.7 billion in international student revenue last financial year, the University of Sydney’s surplus fell from $545 million to $194 million. Related Article Exclusive

AI Thousands of University of Sydney staff to strike over AI Student Dana Kafina, who joined the picket lines, argued growing reliance on AI-generated content risks diminishing the quality of education.



“Some of my main units have lecture materials that are made with just AI,” she said. “It makes it feel impersonal, but also that the quality of learning isn’t as good for students who are paying up to $50,000 in fees.” NTEU branch president Peter Chen warned universities could become the “canary in the coal mine” for the wider workforce. “For those asking why I should care about university teachers on strike, my message is: AI is coming for you as well.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: China’s flood rescue is a no-go zone for foreign media, what does it have to hide?
World.content:
Analysis WorldAsiaFloods China’s flood rescue is a no-go zone for foreign media, what does it have to hide? Lisa Visentin September 2, 2026 — 4:07pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Beijing: Late last Wednesday night, a Tibet Daily reporter filmed a video from inside his car as it pelted down China’s National Highway 219 in heavy rain. He was racing from Lhasa, the capital of the Tibet Autonomous Region, to Gyirong Port at the border with Nepal where a great human tragedy was unfolding. Rescuers observe a moment of silence for the victims of the mudslide near the Gyirong Port in Gyirong County, in southwestern China’s Tibet Autonomous Region. Jigme Dorje/Xinhua via AP They were due to arrive at the port – or what was left of it – around 4am, he explained, their 14-hour drive delayed by the severe weather. “Upon arrival, we will bring you the latest updates on the disaster situation and emergency relief efforts at the scene as soon as possible”, the reporter said in the video posted to Tibet Daily’s WeChat account, a Chinese social media platform.



Loading By that stage, the world had seen the first video of the gargantuan wall of mud and ice that had ripped through the immigration crossing that morning at the Tibet-Nepal border, swallowing everything in its path. That clip would soon be scrubbed from the Chinese internet by censors. The scale of the event would become more apparent in coming days, but by then it was already clear than many people were dead. This scramble – dropping everything and running towards the disaster – is a universal journalistic imperative. It’s what is expected of journalists, especially when your country’s citizens are caught up in tragedy. Credit where it’s due to the Tibet Daily journos. But it’s an imperative the Chinese government has denied foreign journalists like me, despite repeated requests for access to the Gyirong area where there are, based on China’s own figures, five Australians among the more than 500 missing.



On Tuesday, I posed the question again to China’s Foreign Ministry at a press conference in Beijing: why is China refusing access to foreign reporters seeking to cover this tragedy alongside Chinese state media from the disaster zone on the Tibetan side? Related Article Floods Second Australian found after Nepal disaster, ‘grave concerns’ for 42 still missing as death toll passes 1000 I’m far from alone. Other journalists working for international media outlets in China have also sought access. With more than 260 foreigners from 23 countries among the missing, this is a not a mere internal China issue. It took on more significance for Australia on Tuesday, when one of our own was confirmed alive in Tibet. The ministry’s response – essentially, it is too unsafe – is clearly undermined by the authorised presence of local media reporting from nearby the flood ravaged areas.



“Road and communication in the affected area is currently cut off, and there is a significant safety risk of secondary disasters,” spokesman Guo Jiakun said. “Rescue efforts are being carried out in [an] intensive and orderly manner, and we will continue to release the latest information on the disaster situation and rescue operations.” Compare China’s approach with what’s happening in Nepal, which has borne the brunt of the catastrophe, and where the world’s press have amassed since Wednesday. Among them is this masthead’s South East Asia correspondent Zach Hope who dispatched with haste from Singapore, joined by photographer Kate Geraghty from Sydney. They’ve reported harrowing tales of survival amid the devastation. Over the past few days, I have watched clips of state media reporters from the likes of Tibet Daily, Xinhua and China Central Television reporting from the disaster zone, standing on muddy embankments as they carry the government’s message about access and rescue efforts, while tractors work in the background. I don’t wish to impugn the personal dedication or professionalism of these reporters. They are doing gruelling work in challenging conditions, and against the backdrop of mounting casualties, although China has only reported 16 dead so far.



But their reporting is ultimately heavily controlled by their masters: the Chinese government. All state media outlets are regulated by the Publicity Department of the Central Committee of the Chinese Communist Party – better known by its original name, the Central Propaganda Department. We won’t be hearing or seeing anything from those reporters that hasn’t been vetted by editorial staff whose foremost loyalty is to the party’s version of the truth. Chinese rescuers prepare before heading to the mudslide-stricken area near Gyirong Port, Tibet. Xinhua via AP Chinese President Xi Jinping laid out his expectations for state media during a 2016 tour of their newsrooms. “All news media run by the party must work to speak for the party’s will and its propositions, and protect the party’s authority and unity,” state outlet Xinhua quoted Xi as saying at the time.



It may well be that China has a good story to tell about its search and rescue efforts in Tibet. It has massive military resources and advanced scientific equipment, that it can – and says it has – deployed, including troops, aircraft carriers, and drones. But given China’s obsessive control over information, its fixation on positive coverage, and the absence of independent reporters, how can the world be confident it is getting the most full and accurate picture possible of what is happening on the Tibet side of the border? We should also question why almost no survivor accounts have emerged organically on social media from Tibetans or others who have made narrow escapes. What’s this really about? China has long imposed an effective ban on foreign press entering Tibet, rarely granting the permits needed to enter the region unless for closely monitored government-coordinated trips. It’s part of the Beijing’s broader effort to strictly control Tibet, which has sporadically erupted with protests and self-immolation among Tibetans who have pushed for autonomy since China annexed Tibet in the 1950s.

World.title: Sydney Swan Riley Bice ‘not a suspect’ in police sexual assault investigation
World.content:
Exclusive SportAFLCrime Sydney Swan Riley Bice ‘not a suspect’ in police sexual assault investigation Christine Lacy September 2, 2026 — 4:32pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Sydney Swan Riley Bice has been cleared of any criminal conduct in the unfolding police investigation into the alleged sexual assault of exotic dancers at a Melbourne hotel last month. A source with knowledge of the Victoria Police inquiry, but not authorised to speak publicly, also confirmed that detectives have finished a round of voluntary interviews with the four other Swans players but revealed some had not taken part in the process. Swans players (from left) Chad Warner, James Jordon, Isaac Heeney, Riley Bice and Nick Blakey have been suspended for the rest of the season. Artwork: Marija Ercegovac The source said Bice, 25, is now being treated as a potential witness in the case, which is now in its third week. The other Swans stars at the centre of the incident – Isaac Heeney, Chad Warner, Nick Blakey and James Jordon – all remain part of the police investigation.



The developments follow reporting by this masthead of the appointment by the players of different lawyers to represent their diverging interests, with at least three separate counsels now working for the men. The source connected with the investigation said some in the group had declined to provide voluntary accounts of the fateful night at the Pullman Hotel in East Melbourne last month, police can seek to interview them again at any time. In a statement on Wednesday, Victoria Police confirmed three women had made a report about the night and detectives had this week travelled to Sydney to speak to four people. “That process has now concluded,” the statement read. “Investigators also spoke to or will speak to three men believed to be in the hotel room at the time of the incident, who are being treated solely as witnesses at this time.



“Police now believe they have now identified all parties who were in the room at the time of the alleged incident and are not looking for anyone further.” Riley Bice’s manager and the Sydney Swans refused to comment. More to come Be the first to know when major news happens.

World.title: ‘Gaping holes’: North Melbourne give reasons for Clarkson’s sacking
World.content:
North Melbourne have sacked coach Alastair Clarkson after four seasons and with a year remaining on his contract citing “gaping holes” in an inconsistent game plan and muddied messages to players. Players were recalled from leave for an emergency meeting on Wednesday morning to be told the coach had been sacked. Loading Clarkson was told of the club’s decision on Tuesday after a post-season consultation period during which North bosses sought the views of the football department and players, two sources confirmed. In a brutally frank press conference, the club said North’s game plan under Clarkson had “gaping holes” in it, that they failed to implement a modern game style, and that there was muddied messages to players.



North’s football manager, Todd Viney, Clarkson’s long-time friend and ally who came to the club with the coach, said the feedback from players was that the more pressure Clarkson felt, the harder he worked and the more confused the messaging became. Club president Sonja Hood and Viney told the press conference at Arden Street on Wednesday that leadership’s view was that the Kangaroos had made progress under Clarkson, but they needed to extract more from a talented group. When asked what kind of coach North Melbourne needed, Hood said, “One that could coach for the modern game.”



Viney said the game plan was inconsistent, and the club needed a coach who would align the team to modern football.



“I think if there was one thing that Clarko did was he tried too hard in trying to fix that, and then therefore what happens is we get into more meetings, more information, and the players at the end of the day become a little bit confused, and we don’t get the cohesion that we need to win more games,” Viney explained. “There’s still parts of our game plan that we haven’t been able to improve in the four years, and that’s some stuff that we need to get right when we talk to the next coach to bring us in line with where the modern game is right at the moment.”



When asked what the playing group’s reaction was to the news, Hood said they were sad.



“They’re also really excited about what could come in the future,” she said.



In a letter to club members, Hood said it had become clear that “Alastair no longer has the belief from enough people at the club that he is the right coach to take this group forward”. “Once we knew that, it felt disrespectful to him to have him coach into 2027, knowing we would not extend him at the end of that,” Hood wrote. Alastair Clarkson is leaving North Melbourne. Getty Images “Our culture among the players, staff and coaches is undeniably strong, but we need a consistently clear and concise on-field strategy to sit alongside that.” Clarkson issued a statement via his management.



“My time as coach of the North Melbourne Football Club has come to an end,” he said. “We set out to stabilise the club and lay the foundations for a return to playing deep in September. “The challenge was a difficult one that I embraced with my whole being. “My family and I have been privileged to be involved in AFL football for over 40 years, but it is now time for a new chapter.”



Clarkson, who coached Hawthorn to four premierships before departing at the end of the 2020 season, has been with the Kangaroos since his appointment in late 2022. The Roos finished 14th this year with nine wins and 14 losses. They had been in the top 10 with eight wins on June 21 but slumped out of finals contention since. It was their highest result under Clarkson after finishes of 17th in his first two years in charge and 16th in 2025. “We asked Alastair to give our club stability and strength and help return us to the top of the AFL ladder,” Hood said.



Related Article AFL 2026 ‘This is on me, not the club’: Alastair Clarkson opens up on the Roos’ plight “Four years later, we have created an environment where our staff and players want to be at our club. This is a testament to the culture Alastair has helped create and the belief that he has built in this group. “Although we have clearly made progress and won more games, we won’t shy away from our desire to want more from this talented group. “We are incredibly grateful to Alastair for the work he’s done over the last four years and we wish him all the very best for his next chapter.” Viney, Clarkson’s longtime lieutenant and friend, will remain at the club and is expected to be part of the coach search process.



North Melbourne players were spotted emerging from the Roos’ facilities at Arden Street after the meeting but would not comment beyond expressing excitement for next season. As previously reported by this masthead, Clarkson signed a five-year deal worth more than $5 million when he agreed to return to his former club and has a contract that essentially guarantees him the full amount of his 2027 contract, according to sources with knowledge of the deal. North Melbourne, who have received the highest amount of variable funding from the AFL of Victorian clubs over the past two years (surpassing St Kilda who had long held that mantle), have been a relatively frugal club since the 2000s. The Roos wiped off their debt and enjoyed repeated financial benefits from their stint of playing home games in Hobart and now Western Australia. External discussion of Clarkson’s position and future has included the fact that Adam Simpson and John Longmire – both Kangaroos playing greats who went on to coach AFL premierships at other clubs – are not presently employed as senior coaches.



Other potential targets could include Corey Enright and Jaymie Graham, who were contenders for the Carlton and Essendon jobs, respectively, before Josh Fraser and Mark McVeigh were appointed by those clubs. In March, Clarkson told this masthead he was all for someone else taking the top job at North Melbourne if they were better placed for a quicker return to premiership contention. “I came back here to help the footy club. [It’s] nothing to do with ego, nothing to do with anything else except repay to North what they gave to me as a young fellow,” he said. North had not guaranteed Clarkson’s position when pressed on whether he would coach in 2027 as contracted. Western Bulldogs coach Luke Beveridge was shocked when he was told of Clarkson’s fate midway through his press conference on Wednesday.



Related Article AFL 2026 Clarkson’s clause: Frugal Roos would face huge payout if they axed coach early “Really?” Beveridge said. “Jeez.” Beveridge served as an assistant coach under Clarkson at Hawthorn in 2012-14 when the Hawks won two flags and were narrowly beaten by Sydney in a grand final. The Dogs coach said the constant scrutiny on senior coaches right from the start of their tenure was “disconcerting”, even if he accepted it came with the territory. “The difficult thing with what we’re all doing is it’s a different culture now in our code,” Beveridge said.



“We’ve almost become like the EPL where senior coaches’ tenure and your own coaching mortality is speculated about a lot more than it used to be, as opposed to say the NFL, where you can have a winning season and that’s considered a success. “What I’m concerned about is the next generation of senior coaches. Do they actually really want to put them in the situation where, from the start of their tenure, their vocational sustainability is speculated upon? It’s not a nice place to live.” Beveridge paid tribute to Clarkson’s coaching career. “Clarko’s been an amazing coach, amazing custodian of the game, and obviously really outspoken, and someone who’s pushed his own opinions to make the game better,” Beveridge said. Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: Jail time for man who made deepfake images of schoolgirls
World.content:
NationalQueenslandCrime Jail time for man who made deepfake images of schoolgirls Andrew Stafford and Rex Martinich September 2, 2026 — 4:22pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A mother has revealed her anguish over how and when to tell her young daughter she had been targeted by a deepfake image creator who distributed sexualised pictures. A string of women and schoolgirls shared their stories in court, after AI-rendered nudes or sexualised pictures were emailed by former software developer Antonio Rotondo. One took immediate security precautions in their home after discovering the images, while others spoke of the costs of psychological counselling and the stress of the legal process. Rotondo represented himself at trial after pleading not guilty. Dan Peled “What frightens me is knowing that an ordinary photograph can be taken out of my control and transformed into sexual material without my consent,” a victim said.



Rotondo was sentenced to jail on Wednesday after a Brisbane jury found him guilty of 11 counts of stalking. He was also found guilty of five counts of distributing intimate images and one count of distributing child exploitation material involving an image of a 13-year-old girl modified to be sexually “degrading”. The 13-year-old’s mother was among the heartbreaking victim impact statements shared in Brisbane District Court on Wednesday, detailing the toll of being targeted by the 56-year-old. Her teenager has not seen the offensive image. But the mother now feels burdened with keeping that secret and wrestles with how to best tell her about the crime when she was old enough. Rotondo had downloaded public images of female staff and students from a prestigious Queensland school and models who had taken part in a fashion show.



He modified the images to include nudity or sexualised elements using an AI deepfake program, emailing them to the administrators of multiple schools and the fashion event in September 2023. Victims on Wednesday said it impacted not only themselves but also their families. They spoke of feeling humiliated and violated on what were meant to be nights of celebration and personal pride. One said she did not blame the technology, but the people who misused it. “I do not want to be afraid of photography, being photographed or sharing photographs,” she wrote. “Being visible is an important part of my life, my work and the way I express myself.”



Rotondo, who represented himself at trial after pleading not guilty, argued on sentence that he should have faced only two charges, as he only distributed two emails. He also claimed his conduct was not criminal at the time he engaged in it. But Judge John Allen told Rotondo his clear lack of remorse and insight into his offending meant he had to consider other means of deterrence. “It’s a common feature of the victim impact statements that the effects of your offending continue to this day,” he said. Allen, however, found the images fell short of the type of extreme depravity often the subject of such charges.



Rotondo was sentenced to two years in jail. A jury had found Rotondo guilty on Tuesday following a six-day trial. AAP Get alerts on significant breaking news as happens.

World.title: Chalmers backs assault on big tech as Contos sounds alarm on manosphere
World.content:
PoliticsFederalSocial media Chalmers backs assault on big tech as Contos sounds alarm on manosphere Brittany Busch September 2, 2026 — 4:22pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Treasurer Jim Chalmers backs a crackdown on social media algorithms serving “rubbish” to children, as consent advocate Chanel Contos urges the government to better protect young boys from being sucked into the online manosphere. Chalmers became the latest cabinet minister to weigh in on the persistent dangers posed by harmful social media content on Wednesday, after Social Services Minister Tanya Plibersek last weekend sounded the alarm on the prevalence of sexual choking in online pornography. Treasurer Jim Chalmers said algorithms were feeding “rubbish” to kids online. Alex Ellinghausen “I find it really disturbing the rubbish that is fed to our kids, and to our population more broadly, with these algorithms,” Chalmers said on Wednesday. “It’s self-evident that social media, and particularly the way these social media algorithms work, are not doing us a lot of good.” Algorithms push content into users’ social media feeds based on their online activity and personal data. Advocates like Contos are calling for default feeds to be algorithm-free.



Labor is strengthening its attack on big tech after Prime Minister Anthony Albanese flagged online safety as a key platform for a third term, with cabinet considering mandating an algorithm opt-out function in its impending digital duty of care reforms. Global momentum to regulate big tech is building after Australia’s teen social media ban, the European Union’s crackdown on algorithms, and Meta’s landmark $25 billion settlement in the United States that also extracted promises from the tech giant to limit its appeal to children. Chanel Contos at the press club on Wednesday afternoon. Alex Ellinghausen But reform has proven difficult. Many Australian teens remain on social media, and in Europe, tech companies complied with an opt-out mandate, but disincentivised uptake by limiting other features, sparking a lawsuit in the Netherlands and an investigation by Ireland’s tech regulator. Nationals leader Matt Canavan agreed online content was toxic, but blamed the “feminisation of our curriculum” for driving young boys towards it.



“They’re sick and tired of getting lectures about how bad men are at school, and so they go to other places,” Canavan told Nine’s Today. “They’re sick and tired of the feminisation of our curriculum and the lack of direction and leadership that they’re given. Maybe we should look at getting more male teachers in,” he said, adding boys felt patronised, not cherished, at school. Nationals leader Matt Canavan. Alex Ellinghausen Contos, who shot to national prominence in 2021 by documenting sexual violence in Sydney schools and successfully campaigned to mandate annual consent education in schools, said the consent curriculum was about promoting healthy intimacy. “It is absolutely not an attack on men or boys at all. It’s to make their sex lives happier and healthier and their relationships better,” the Teach Us Consent chief executive said when asked about Canavan’s comments following a National Press Club address in Canberra on Wednesday.



“But of course, we also need to hold all of that while acknowledging that sexual violence is majority perpetrated by boys and men, and that shouldn’t be shameful for the individual, but it should mean that they’re willing to be part of a system to change that statistic.” Related Article Exclusive

Privacy Albanese attacks algorithm but no ban for ‘pervert glasses’ in privacy overhaul Greens communications spokeswoman Sarah Hanson-Young accused Canavan of stoking a culture war and criticised him for blaming female teachers for boys behaving badly. “Senator Canavan has shown himself to be a fool when talking about these issues,” she told reporters in Canberra. The Greens have backed Contos’ call for the government to go further on reining in social media by requiring algorithms to be opt-in.



In her speech, Contos said algorithms were preying on the insecurities of boys, funnelling them from lifestyle and dating advice into misogynistic content. She said research indicated that it took just 23 minutes for a new male social media profile to be served up misogynistic content, as teen boys overtake men as the most likely to perpetrate child sexual abuse. Related Article Opinion

Cyber bullying If we’re serious about social cohesion, these big tech hate machines must be reined in Chanel Contos Founder of Teach Us Consent “We owe it to our boys and young men to not hand-deliver them to an industry that takes their valid concerns, fuels the fire with unfounded grievance, and then extracts their strong emotions for profit,” she said. Contos is calling for social media feeds to be limited to the pages deliberately followed by users and presented chronologically, with the option to switch on an algorithm to feed them curated suggested content. Contos said social media companies’ business model was to push content that would keep eyes on screens longer, rather than what people would choose to see.



“Our screen time fills big tech’s pockets, and the more outraged we are, the more time we spend on their screens,” she said. Contos conceded people would still choose to use the social media algorithm, but said it was about giving them a choice. “As a society, we put parameters around other addictive substances like gambling, alcohol, and smoking, and people still do those things,” she said. “But we’re trying to make it safer.” Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. World.title: Chalmers admits tax reforms helped drag down house prices
World.content:
Breaking PoliticsFederalAustralian economy Chalmers admits tax reforms helped drag down house prices Shane Wright Updated September 2, 2026 — 4:21pm ,first published 11:58am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Treasurer Jim Chalmers has admitted the government’s budget overhaul of property-tax concessions is contributing to the fall in home values as a new snapshot of the economy shows cash-pressed consumers are splurging on EVs but giving up their overseas holiday plans. As private sector economists forecast property values to continue falling through the rest of this year and well into 2027, Chalmers said higher interest rates and the turmoil facing the economy from the war in Iran were also adding to downward pressure on home prices. The June quarter national accounts, released on Wednesday, showed the economy expanded by 0.4 per cent, taking annual growth down from 2.5 per cent to 2.1 per cent. Half of the growth was due to a lift in household spending with most of that coming through a record purchase of new cars.



The bureau noted that there was a record sale of EVs and hybrids as people sought to avoid the surge in oil prices caused by the US’s war against Iran and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz. Spending on transport actually fell, due to the lift in pump prices. The surge in EV purchases has continued into the current quarter. Figures from the Electric Vehicle Council covering Tesla and Polestar showed another rise in purchases through August to be 91 per cent up on the same period last year. It said other areas of discretionary spending were “subdued” due to rising cost-of-living pressures. This was most evident with a sharp drop in international tourism, as Australians abandoned their northern-summer plans for travel to Europe and the United States. People buying EVs and hybrids was a major contributor to GDP growth in the June quarter. Bloomberg Essential spending also fell, particularly on electricity and gas caused by the warmer-than-normal winter.



Home construction continues to grow, up by 1.6 per cent in the quarter to be 5.8 per cent stronger over the past year to be at its highest level since early 2019. But there are doubts how much longer the lift in new-home builds can continue given the slowdown in the overall property market, the increase in the cost of construction – which is partly due to the surge in oil prices and strong demand – and the government’s budget tax measures. Chalmers, who noted Australia remained equal with the US as one of the fastest-growing economies in the world, described the overall result as “robust” given the headwinds facing the economy. Pressed on forecasts by the Commonwealth Bank that property prices could fall by as much as 13 per cent in Sydney, Chalmers said the budget changes in areas such as negative gearing and capital gains tax were weighing on the market along with other factors. “We’ve said on a number of occasions that that is not the only factor. It’s a factor but not the only factor, and the evidence of that,” he said.



“What is too frequently ignored, is that house prices and auction clearance rates were softening before the budget, and that’s because of movements in interest rates and developments in the economy more broadly.” Related Article Property prices $40,000 wiped off the value of the average house over winter Shadow treasurer Tim Wilson accused Chalmers of deliberately trying to tank the property market. “This was by design. This is the economy that Labor has designed,” he told News24. The bureau said there was also growth due to public demand and net trade thanks to a lift in exports. It was the first positive contribution to growth from the trade sector since late 2023.



Private investment, which was a key factor in the March quarter, was flat in the June quarter due to a sharp fall in the imports of data processing equipment used in new data centres. But business investment was flat despite firms continuing to construct new buildings for data centres. There was also a lift in engineering construction for new renewable and mining projects. There continued to be concerning signs about the nation’s economic foundations. Productivity was flat in the quarter to be down by 0.2 per cent over the full year. Unit labour costs jumped by 0.9 per cent in the quarter to be 0.5 per cent higher since June last year. The Commonwealth Bank’s head of Australian economics, Belinda Allen, is one who expects the overall economy to slow as investment in new homes ebbs as interest rate increases bite and property prices ease. “But this will not be enough to stop another interest rate hike from the RBA in November given recent inflation data indicating upside risks have materialised,” she said.



Sunny Nguyen, Moody’s Analytics head of Australia economics, said the figures confirmed that higher interest are biting into households’ spending plans. She said while household nominal income grew by 1.5 per cent in the quarter, they had only spent 0.4 per cent of it. “In the March quarter, they drew on savings buffers to cover essentials; now they are rebuilding them,” she said. EY Australia chief economist Cherelle Murphy said the economy’s long-term problems had been exposed by the figures. “Australia’s economy is caught between resilient demand and weak supply-side performance. These national accounts will do little to ease the Reserve Bank’s concerns about the inflation outlook, and we continue to expect that another rate rise will soon be delivered,” she said. World.title: AI jobs war erupts at Sydney university as staff walk out
World.content:
NationalNSWEducation AI jobs war erupts at Sydney university as staff walk out David Barwell September 2, 2026 — 4:12pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Classrooms at the University of Sydney’s Camperdown campus fell unusually quiet on Wednesday as hundreds of staff walked off the job amid a growing dispute over artificial intelligence, workloads and job security. Up to 600 staff members established picket lines across campus entrances as part of a 24-hour strike, forcing most classes online and shutting laboratories. The action, led by the National Tertiary Education Union (NTEU), highlights mounting tensions across higher education as universities increasingly integrate AI into teaching. Academics at the University of Sydney walked off the job on Wednesday. Dominic Lorrimer Alongside claims for a 20 per cent pay rise and 17 per cent superannuation for casual staff, the union is seeking legally binding protections governing artificial intelligence, including guarantees AI will not be used to cut jobs or replace human interaction in teaching. NTEU NSW secretary Vince Caughley said academics were already seeing AI avatars and chatbots used in course delivery.



“For us, it’s not simply about our jobs. It’s about the nature of what a university is,” Caughley said. The University of Sydney has positioned itself as one of Australia’s most enthusiastic adopters of AI, with academics using its custom-built platform Cogniti to create chatbots and interactive learning tools. NTEU USYD branch president Peter Chen and NTEU NSW state secretary Vince Caughley speak during the rally. Dominic Lorrimer Tensions escalated after the university released a discussion paper last month outlining a future in which AI could provide personalised learning support to students while reducing staff-student contact hours. The proposal intensified concerns among academics that automated systems could eventually lead to job cuts and fewer staff teaching larger student cohorts.



Computer science lecturer Alan Fekete, who has taught at the university for 38 years, said staff were already managing heavier workloads. “The fact that they keep putting up the work we have to do, and having fewer people to do it, increases the stress and increases the risks of losing one’s job,” Fekete said. The strike resulted in most classes taught online on Wednesday. Sitthixay Ditthavong As part of enterprise bargaining negotiations, the union is also seeking consultation over AI deployment, transparency around algorithms and the right for staff to challenge automated decisions. The university, in a statement, described the strike action as “premature” and said it was committed to engaging at the bargaining table.



“Human judgment, accountability and relationships are essential to everything we do, and can never be replaced by technology,” the spokeswoman said. Staff at the University of Sydney set up picket lines on Wednesday, Sitthixay Ditthavong The strike comes as universities grapple with broader financial pressures. Despite generating $1.7 billion in international student revenue last financial year, the University of Sydney’s surplus fell from $545 million to $194 million. Related Article Exclusive

AI Thousands of University of Sydney staff to strike over AI Student Dana Kafina, who joined the picket lines, argued growing reliance on AI-generated content risks diminishing the quality of education.



“Some of my main units have lecture materials that are made with just AI,” she said. “It makes it feel impersonal, but also that the quality of learning isn’t as good for students who are paying up to $50,000 in fees.” NTEU branch president Peter Chen warned universities could become the “canary in the coal mine” for the wider workforce. “For those asking why I should care about university teachers on strike, my message is: AI is coming for you as well.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: China’s flood rescue is a no-go zone for foreign media, what does it have to hide?
World.content:
Analysis WorldAsiaFloods China’s flood rescue is a no-go zone for foreign media, what does it have to hide? Lisa Visentin September 2, 2026 — 4:07pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Beijing: Late last Wednesday night, a Tibet Daily reporter filmed a video from inside his car as it pelted down China’s National Highway 219 in heavy rain. He was racing from Lhasa, the capital of the Tibet Autonomous Region, to Gyirong Port at the border with Nepal where a great human tragedy was unfolding. Rescuers observe a moment of silence for the victims of the mudslide near the Gyirong Port in Gyirong County, in southwestern China’s Tibet Autonomous Region. Jigme Dorje/Xinhua via AP They were due to arrive at the port – or what was left of it – around 4am, he explained, their 14-hour drive delayed by the severe weather. “Upon arrival, we will bring you the latest updates on the disaster situation and emergency relief efforts at the scene as soon as possible”, the reporter said in the video posted to Tibet Daily’s WeChat account, a Chinese social media platform.



Loading By that stage, the world had seen the first video of the gargantuan wall of mud and ice that had ripped through the immigration crossing that morning at the Tibet-Nepal border, swallowing everything in its path. That clip would soon be scrubbed from the Chinese internet by censors. The scale of the event would become more apparent in coming days, but by then it was already clear than many people were dead. This scramble – dropping everything and running towards the disaster – is a universal journalistic imperative. It’s what is expected of journalists, especially when your country’s citizens are caught up in tragedy. Credit where it’s due to the Tibet Daily journos. But it’s an imperative the Chinese government has denied foreign journalists like me, despite repeated requests for access to the Gyirong area where there are, based on China’s own figures, five Australians among the more than 500 missing.



On Tuesday, I posed the question again to China’s Foreign Ministry at a press conference in Beijing: why is China refusing access to foreign reporters seeking to cover this tragedy alongside Chinese state media from the disaster zone on the Tibetan side? Related Article Floods Second Australian found after Nepal disaster, ‘grave concerns’ for 42 still missing as death toll passes 1000 I’m far from alone. Other journalists working for international media outlets in China have also sought access. With more than 260 foreigners from 23 countries among the missing, this is a not a mere internal China issue. It took on more significance for Australia on Tuesday, when one of our own was confirmed alive in Tibet. The ministry’s response – essentially, it is too unsafe – is clearly undermined by the authorised presence of local media reporting from nearby the flood ravaged areas.



“Road and communication in the affected area is currently cut off, and there is a significant safety risk of secondary disasters,” spokesman Guo Jiakun said. “Rescue efforts are being carried out in [an] intensive and orderly manner, and we will continue to release the latest information on the disaster situation and rescue operations.” Compare China’s approach with what’s happening in Nepal, which has borne the brunt of the catastrophe, and where the world’s press have amassed since Wednesday. Among them is this masthead’s South East Asia correspondent Zach Hope who dispatched with haste from Singapore, joined by photographer Kate Geraghty from Sydney. They’ve reported harrowing tales of survival amid the devastation. Over the past few days, I have watched clips of state media reporters from the likes of Tibet Daily, Xinhua and China Central Television reporting from the disaster zone, standing on muddy embankments as they carry the government’s message about access and rescue efforts, while tractors work in the background. I don’t wish to impugn the personal dedication or professionalism of these reporters. They are doing gruelling work in challenging conditions, and against the backdrop of mounting casualties, although China has only reported 16 dead so far.



But their reporting is ultimately heavily controlled by their masters: the Chinese government. All state media outlets are regulated by the Publicity Department of the Central Committee of the Chinese Communist Party – better known by its original name, the Central Propaganda Department. We won’t be hearing or seeing anything from those reporters that hasn’t been vetted by editorial staff whose foremost loyalty is to the party’s version of the truth. Chinese rescuers prepare before heading to the mudslide-stricken area near Gyirong Port, Tibet. Xinhua via AP Chinese President Xi Jinping laid out his expectations for state media during a 2016 tour of their newsrooms. “All news media run by the party must work to speak for the party’s will and its propositions, and protect the party’s authority and unity,” state outlet Xinhua quoted Xi as saying at the time.



It may well be that China has a good story to tell about its search and rescue efforts in Tibet. It has massive military resources and advanced scientific equipment, that it can – and says it has – deployed, including troops, aircraft carriers, and drones. But given China’s obsessive control over information, its fixation on positive coverage, and the absence of independent reporters, how can the world be confident it is getting the most full and accurate picture possible of what is happening on the Tibet side of the border? We should also question why almost no survivor accounts have emerged organically on social media from Tibetans or others who have made narrow escapes. What’s this really about? China has long imposed an effective ban on foreign press entering Tibet, rarely granting the permits needed to enter the region unless for closely monitored government-coordinated trips. It’s part of the Beijing’s broader effort to strictly control Tibet, which has sporadically erupted with protests and self-immolation among Tibetans who have pushed for autonomy since China annexed Tibet in the 1950s.

World.title: Floating rates rise after official cash rate increase
World.content:
Westpac says it is increasing variable interest rates for borrowers and some savers, after Wednesday's increase to the official cash rate.

The OCR was lifted by 25 basis points, to 2.75 percent.

Westpac's variable home and business lending rates will increase by 0.25 percent, effective Monday for new customers and Thursday for existing customers.

Its Bonus Saver and Business Online Saver, will also increase by the same amount from Monday.

"New Zealanders have shown resilience in the face of cost pressures and uncertainty, and our data suggests they remain well-placed to manage further rate rises," said managing director of product, sustainability and marketing, Sarah Hearn.

"Most of our home loan customers are on fixed rates and there are no changes for them today.

Is there any point in KiwiSaver if I'm on a total remuneration package? No Stupid Questions with Susan Edmunds Download MP3 10m

"However, we recognise some customers will be worried about rising rates. We're here to help borrowers and savers manage their money through an increasing OCR cycle and we encourage them to contact us if they need any help or advice."

Mortgage adviser Campbell Hastie said few borrowers would be surprised by the OCR increase.

"We were all expecting the rate to go up... I don't think anyone wants to hear that interest rates have gone up but I think there is a general expectation that this is going to happen and it'll eventually flow through into fixed rates.

"I think that's what people are expecting. Whether it happens or not is a different question but I don't think it's going to be a surprise to anyone."

He said interest rates were unlikely to rise enough to go back to their levels of two years ago.

"It's more than what it was six months ago but not like what it was two or three years ago."

Cotality chief property economist said the increase was not likely to have much of an effect on the housing market.

"The mood amongst buyers and sellers certainly remains fairly cautious, and those with mortgages will be wary of the recent interest rate increases on popular terms such as the two-year fix," he said.

"That being said, although floating rates may well shift higher to some extent after today's OCR rise, it's arguably already been priced in to prevailing fixed rates, so they might not show too much movement in the coming days.

"Of course, looking out over the next few months, there still seems a greater likelihood of higher mortgage rates rather than flat or down.

"The resilience of employment ...will tend to offset the housing effects of higher interest rates to a degree. But the looming election is another key factor at the moment, especially for property investors as they wait any indications from the opposition about interest deductibility."

World.title: Almost 50 jobs could go at National Library and Archives, PSA warns
World.content:
A proposal to cut 12 percent of the workforce at the National Library and Archives NZ will decimate both organisations and have a significant impact on service levels, says the Public Service Association (PSA).

The PSA said staff on Wednesday learned of the restructure proposal to cut 47 full time equivalent roles.

The proposed job cuts come on top of previous job cuts, and the PSA estimated that if the the plan goes ahead, the total workforce at both organisations will be 15 percent smaller than it was two years ago, with 350 staff.

The PSA said it understood the proposed cuts were to take effect as of 30 November.

The PSA said the Department of Internal Affairs (DIA) itself admitted to staff today that the cuts "will likely have impacts on service levels".

Chief Archivist Anahera Morehu and National Librarian Rachel Esson said in a joint statement to RNZ that they were currently consulting on a proposed organisational change affecting the National Library and Archives NZ.

"Supporting and engaging with our people is a priority. We are focused on delivering better public value for money and delivering customer needs in new and more sustainable ways.

"The proposal is part of our internal process and no final decisions have been made," the statement said.

PSA national secretary Fleur Fitzsimons said police, the courts and the health system, which all rely on records kept by archives NZ, will also be impacted, as well as people's ability to access their own records.

"It will be questionable whether basic legal requirements around record keeping can be met if cuts go ahead.

"This proposal would decimate National Library and Archives, and we oppose it," she said.

"This should not be occurring 10 weeks out from a general election, we are calling on DIA and the government to stop this in its tracks," she added.

PSA national secretary Duane Leo said the proposed cuts were an attack on New Zealand's precious Taonga.

"Our dedicated archivists, researchers and others are paying the price for that when they have more to give, and more valuable work to do for all of us as collections grow. It makes no sense," he said.

He said the DIA admitting in writing that its own cuts will hurt the public showed the "truth is laid out in black and white" that it was on the government.

The PSA said workers were concerned that the plan would make it more likely that they could only do the bare minimum of critical work required under the legislation - putting at risk the access to and the preservation of millions of precious items that spoke to Aotearoa's history.

It said workers feared that the cataloguing backlog will grow, and families, historians and genealogists will face delays accessing items, or not be able to find items. Researchers' capacity to help people researching family histories, writing books and understanding the past, will also be affected.

Leo said AI would not be able to plug the gaps, as the government promised.

"AI won't be able catalogue the ever-growing collection of material donated to Archives. AI won't be able to help people navigate millions of records.

World.title: Parent questions delay after Kaikōura school bus route restored
World.content:
A Kaikōura school bus route has been reinstated using a four-wheel-drive bus, two months after the inland highway was damaged by flooding, with one parent questioning why it was not able to happen sooner.

The Cribb Creek Bridge was damaged during heavy rain on 7 July and the road was closed, before re-opening to four-wheel-drive access a week later. A temporary road has been built across Cribb Creek, but permanent repairs to the road are estimated to take six months.

Parent Bub Taylor said getting her children to school was a 106km round trip and, for the last two months, several other families on the Inland Road had faced a long commute or were staying with friends in Kaikōura.

She had asked both the Ministry of Education and the bus operator if a four-wheel-drive bus could be used so it could travel the full route, but had no success.

"Everybody just kept fobbing me off when I asked the obvious."

About six weeks after the road first closed, with the help of the Kaikōura District Council and Blenheim Toyota, the families were loaned a Hiace van. Taylor said they created a roster of drivers, with up to eight children picked up and dropped off each morning to meet the school bus near the washed-out Cribb Creek Bridge.

Days after the van service got underway, the Ministry of Education said the bus operator would trial a four-wheel-drive bus to see if it could reinstate the route.

Taylor was driving the van on Tuesday morning and had picked up four of the children when she came across the school bus sitting at its first stop, much to her surprise.

"The bus is now reinstated which is fantastic and we're really thrilled, but we should never have gotten to this point, we shouldn't have had to wait that many weeks for an answer and we certainly shouldn't have had to go public with the story to get some action."

The parents were responsible for the cost of fuelling the van and Taylor said they had sought funding, which had been provided by a local business and Fern Energy.

"It's so frustrating because we'd just gone and got thousands of dollars worth of fuel funding and now I'm having to go back to those fuel companies and say, thank you so much, we're so grateful, but you can have it back now."

Taylor said the van had been loaned to them for six months and they would keep it as a backup in case there was any further heavy rain or damage to the road.

Ministry of Education general manager for school transport James Meffan said the bus operator trialled a four-wheel-drive bus on Monday and the full route was reinstated on Tuesday.

He said any questions about the trial or its timing should be directed to the operator.

World.title: Dunedin City Councillor Benedict Ong to be trespassed from Otago University Students' Association premises
World.content:
The Otago University Students' Association plans to trespass controversial Dunedin City Councillor Benedict Ong from its premises after reports from students of inappropriate and unwanted behaviour.

The association's president Daniel Leamy said it took student wellbeing seriously and was taking action to ensure students feel safe and supported.

The association wanted the University of Otago to follow suit and trespass Ong from the campus.

A university spokesperson said it was in discussions with the association and was not in a position to comment.

In a social media post, Ong described the move as a "politically motivated false attack" because "of the support I have across our community and a number of my statements in my posts".

He attached an image of himself with a group of young women and performers from the University of Otago Capping Show at what appears to be the Dunedin student bar U-Bar.

In May, Ong was suspended from all committees and subcommittees for nine months because of concerns about his behaviour.

He faced a code of conduct complaint after revealing details about a potential hotel development at Forsyth Barr Stadium to reporters in April.

Last month, Ong was kicked out of a council meeting discussing its amalgamation plans and, in the weeks leading up to that, had been asked to leave a University of Otago student protest and a health debate hosted by the Big Hairy Network.

Speaking to RNZ after the council meeting, Ong said he had been "wrongfully barred, blocked and banned" from his right to vote.

On 29 July, Education Action Group 26 organised a protest and sit-in at the university's St David's complex to protest against tertiary education cuts.

Spokesperson Annabel Hankin said Ong was among many others who put their hands up to speak in response to a question during the sit-in.

When he was not selected, he stood up and spoke loudly before being told to settle down and not to interrupt others.

She described his behaviour as "a little bit disorderly and distracting", but that it was "pretty harmless" and easily dealt with.

World.title: Water leak found near Seddon after 3000 cubic metres lost
World.content:
The leak in a Marlborough water main has been identified after about 3000 cubic metres of water was lost.

About 750 residents in rural Marlborough were asked to conserve water after the major leak was discovered late on Tuesday night.

The council said the location of the leak was identified on Wednesday afternoon in the 225mm water main, about two kilometres southwest of Seddon on Marama Road.

Marlborough Waters chief executive Richard Coningham said the good news was that the leak was not under the Awatere River bed as previously thought, making the repair much more straightforward.

"However we are not through the woods yet and it is still important that people in Seddon and on the Awatere Rural network conserve their water use as much as possible."

Council engineers are investigating whether there are any other leaks on the network.

Water had been trucked into the Awatere area since 8.30am on Wednesday after about 3000 cubic metres of water, more than the volume of an Olympic-sized swimming pool, was lost.

Residents around Seddon were asked to urgently conserve water after the Rural Awatere water supply storage tanks ran dry and the Seddon water supply tank fell to about 40 percent capacity.

The additional water was helping to maintain supply, but conserving water remained extremely important because of supply constraints, Coningham said.

"Trucking water into the area means we can begin replenishing both the rural Awatere tanks and the Seddon tank while crews continue working on the leak," Coningham said.

"However, we still need everyone connected to these supplies to use as little water as possible. Please keep water use to essential drinking, cooking and hygiene needs and avoid all non-essential use."

People in Seddon are advised to boil water as a precaution and those on the rural Awatere supply remain under a long-standing boil-water notice.

Coningham said the precautionary boil-water notice was necessary for Seddon because, while the trucked-in water was safe, some of it was food grade and not classed as potable grade under water regulations.

Water should be brought to a rolling boil for at least one minute and allowed to cool naturally before use. The notices will remain in place until the council advises otherwise.

The council will continue trucking water into the area as required and is closely monitoring storage levels.

The pipe supplied Seddon, Seaview, Grassmere and rural areas south of the Awatere River.

World.title: Ellerslie homicide: Accused's church friend went to pastor over murder plot, court told
World.content:
Lok Fung Lorrence Li roped in a church friend to help him murder his landlady and the friend told his pastor, says the Crown.

Li is on trial for the murders of Auckland couple Fuk-Fu Joseph Kwok and his wife Mei Han Chong in 2023.

He is also charged with conspiring to murder his former landlord.

A jury heard today that the man Li allegedly plotted with told a church leader about the alleged murder plot on his landlord, two months before the Kwoks were killed.

Li's former landlord - who can not be named - gave evidence today through an interpreter about some paint which mysteriously appeared on her security cameras, just days before the Kwoks were killed.

"My husband saw the paint on the ground and the camera, and then asked me to come out and have a look, so we also noticed the sensor lights were painted," she said.

The Crown said Li and another man - Shu Man Poon - went to the landlord's home with murder on their mind, but were spooked off.

Poon pleaded guilty to his role in the Kwok killings, and was expected to give evidence later in the trial.

Jurors later heard from Shing Shan Yim, a part-time pastor of Li and Poon's church.

Speaking through an interpreter, Yim said he visited an anxious Poon in September 2023, with another pastor.

"Poon is owing somebody some money, and forcing him to do something as part of the favour," Yim was told.

He said it was Lorrence Li, another member of their church, who he owed money to.

Poon showed him a weapon, and said he was being made to rob someone.

"He mentioned about going to tie them up then rob their money."

During the confessional, Poon was called by Li. The call was put on speaker phone where the church leaders heard Poon pleading with Li not to go ahead with the plan.

"We shouldn't do this, and we should stop right now," Poon said.

Yim and the other pastor convinced Poon to go to the police, driving him to the Auckland Central station.

In the Crown's opening, jurors heard Poon told police he was $7000 in debt to Li, and that Li said he could clear the debt by taking part in the alleged murder.

"Mr Poon told that front-counter staff member he'd been trying to deter Mr Li from the plan but felt the only way out was to kill himself," Crown Prosecutor Harrison Bell said.

"He mentioned he had been struggling with his mental health and that he'd taken a bunch of pills and began crying out in pain, clutching his head."

He was taken to hospital, and the date of the alleged planned murder was pushed out.

It was later in early November that year that the pair allegedly went to the landlord's property, days before the Kwoks were killed.

World.title: MP Paulo Garcia valedictory: 'Let hateful words be the undoing of those who wield them.'
World.content:
In one of two farewell speeches from retiring MPs this week, two-term National Party MP Paulo Garcia - the first ethnic Filipino to be elected to New Zealand's Parliament - brought both thanks and also a gentle admonition to his colleagues.

Paulo Garcia : ‘Let hateful words be the undoing of those who wield them.’ The House Download MP3 6m

Along with the more usual gratitude, thanks and humble pride to be a representative of his community, Garcia raised the uglier side of politics, including isolation, and the personal and physical implications of hate.

"I've almost been run over, threatened, had cans thrown at me, and [been] attacked while in my car. My wife and I have had to move house. It isn't real until it happens to you. This takes an emotional toll for some more than others. It threatens our peace."

He drew a direct line between this violence and the language used by some in politics.

"Parliament is a study in human behaviour and motivations. It's also a reflection of the public. Instead of thriving in our shared humanity, some choose to condemn and divide. Language is weaponised to foster hate and division and doubt and suspicion. Many of the public, often the most vulnerable, hear words spoken in this House, take them, and action that hate."

The Hansard record of Paulo Garcia's full valedictory statement is below.

It is such a privilege to be able to stand again, this time to do a valedictory. I went through a range of emotions preparing this speech. I hope to convey only the best of those emotions: my wonderment, my gratitude, and my joy.

My wonderment at actually being a member of Parliament in New Zealand-my mother and father, visiting in winter 2006, soon after my family had just arrived, saw how we needed to ration heat in our rented home. Fourteen years ago, our family did a road trip to Wellington. We parked at Molesworth Street and we jumped out with our little kids and we took photos in front of Parliament. I wanted to begin by saying mom and dad, mom and pop, thank you for advocating for us in heaven. Gratitude for the opportunity to take the Filipino migrant story in New Zealand all the way to Parliament, by God's grace and the trust and hard work of many, as the first ever member of the New Zealand Parliament of Filipino descent.

Melissa Lee, Peter Goodfellow, Simon Bridges, Alastair Bell, Andrew Hunt, Peter Kiely-thank you. I understand that I'm only the third Filipino adult migrant to have been elected into a legislature outside the Philippines in history.

Gratitude for the privileged experience working as an MP with my colleagues; the Parliament team; the clerks and staff; my outstanding executive assistant Winin Wilson; Sally, Diane and Thomas, among others; my electorate office team with former MP Marie Hasler, Andre Bonilla, and James Rutherford; Lisa, Paul, and Ben at the library; the security team, in particular, Carl, Sam and Gino; and the cleaning staff for your genuine smiles and nods of acknowledgement and encouragement which helped so much, especially when I have been invisible to many.

Joy in being able to return to the country of my birth, the Philippines, as a New Zealand member of Parliament twice-during the 52nd Parliament in January 2020 for an official parliamentary bilateral visit to the Philippines with the National Party leadership team of Simon Bridges, Gerry Brownlee, and Mark Mitchell, to meet with our Philippine counterparts and the presidential candidates for the 2022 elections there, and a special visit with the Philippines Cardinal Luis Antonio Tagle, and again during this parliamentary term in April 2024 for an investment mission to Singapore, Thailand, and the Philippines with the Prime Minister, Minister Simon Watts, and 25 CEOs of New Zealand. At the behest of the Prime Minister, I walked down the red carpet from the plane alongside him, which was not protocol. Thank you, Mr Prime Minister. Then to Rome in October 2025 as I was invited to speak as the Filipino New Zealander MP at the Filipino diaspora conference during Pope Leo and Cardinal Tagle's week of prayer for migrants.

Gratitude for the amazing friendships and network built over these years, many of whom are in the gallery tonight: our New Lynn hoardings and support team; my campaign managers Romil Fernandez and Kevin Ryan; my psychiatrist friend, or, should I say, my friend the psychiatrist, Dr Tony Fernando, who I know has been watching over my mental health all this time; the many amazing constituents in New Lynn; the Kasamas, the National core group; Knights of Rizal; my Welly whānau; the very many hard-working Filipinos from Kaitāia to Invercargill, mga kababayan; the diplomatic corps in Wellington, especially the fantastic Philippine Ambassador to New Zealand Kira Azucena and their embassy team; and my former colleagues at the Auckland Consular Corps, Peter, Gregg, and Boguslaw. It is all about strong relationships.

I am humbled in knowing each of you. This is community.

National MP Paulo Garcia delivers his valedictory statement. VNP / Phil Smith

Getting into politics has been like getting on a train that doesn't fully stop. You have to grab hold, battle others to get in, and take a seat as the train quickly enters into a very tight tunnel. If you pop your head out-unless you're Tom Cruise-it could well be knocked off. One of life's greatest challenges is not to think that we are bigger and better than who we really are-all the more as members of Parliament. There's a huge temptation to think that we are like the great big tractor wheels of a tractor and that the tractor won't work without us, when the reality is that we are actually just the clumps of soil that are stuck on them. Conversely, the toxicity of politics can actually make us feel even less. The human need to be seen, heard, and acknowledged can become overwhelming. In wanting to be the big wheels, we miss the fact that the clumps of soil, formed together, make up the field that's infinitely more valuable than the great, big tractor wheels that may often need to be replaced.

Politics is also like a marathon. Some have trained for it all their lives, some get into it to see what they can contribute, and some for the perks and praise of winning at all costs. Because intense focus and long work hours are the rule, many would have run the full distance without real connection and engagement-many times to the detriment of our own teams, our friends, and our families. Despite the huge platform for engagement and community it presents, politics can be hugely isolating. We can end up siloed and thinking that everything is about us. There is so much to do to keep New Zealand afloat and going in the right direction-amid the onslaught of threats and the barrage of hate and calumny, and risks to personal safety, on top of the unrelentingly fast pace and volume of work. Even the greatest of intentions to see, hear, and acknowledge others are lost in some. But what I've realised is-apart from a few exceptions, possibly-this is no one's fault. It's simply the nature of the beast that politics is.

I'm grateful to have met so many amazing people and learnt so much. Parliament is a study in human behaviour and motivations. It's also a reflection of the public. Instead of thriving in our shared humanity, some choose to condemn and divide. Language is weaponised to foster hate and division and doubt and suspicion. Many of the public, often the most vulnerable, hear words spoken in this House, take them, and action that hate. I have had more than a lifetime's worth of profane gestures and nastiness through my time as a member of Parliament. I've always believed in a final judgment, not expecting that judgment happens here. For the first time in my life, I was screamed at over the phone over a sustained period where a friend walking beside me exclaimed, "Wow, who was that?" I've almost been run over, threatened, had cans thrown at me, and attacked while in my car. My wife and I have had to move house. It isn't real until it happens to you. This takes an emotional toll for some more than others. It threatens our peace.

National MP Paulo Garcia delivers his valedictory statement. VNP / Phil Smith

I take from the words of a person I follow closely: "Peace is not merely a political or institutional reality. It is the fruit of conscience, where resentment, indifference, and hatred can either be escalated or reconciled. Words can open paths or close them. They can illuminate reality or distort it to the point of making encounter impossible." I mentioned this in my maiden speech: "Let hateful words be the undoing of those who wield them." We who hold public office have a special obligation to be mindful of our words in order to disarm language instead of weaponising it. Firmness does not mean contempt. Disagreement does not affirm hate. Alleging the contrary is simply false and misleading. Respect cannot be demanded when it's not lived. It is in this respect for others that arises the duty to safeguard the space where their convictions, their conscience, and their relationships-some involving a faith in God-lie.

It is this inner realm that allows for a better understanding of increasingly divisive issues for every democratic society: freedom of thought, conscience, and religion-fundamental rights that protect the most intimate sphere of persons. The freedom upon which the contemporary State is built, if it is authentic, recognises the religion, the religious dimension, of the human person, respects it, and protects it, and it ensures that having faith is not a reason for which a person has to forfeit his or her contribution to society.

I finish with a tribute to my family: my brother Dr Vicente Garcia and his wife, Pearly, who have taken time off their extremely busy lives in Connecticut to be here with me tonight. My family in faith and very close friends, thank you for being here. For my daughters Maryana, Rocio, Lucia, and Ana Car, I learn from your example. Thank you for your wise counsel and your prayers. My father's heart wishes for you all to be here with me this evening. To the love of my life, Malu, the one vote I was determined to retain and maintain, my heart sings with joy at the prospect of spending more time with you-unhurried coffees. Thank you for being my greatest ally and sounding board, even if you do tend to get sleepy whenever I talk about my reckons. You have made me feel whole and affirmed me when I felt in pieces. I am excited for our next adventure.

Thank you everyone. Thank you everyone, really. I leave you with a hope that through the challenges we all have in our respective lives, we can pause more often, smile more, and be thankful.

I have asked the Auckland Choral Ensemble to help us remember how truly blessed we are living in New Zealand through a song entitled "Paraiso"-in English, "Paradise".

National MP Paulo Garcia delivers his valedictory statement. VNP / Phil Smith

You can watch video of Paulo Garcia's valedictory speech here.

World.title: Family of young woman killed by truck driver fight for law change
World.content:
Call for stronger accountability for preventable road deaths Checkpoint Download MP3 5m

Preventable deaths on our roads deserve stronger accountability - that's the message from a family grieving the loss of a daughter and her unborn child.

Jade Evans, 18, was killed near Palmerston North in November last year when a truck driver drove through a stop sign.

The driver pleaded guilty to careless driving causing death, and was sentenced to two months' community detention. He also lost his licence for 12 months and must pay reparations of $8000 to the family.

The maximum sentence possible under the law is three months' imprisonment. But Jade's mother, Kathryn Stothers, says that does not reflect the seriousness of the driver's deliberate - and fatal - choice.

She told Checkpoint on Wednesday the next part of the family's healing process was an initiative called Jade's Law.

"Jade's story has shown us that a preventable road death has devastating consequences for us as an entire family and also in the community, so we really want to turn that loss into meaningful change and make New Zealand roads safer."

She said at present, the law does not differentiate between genuine mistakes and deliberate decisions.

"The level of accountability is just the same if there was an accident that resulted because of water on the road or sunstrike, or anything like that. There's no deterrence for somebody that has deliberately breached road rules."

On 18 November, Jade was on her way to her parents' for dinner. The truck driver "looked left and right and continued to drive through" a stop sign, Stothers said.

"The truck driver has collided with our daughter Jade, and upon impact she's received devastating brain injuries and lost consciousness instantly and never regained it again."

Stothers said police and the courts did "everything they can" to hold the driver accountable, but the law did not differentiate between careless driving causing injury, and careless driving causing death.

"This is why we're pushing for stronger accountability to close the legislation gap. There's a gap in our current law when a fundamental road rule is broken and someone loses their life. This is to strengthen deterrence and restore public confidence that the law reflects the seriousness of a life lost.

"We don't want to make it that every single offence is charged at a higher charge. What we're asking for is to have more of a tiering section in the law so that the police and the court can charge appropriately when something like death occurs, because there's been a breach of a fundamental road law. We're not trying to take away from genuine accidents."

Stothers said Jade was a "strong, young, energetic, enthusiastic person" and her death left a hole in their lives.

"What we want to prevent is for other families to be in our situation where we're looking across the dining room table where there's a person missing. We want to reduce the possibility of other families sitting in the place we have, because it's a terrible place to sit."

World.title: Clarkson sacked as Kangaroos hunt 'coach for the modern game'
World.content:
North Melbourne has parted ways with coach Alastair Clarkson after four AFL seasons.

Clarkson, who guided Hawthorn to four premierships as a coach, has been unable to lead the Kangaroos to the finals during his time at Arden Street.

Clarkson was contracted with the club until 2027, but the Kangaroos opted to end his tenure early.

Live Moment Look back at North Melbourne president Sonja Hood and football boss Todd Viney's press conference after Alastair Clarkson was relieved of his duties as Kangaroos coach. What was going to happen next year? Did the North Board refuse a contract extension prior to the 2027 season? Did the want Clarkson to coach for his future? - Roos Member From what Hood said, they determined that they weren't going to extend Clarkson beyond 2027, therefore believed that it would be unfair to expect him to coach next season. Is it time for Simpson or Longmire? I think it's the right thing to do. He has laid a foundation but it needs a new voice to get that bit more. I prefer Simmo to Horse and think he could really push this group forward. - Nathan Hood wasn't prepared to say they're the preferred candidate, but both of their reactions will be interesting. The stuff about a modern coach makes me think they'll go for a highly-credentialled assistant. Should the players be blamed? Why get rid of a 4 time premiership coach with 1 more year left. Makes no sense. Maybe players should be held more accountable. - Davo It is interesting, Davo, that the players often seem to skirt responsibility with this kind of stuff. I guess it's easier to remove one employee than multiple. At the end of the day, this is a players' league. Show more

North Melbourne president Sonja Hood said the Kangaroos were in a better position now than when Clarkson took over, but the club wanted more success.

"We asked Alastair to give our club stability and strength and help return us to the top of the AFL ladder," Hood said.

"Four years later, we have created an environment where our staff and players want to be at our club. This is a testament to the culture Alastair has helped create and the belief that he has built in this group.

"Although we have clearly made progress and won more games, we won't shy away from our desire to want more from this talented group.

"We are incredibly grateful to Alastair for the work he's done over the last four years and we wish him all the very best for his next chapter."

Under Clarkson, North won 20 of their 82 AFL matches, including nine this season. Clarkson took over the Kangaroos after the club had collected back-to-back wooden spoons in 2022 and 2021, while also finishing second-last in 2020.

North have not made the finals in a decade, when the club made consecutive preliminary finals in 2014 and 2015 and an elimination final in 2016 under Brad Scott.

The 2026 season was North's best under Clarkson, and most successful since 2019, with the Kangaroos finishing 14th on the ladder with nine wins.
