World.title: Ferrari's Schumacher-inspired livery, F1 leader to cop penalty in Italy
World.content:
Ferrari will be celebrating the legacy of Michael Schumacher this weekend at its home race, with a special livery dedicated to the seven-time Formula 1 world champion.

This year marks 30 years since Schumacher joined the Scuderia, and 20 years since his final F1 victory in the 2006 Chinese Grand Prix.

Piastri searching for answers as teammate re-enters F1 title picture Oscar Piastri's "disappointing" end to the Dutch Grand Prix leaves the Australian and his McLaren team searching for answers, while his teammate has roared back into the Formula 1 title picture.

With Schumacher at the wheel, Ferrari rose to the top of F1 after years spent without championships.

Ferrari's constructors' championship win in 1999 ended a 16-year wait in the teams' competition, while Schumacher's drivers' championship triumph in 2000 made him the first Ferrari race to become world champion since Jody Scheckter in 1979.

Schumacher won five of his seven drivers' championships with Ferrari, from 2000-2004.

This weekend at the Italian Grand Prix in Monza, a race Schumacher won five times with Ferrari, the Scuderia has a one-off livery which pays tribute to the F1 champion.

Among the features are seven stars on the nose of the car, representing Schumacher's world titles, and drivers Lewis Hamilton — the sport's other seven-time world champion — and Charles Leclerc will wear racing suits that also feature the seven stars and Schumacher's logo.

F1 championship leader to take grid penalty at Monza

Kimi Antonelli has celebrated his 20th birthday as the Formula 1 drivers' championship leader, and heads into his home grand prix with a significant 59-point advantage over his two nearest rivals.

F1 drivers' championship leader Kimi Antonelli is set to start the Italian Grand Prix from the back of the grid. (Reiters: Benoit Tessier)

But the youngest-ever leader of the F1 championship heads into this weekend's race at Monza knowing he has work to do to be near the front of the grid.

Mercedes announced during the previous race weekend in the Netherlands that Antonelli will take an engine penalty this weekend.

F1 teams have an allocation of power unit components they can use in a season. When a driver is fitted with a power unit component that exceeds the allocation, they are handed a penalty at the first event that new part is used.

Mercedes has had multiple power unit issues this year, with Antonelli failing to finish in Barcelona and teammate George Russell suffering issues in Canada and Belgium.

Despite the Italian Grand Prix being Antonelli's home race, Mercedes boss Toto Wolff said now was the right time to do it for the championship leader.

"Our calculations say that that's the best track to take it," Wolff said.

"Obviously, algorithms don't take their nationality into consideration. We're here to fight for a championship and not get the most PR. So yeah, that's what we're going to do."

Monza, known as the Temple of Speed, is expected to be a strong track for Mercedes, which is likely why it is taking the penalty now.

With long straights, there should be plenty of opportunities for Antonelli to pass with his impressive Mercedes power unit.

Monza has been the scene of impressive drives through the field in recent years.

Pierre Gasly won from 10th on the grid driving for AlphaTauri (now Racing Bulls). Max Verstappen won in 2022 after taking a five-place grid penalty, while Lewis Hamilton charged from the last row on the grid to place fifth.

Last year, Isack Hadjar started in the pit lane for Racing Bulls and was able to finish 10th.

ABC Sport will have a live blog of the Formula 1 Italian Grand Prix from 9pm AEST on Sunday, September 6.

World.title: Bledisloe Cup quadruple-header announced as sevens added to ticket
World.content:
Australia's sevens teams will share the stage in a scheduling first, with the Wallabies and Wallaroos creating a Bledisloe Cup quadruple-header in Sydney.

The Stadium Australia Test against the All Blacks on October 17 already had a support act secured, with the Wallaroos due to host Scotland for the first time in their WXV Global Series clash.

Kick-off times for Bledisloe Cup in Sydney Wallaroos v Scotland, 12pm

Australian sevens men v Fiji, 2:05pm

Australian sevens women v New Zealand, 2.25pm

Wallabies v New Zealand, 3:45pm All times in AEDT

Now two more fixtures will be added to the ticket, with Australia's world champion sevens women to face rivals New Zealand and the men up against two-time Olympic gold medallists Fiji.

"This is an historic moment for Australian rugby, with all four of our Teams In Gold competing on the same pitch, on the same day, on an unmissable occasion," Rugby Australia chief executive Phil Waugh told AAP.

"The day will showcase the very best of rugby with our elite male and female players across the XVs and Sevens formats taking on famous rivals from around the world in an unprecedented line-up of international rugby.

"We look forward to celebrating this extraordinary occasion with our great Australian rugby community and we thank our friends from New Zealand Rugby, Fiji Rugby Union and Scottish Rugby for helping make this day a reality."

The Wallaroos will begin the action before the men's and women's sevens outfits take the field, followed by the Wallabies, who will complete the four-course menu with a late afternoon kick-off at the venue set to host next year's World Cup final.

AAP

World.title: Thea Frodin, Serena Williams's body double in movie, makes US Open debut
World.content:
Making a US Open debut as a teenager is a daunting task, but American Thea Frodin is no stranger to the bright lights.

The 17-year-old played at her home slam for the first time, going down in straight sets to world number two Elena Rybakina 6-3, 6-2.

There were plenty of fans at Grandstand who were there to see Rybakina, this year's Australian Open champion, but Frodin was a mini-celebrity in her own right.

Frodin, from California, was a body double at the age of 12 in the 2021 film King Richard, a movie starring Will Smith about the rise of Serena and Venus Williams with the help of their father, Richard Williams.

Fordin was the body double for actor Demi Singleton, who played Serena in the film, and is now forging her own path at Flushing Meadows.

There was no Hollywood screenwriting for Fordin's debut, with Rybakina never troubled in the win that came after a near three-hour rain delay.

Fordin was not disgraced in the straight-sets defeat. Down 1-5 in the second set, the teenager fired four aces, saving three match points, to extend the match just one extra game.

"She played really well today, and she has great shots," Rybakina said of her teenage opponent.

Fifth seed comes from behind to avoid another US Open boilover

Italian fifth seed Flavio Cobolli has rallied from two sets down to win his first-round match at the US Open, avoiding another early upset on the men's side.

Flavio Cobolli needed more than four hours, and five sets, to make it to the US Open second round. (Getty Images: Julian Finney)

The French Open runner-up beat Francisco Comesana 3-6, 2-6, 6-3, 6-4, 6-4, finishing his match that lasted 4 hours, 12 minutes, not long after some sun had broken through the clouds and allowed play to start on all the outside courts after a morning of rain.

Cobolli made his first career two-set comeback to avoid joining Novak Djokovic (fourth seed) and Arthur Fils (10th seed) among early losers in a men's draw that was already missing top-ranked Jannik Sinner due to injury.

Cobolli said he took a bathroom break after the second set and decided to change everything.

"So I changed all the dress that I started with today and it works," Cobolli said.

"In grand slams it's never done. You have to fight until the last point."

Ninth seed Taylor Fritz, the 2024 runner-up, rolled to a 6-3, 6-2, 6-4 victory over 18-year-old fellow American Darwin Blanch.

Kokkinakis withdraws from US Open before hitting a ball Thanasi Kokkinakis concedes he may have contested his last US Open without even hitting a ball after the cursed star's body failed him once again.

Madison Keys was the only other player to move into the second round early in a tournament where rain threatened to hamper the schedule for a couple of days.

Showers that began Monday night, local time, and could be on and off through the middle of the week delayed play on all the outer courts, allowing action only in Arthur Ashe Stadium and Louis Armstrong Stadium, which have retractable roofs.

Keys, the 22nd seed, beat 19-year-old Alina Korneeva 7-5, 6-4 in the leadoff match in Ashe. The 2017 US Open runner-up was knocked off in the first round last year in Flushing Meadows.

"It's always tough playing someone young and up-and-coming, and they're going after their shots," Keys said.

"And it's so hard to play a first round of a Grand Slam, so nervous and just wanting to do so well. So, really happy I was able to kind of fight through that and win today."

Coco Gauff, the 2023 US Open champion, 17th seed Alex Eala, and men's first seed Alexander Zverev are scheduled to play later on the final night of round one matches.

ABC/AP

World.title: Aussies march on at US Open, De Minaur washed out, Kokkinakis withdraws
World.content:
Diminutive Dane Sweeny and qualifier Tristan Schoolkate have stormed into the US Open second round to continue Australia's excellent start to the season's final grand slam.

Sweeny was leading the crafty Corentin Moutet 7-6(4), 6-4, 3-0 when the Frenchman retired injured on Tuesday, local time.

Schoolkate then celebrated like Lleyton Hewitt when he finished off American qualifier Nishesh Basavareddy 7-6 (4), 3-6, 6-3, 6-4 in a tick over three hours.

The 25-year-old Sweeny marked his maiden appearance in the US Open main draw with a first-ever victory at an overseas grand slam.

The wildcard next faces either Italian 13th seed Lorenzo Musetti or rising Brit Arthur Fery for an improbable place in the last 32.

Schoolkate is into round two for a second time and will next play Italian fifth seed Fabio Cobolli, the 2026 French Open runner-up.

Sweeny, who only stands 170 centimetres high, and Schoolkate give Australia at least seven players in round two, joining Taylah Preston, Kim Birrell, Maya Joint, Alexei Popyrin and James Duckworth.

Men's sixth seed Alex de Minaur will have to wait another day to try to follow suit after more rain in New York wiped out the day-three night session.

De Minaur did not even make it onto The Grandstand for his first-round clash with Italian qualifier Andrea Guerrieri.

Injured Kokkinakis withdraws from US Open before hitting a ball

Thanasi Kokkinakis concedes he may have contested his last US Open without even hitting a ball after the cursed star's body failed him once again.

Kokkinakis formally withdrew from the season's last grand slam after being unable to take the court for his scheduled first-round clash with Spanish wonder boy Rafael Jodar because of an ankle sprain.

Thanasi Kokkinakis has pulled out of the year's final grand slam. (Getty Images: NurPhoto/Robert Szaniszlo)

The Australian suffered his latest injury in Cincinnati two weeks ago and has been racing the clock to be fit for the Open ever since.

He ran out of time and, after a decade battling endless back, shoulder, abdominal, knee and arm injuries, Kokkinakis admits he is losing patience.

"It is a possibility for sure," the 30-year-old told AAP when asked if his US Open career might be over.

"I'm not going to say never. The thing is, I feel like the tennis part, I've still got a lot of good tennis left in me.

"On the limited matches that I've played, I've shown that I'm more than good enough to still compete and then beat some good players.

"But, to be honest, I'm sick of going into tournaments not feeling like I can do it physically and everyone asks me how my body is."

The 30-year-old used — or "wasted" — the fifth of nine injury-protected ranking entries available to him to make the US Open draw.

The one-time Roger Federer slayer now plans on continuing his recovery and trying to be fully fit for the Australian summer.

"I want to go into it being confident in myself and, if I do win, give myself a chance to back up and try and play again," Kokkinakis said.

"That's always the thing. So it's about feeling strong in myself.

"I'll definitely obviously give the next Aussie a crack and see where I'm at after that."

AAP

World.title: Adelaide MotoGP project is more than the track. Here's what's planned in the parklands
World.content:
Headline announcements have a habit of overshadowing, if not totally obscuring, finer details, and the future of the Australian MotoGP has been no exception.

On Sunday, the SA government released its long-awaited plan for the design of a $96 million Adelaide street circuit set to host the race from 2027 — a development that will involve the cutting down of nearly 400 trees to make way for the new track.

The announcement came amid environmental acrimony. The government is currently facing protests and a federal court challenge over its actions in another part of the Adelaide parklands to redevelop the North Adelaide Golf Course.

But the MotoGP project will be about more than the track and the trees — the government is promising what amounts to a sweeping upgrade of the areas around Victoria Park in Adelaide's eastern parklands.

Here's a look at the plan that is currently out for community consultation.

Canopy and habitat

Of all the ramifications of the MotoGP project, the impact on the environment is perhaps the most politically sensitive.

But the government has been keen to spruik what it has described as a "nature-positive outcome" and has promised to plant many more trees than it removes, "meaning a net increase of at least 3,393 trees".

It has also committed to a $15 million environmental spend on "greening, rewilding and revitalising projects to restore habitat and strengthen biodiversity".

Shared-use paths are part of the concept plans. (Supplied: SA government)

Those projects will include work to reduce pollution entering the River Torrens and to support wildlife such as local butterfly populations.

Asked about how soon the works would be completed, SA Premier Peter Malinauskas spoke of "the next few years".

"We've got a timeline that we want to work within in terms of the release of that funding," he said.

"There'll be capacity constraints about when some projects will be delivered.

"Some of the projects will require a fair bit of design work around the stormwater work that we're doing … to be able to help grow the tree canopy at a faster rate than what otherwise [would be] the case."

Grey-headed flying foxes — which are prone to summer heat stress — will get improved cooling infrastructure and habitat regeneration.

Bat Rescue SA's fundraising coordinator, Judith Bemmer, welcomed the commitment, but also expressed concern about habitat loss as a result of the removal of trees.

"We're worried that there's the potential for starvation of the baby bats, because they won't have some of those trees to fly out to," she said.

"Having said that, the trees close in to the parklands, where their colony is, and the fig trees are all still there.

"We're very hopeful that in the future, as these other trees mature, it will provide both cover and forage for these bats."

Grey-headed flying foxes at Adelaide's Botanic Park. (Supplied: Craig Greer)

Mr Malinauskas said environmental works would also include steps to contribute to platypus rewilding efforts in the Torrens by ecology group Green Adelaide.

"We are putting funding in place to accelerate that work and get it done. There is a bit of work that is required here," he said.

Adelaide Park Lands Association president Mat Monti said that, on their own, tree planting, revegetation and environmental investment were commendable — but that, when coupled with tree removal, they amounted to "greenwashing".

"We don't want them to do it just to excuse the destruction of the eastern parklands for MotoGP," they said.

Fringe benefits

The design for the new street circuit will see MotoGP bikes race along Rundle Road, between Rymill and Rundle parks.

During Adelaide's so-called Mad March festival season, those parks are occupied by Fringe venues Gluttony and The Garden of Unearthly Delights.

Rundle Road — an extension of Rundle Street — will host part of the race. (Supplied: SA government)

The government said the venues stood to gain from the redevelopment works, through upgrades to water, electricity and sewerage infrastructure.

"When Fringe and Gluttony set up down in the East End around Rymill Park, there is often temporary infrastructure they have to bring in at substantial cost," Mr Malinauskas said.

"If we can put some permanent infrastructure in the ground, that makes it easier for them to set up and pack down."

Sport and recreation

The main part of the MotoGP circuit will be in Victoria Park, which currently hosts Adelaide's Supercars races and formerly hosted the F1 Grand Prix.

The heritage grandstand in the park — a hangover from its time as a horseracing venue — will be closer to the race, thanks to a track redesign involving a revised turn-off from Wakefield Road.

The redevelopment could accommodate new playing courts. (Supplied: SA government)

But the government is also promising other works in Victoria Park for community benefit, such as an upgraded soccer field, with lighting, and community space near the grandstand.

It said there would be new running tracks through the eastern parklands, including a 2-kilometre loop in Victoria Park itself.

It also said there would "potentially" be a new skate park and playing courts near Fullarton Road.

"They could be pickleball courts, they could be basketball courts, they could be netball courts," SA Motor Sport Board chief executive Mark Warren told a parliamentary inquiry on Monday.

Mark Warren says the redevelopment will include playing courts and a cycling criterium circuit. (ABC News: Daniel Taylor)

A new water jump will be installed for the Adelaide Equestrian Festival — an annual three-day horse trials event and Olympic qualifier held in the eastern parklands.

"This will give our event a bit of a boost because we won't now have to fund it ourselves, which is great news," board member Karlene Maywald said.

"We're also working closely with the Motor Sport Board and the government to ensure we can deliver our event next April."

Pedal power

Several of the elements of the new design relate to cycling — including plans for the Tour Down Under.

The government said the Victoria Park circuit would be hosting the return of the Tour Down Under classic, a pre-tour street race, from 2028.

The heritage grandstand will be closer to the action because of a track re-design which will also accommodate cycling events, the government says. (Supplied: SA government)

The Motor Sport Board said a new 1.2-kilometre criterium loop would provide space for cycling races and Pedal Prix events.

"That's quite critical because right now the criterium loop that exists has a crossover between park users," Mr Warren said.

"It was important to, in the design, look at how we can have an unobstructed cycling criterium loop, and we believe the current design as it's been put out for consultation will achieve some of that. There's been some discussion already with cycling clubs."

There are also plans for new shared-use paths, and a pedestrian and cyclist refuge on Wakefield Road.

Consultation on the plans is open until September 20.

World.title: Ben Stokes joins Adelaide Strikers for BBL summer
World.content:
Former England cricket captain Ben Stokes will take part in the upcoming Big Bash League season after signing with the Adelaide Strikers, the team has confirmed.

The all-rounder's move had been tipped earlier in the week, but has now been locked in by the Strikers, who said they were looking forward to capitalising on Stokes's "world-class talent" and ability to put in "match-winning performances with both bat and ball".

Stokes retired from international cricket in June, a decision that caused shock waves when it was revealed during a Test match.

His arrival in Adelaide will follow a previous BBL stint, at the Melbourne Renegades in 2015.

"Ben is one of the greatest all-rounders the game has seen, a proven match-winner and a competitor who thrives under pressure," Adelaide head coach Tim Paine said in a statement released by the Strikers.

"We're thrilled to have a player of his ability join our squad."

In the same statement, Stokes said the opportunity to join the Strikers was one he "couldn't pass up".

"Adelaide Oval is an incredible place to play cricket, the Big Bash is a fantastic competition and the Strikers have an exciting group," he said.

"I can't wait to get started, create some special memories with the group and give Strikers fans plenty to cheer about."

Stokes — who made his Test debut in Adelaide in 2013 — will be available for the full BBL summer, the Strikers said.

The hard-hitting, fast-bowling all-rounder captained the England side that was widely expected to challenge Australia for the Ashes in the 2025/26 summer, but was defeated 4-1.

His decision to quit international cricket was revealed shortly before the tea break on day four of the third Test between England and New Zealand at Trent Bridge.

During the series, Stokes made front-page news after being dropped by England for the second Test amid an investigation following a night out with a teammate after the first Test at Lord's.

The 35-year-old is widely recognised as one of the most impactful and talismanic cricketers of the current era, and scored more than 11,000 international runs across T20, ODI and Test formats.

His match-winning performances have included a whirlwind 135 not out against Australia at Headingley in 2019, which steered England to an astonishing one-wicket triumph, and a rearguard 84 not out against New Zealand in the World Cup final the same summer.

His innings of 155 against Australia in a losing cause at Lord's in 2023 occurred in the match made notorious by the controversial run-out of wicketkeeper Jonny Bairstow.

World.title: Beach sprinting was just the start of Damien Cook's NRL story
World.content:
With a bit of luck, they'll tell the old Damien Cook story one more time.

This weekend, the 35-year-old St George Illawarra skipper will play his final NRL match before heading to Super League side Castleford next year.

His farewell will be at Wollongong Showground, the closest ground in the league to the ocean. When the swell's big, you can almost hear the waves crashing on City Beach from the hill.

Maybe it will be when Cook runs out for the 263rd and last time, or perhaps he'll dart out from dummy half to take on the Parramatta defence with a glimpse of the old quickness.

Maybe it'll be the commentators who say it, maybe it'll just be fans in the stands, but someone, somewhere will almost certainly tell somebody else "you know, he used to be a champion beach sprinter."

It's a story nobody seems to tire of telling — Cook himself still hears about it all the time.

"It's the great Dane Gagai's fault. He mentioned it one day when I was doing media — a few people knew about it, but he said it real loud, the journo I was speaking to did a story on it and it got out from there," Cook said.

"It's never stopped; I still get it every day. Commentators say it, I get it in comments, DMs, Instagram stories; if people see a post about a beach sprinter they tag me in it. You have to laugh."

The yarn got its greatest play during Cook's ascent to becoming one of the best hookers in rugby league, which came almost 10 years ago now, and it's worth breaking it out one more time to celebrate the end of an NRL career with an extraordinarily long tail.

It took a while to get going. Cook spent plenty of time as a second-stringer on second-rate teams.

Cook's NRL career took a while to get going. (Getty Images: Brett Hemmings)

He did not make the run on side for an NRL match until he was almost 23 and wasn't a full-time starter at hooker until the year he turned 27.

But after taking the long way, he made up for lost time immediately, and once the beach sprinting tale got used up, we started to tell others.

Cook can't pick his favourite himself. He is overwhelmed by the memories he's made because there are so many.

This late starter has now played the seventh-most matches of any dummy half in the history of the game, so when you ask him about his favourite match there's so much to choose from.

There's the first grade debut back in 2013, of course, which came for St George Illawarra against Wests Tigers at the Sydney Cricket Ground in Heritage Round. The retro jerseys and brown football made it feel like history even while it was happening.

There was the first game at Wollongong a week later. Cook is proud to finish his NRL journey there, given it's where he grew up watching football and where he played his junior grand finals for Helensburgh.

In a nice full-circle moment, his first match there in the top grade came against the Eels, just like his last will.

"The big one that day was when I got under Fuifui Moi Moi — it wasn't me being brave, he was coming straight at me," Cook said.

"I didn't have much of a choice."

Cook is one of the best dummy halves in New South Wales Origin history. (Getty Images)

There's the late-season cameo for Canterbury in 2015, which first made Cook's name and proved he could ride the lightning, and his debut at South Sydney, where he played more than 200 games and spent his most glorious times.

There's his first State of Origin match in front of 90,000 at the MCG in 2018, when he was one of 11 New South Wales debutants alongside players like Nathan Cleary, Tom Trbojevic, Latrell Mitchell and Cameron Murray.

Cook was the best of them that night in a magnificent beginning, and he always seemed to find something extra for the Blues — among dummy halves, only Ben Elias and Danny Buderus have worn the jersey more.

The 2019 decider, when he scored a scorching try right through the heart of the Queensland defence, was perhaps his single greatest highlight in rep football, but playing for Australia against Tonga in Auckland later that season was another special night.

As the Tongan anthem rang out through the night, Cook thought he'd be crushed by the noise.

"All the Tongans were singing their anthem, just this sea of red. I thought 'bloody hell, nobody is going to sing our anthem; we're up against it here'," Cook said.

"But then all the Tongans sang our anthem as well. The sound of it, I'll never forget it."

The pandemic ravaging international football and the eventual emergence of Harry Grant kept Cook to just four Tests, but he did get the special honour of playing one in Wollongong the following season and duly marked it by scoring a try.

It was no barge-over from close range though — it was an intercept that Cook took 70 metres all the way home.

He could have run along Lawrence Hargrave Drive, across the Sea Cliff Bridge, and up the hill all the way back to Helensburgh and the Kiwis wouldn't have caught him.

Cook ran all the way into an Australian jersey. (Getty Images: Mark Metcalfe)

Then there's all the club wars as well, because once Cook became one of the best he liked nothing more than testing himself against the top sides.

He says he relished the days where South Sydney had a real shot at being pride of the league again and had it out with the likes of Melbourne, Penrith and the Sydney Roosters with everything to play for and no quarter asked for or given.

All told, when asked to pick a single favourite game, Cook named almost a dozen. He just couldn't leave anything out.

"I know you asked for one, but rugby league has given me so much," Cook said.

"The mates, the moments, the memories, it's why you do it."

Cook himself gave plenty of people similarly glorious memories.

He was fast enough that a dart from dummy half would make the crowd rise, fast enough that he could break into space and round the fullback from anywhere, fast enough that when Wayne Bennett came out favouring the NRL's proposed set restart rules in 2020 some said the wily old coach was doing it just to suit Cook.

But there was more to Cook's game than raw pace. He's a cannier playmaker than some might think — in 2019 he accumulated 18 try assists, more than Grant has ever managed in a single season and equal to Cameron Smith's career high.

Cook was also among the top four players in the league for tackles made in seven of his first eight seasons.

If he gets through 25 tackles on Sunday, which is light work so long as he plays big minutes, he'll pass 10,500 of them for his career, and given the middle of the field is where the giants live, he'll have given up size and weight on just about every one of them.

Cook has never shirked the tough stuff through his long NRL career. (Getty Images: Bradley Kanaris)

Somehow, he has gotten through those 10,000 blows without ever being seriously broken — this year marks the 10th season in a row Cook will manage at least 23 games.

That's a point of pride for Cook. Once he got a taste of his dream coming true, it became a prize beyond value.

"It took a while to get there, so once I did I never wanted to let it go. I'm very proud of that because I put a lot of time into recovery and working hard and staying fit and being ready for every pre-season so I can get the most out of it," Cook said.

"I've set high standards for myself, which is why I've been able to play consistently. Even in NSW Cup I tried to do that.

"Touch wood, I haven't had a bad injury since I was at the Dogs when I broke my thumb — the other games that ruin my record were getting rested or COVID protocols, and I wish we could take those off.

"Longevity and consistency are something I'm really proud of."

Both Damien Cook and his club have done it tough in 2026. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

In the end, being there all day every day has taken its toll on Cook. It has slowed him down, and the ravages of age have finally overtaken whatever benefits he gained from his late start.

He has just two try assists and one line break for the season and has spent time on the bench and as 18th man. It feels like this change has come at the right time for him.

The wins have not come as Cook or St George Illawarra would have liked in the two seasons since he joined, but that doesn't mean he won't leave a legacy.

The Dragons have a host of young players who hold the future in their hands, perhaps none more than 23-year-old backrower Hamish Stewart.

Despite recent struggles, Cook's efforts have never wavered. (Getty Images: Brett Hemmings)

"It's me, Gutho [Clint Gutherson] and Cooky in the gym. You see him, day in and day out, and he has the most energy of anyone. He never skips a rep," Stewart said.

"He's been massive for all us young blokes, showing us how to run a team and how a club really works.

"I love how he goes about life off the field as well — I feel like I can go to him about anything."

Stewart has played every game this season and earned plenty of plaudits despite the Red V's struggles.

Along with the Couchman brothers, Dylan Egan and Loko Pasifiki Tonga, Stewart is part of the sun that can break through the clouds and of all those players, his tomorrows may be the brightest.

The Dragons have found wins hard to come by during Cook's time with the club. (AAP: Mark Evans)

If Stewart does go on and makes the most of it, Cook will play a role even if they're not packing down together.

The veteran is the kind of guy who can hold a beaten-down town together, and even if the team hasn't been winning, that doesn't mean Cook hasn't been teaching.

In trying to impart the hard-won wisdom of his rise, Cook is leaving behind something that will last once he's gone. His lessons will remain, like footsteps in the sand.

"You have to make sure you're doing the right things all the time, to lead by example. You have to push right along to the end of the season, even if it's a tough one," Cook said.

"It's easy to tick the boxes when you're winning games, but when you're up against it you still have to push hard every day.

"That's a good value to have, and a lot of the players here have that."

If he's right, that could be the longest tail of all for Cook, who leaves the club in a far better place than he found it.

He has shown these boys how to live, but now they must become men without him.

"He's always got a smile on his face every day. You see him when you walk through the doors and you know you're gonna have a good day," Stewart said.

"That's what I'll miss the most."

Cook's ultimate legacy is the players he leaves behind at St George Illawarra. (Getty Images: Bradley Kanaris)

For Cook himself, this is an end but not the end.

He's excited about playing for Castleford next year, to have a new challenge in a new place, to have something to prove again, to do the work and love it and to give it everything he's got, which Cook says is all he's ever done.

He's excited for Sunday, to see family and friends in the crowd and, one last time, to live that dream he would not surrender during the hard times.

There's no beach, but it'll be a fine day to get a sprint in.

"If I told my younger self what would happen over the past 14 or 15 years, I don't think he'd believe me," Cook said.

"Definitely after the season it will [sink in], especially when I'm packing up the house and going through some jerseys. That'll bring back the memories.

"But there's still more to do."

Tech.title: This new Roomba seals itself to your carpet
Tech.content:
is a senior reviewer with over twenty years of experience. She covers smart home, IoT, and connected tech, and has written previously for Wirecutter, Wired, Dwell, BBC, and US News.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

iRobot has announced a new flagship robot vacuum, which it will showcase at IFA in Berlin this week, the company’s first big tech trade show in years. The Roomba maker will be exhibiting under its new owner, Picea Robotics, the contract manufacturer that purchased the once-troubled American robotics company out of bankruptcy in January.

The $1,199 Roomba Max 875 Combo is the company’s newest top-of-the-line robot vacuum and mop, and it debuts alongside the $899 Roomba Plus 678 Combo. Both models are available now at irobot.com.

The key vacuuming improvement is a new sealing system iRobot is calling SealForce that takes vacuuming “to a level beyond what’s previously been possible,” iRobot chief engineer Adam Pope said.

This works by lowering a sort of skirt around the cleaning head when it detects carpet, enabling a better seal that directs airflow deeper into the carpet. Paired with a new vane-type blower motor that Pope says moves 20 L/s (liters of air per second), SealForce helps the Roomba 875 deliver three times deeper carpet cleaning than without the feature.

Previous Next





1 / 4 The Roomba Max 875 Combo comes in black or white Image: iRobot

The 875 offers 35,000 Pa suction power, the highest iRobot has ever published—for years, the company refused to publish detailed suction-power specs. It uses a single rubber brush rather than the company’s signature dual rollers (my favorite for pet hair on carpet). Pope says this is to accommodate that better seal against the carpet. It uses lidar and camera-based vision to navigate and detect obstacles and has a slimmer footprint than the Roomba 775. It can also climb thresholds up to 3.5 cm high.

The 875 has a roller mop that can extend to the side to clean edges and a new hair-cutting anti-tangle brush.

The 875 Combo is also a mopping robot, with a self-cleaning roller mopping system that adds more downward pressure than the 775, plus a new heated mist feature called ThermaMist, which sprays ahead of the mop to pretreat stains. The mop includes a retractable mop cover that extends during vacuuming to keep carpets dry and can extend to get along edges. The robot comes with an auto-empty / wash dock that automatically washes the mop with hot water and dries it with hot air.

This SealForce tech is new to iRobot, but not to robot vacuums; Narwal and Dreame have variations on this on their latest flagships, the Narwal Flow 2 and Dreame X60 Max Ultra. But it is novel in the space, and combined with ThermaMist, a new hair-cutting anti-tangle main brush, and an anti-tangle side brush, the 875 shows that iRobot is inching closer to catching up with its competition than with its last relaunch.

Previous Next

1 / 2 The 678 squirts cleaning solution on dried on messes then returns to mop them up.

The company is releasing a midrange version of the 875, the Roomba Plus 678 Combo. This also has a roller mop and the new SealForce tech, but it drops to 30,000Pa suction power and 18 L/s of airflow, and there’s no ThermaMist or mop cover.

Instead, the 678 has its own treatment system called SprayForce, which sprays cleaning fluid on stains to presoak them, then comes back later. It lifts its mop 10mm when it detects carpet. Both new models work with Amazon Alexa, Google Home, and Siri Shortcuts, and are currently going through Matter certification, according to Pope.

A robot vacuum with better vacuuming is less flashy but more practical than those that sprout legs and arms. We’re seeing several manufacturers adopt this type of sealing technology — one upright vacuum makers have been trying to perfect for decades. It will be interesting to see if Roomba’s version solves that very real problem when it comes to cleaning carpet.

Tech.title: Google needs Hollywood more than the studios need AI
Tech.content:
Google has reportedly been reaching out to a number of Hollywood’s biggest studios, hoping to strike licensing agreements that would allow it to train its AI models on copyrighted material in exchange for massive piles of cash. In theory, these deals would be a win-win: a huge financial boon to the studios that would also give Google a significant advantage in its race to outpace other AI companies. But while there’s little downside for Google, these deals pose a distinct set of risks to each of the studios that might be thinking about going all-in on AI. Getting into bed with Google this way might benefit Hollywood in the short term, but it could just as easily backfire and leave the public feeling burned by the entertainment industry.

Though Google has not yet been able to get Disney, Warner Bros. Discovery, or Universal to agree to anything officially, the company’s executives have been reaching out to multiple studio representatives with pitches focused on its AI technology, according to unnamed sources speaking to The Los Angeles Times. Google wants permission to train its AI models on the studios’ vast libraries of copyrighted content, and it’s willing to spend hundreds of millions of dollars to get ahold of them. Per The LA Times, Google could pay a studio like Disney / Pixar around $40 million just for the rights to generate outputs featuring a single copyrighted character. That payout could swell well into the billions the more characters Google’s deals encompass, and studios might be able to secure a portion of however much advertising revenue Google makes from AI-generated content featuring that IP on platforms like YouTube.

As expensive as these partnerships would be for Google, they would also be an invaluable tool as the company continues to crystalize its position as one of the most prominent players in the AI game. Gemini being able to spit out Disney-approved images of Darth Vader and Snow White might not seem all that significant on its face, but that’s exactly the sort of thing that could get more ordinary, non tech-obsessed people seeing generative AI in a more positive (if innocuous) light. After years of hearing AI companies boast about their plans to disrupt society and eliminate jobs, public sentiment — especially among young people — about the technology has shifted into the negative. Even with tools like ChatGPT being as popular as they are, the larger AI industry has been so mired in controversy and plagued by concerns about its real world harms that it would now be hard-pressed to put out products that would immediately curry widespread goodwill. Striking deals with film and TV studios would give Google a convenient way to shift the larger narrative about its AI ambitions.

The content developed through these partnerships would presumably look better than the slop currently being churned out by models trained on ill-gotten source data, and having Google’s name and logos slapped all over official AI-generated Disney content would do wonders to legitimize this technology in people’s minds. But even if it didn’t, the partnership would still signal to the public that the entertainment industry sees generative AI as a tool worth embracing. It’s hard to quantify how valuable that framing would be to Google, whose DeepMind arm struck a $75 million investment deal with A24 earlier this summer. But it’s very easy to imagine how taking Google’s AI cash could put studios on a path that ultimately alienates their workers and audiences.

Regardless of whether a studio were to incorporate AI tools into their production workflows or simply feature user-generated AI content on their platforms (which was Disney and OpenAI’s plan before their partnership collapsed), striking a licensing agreement with Google would be a watershed moment.

Lionsgate, a notable studio but not a major player, struck a licensing deal with Runway in 2024. So far, nothing concrete has come out of that partnership, but the companies say they’re working on a plan to release AI-generated shorts. Once any one of the big legacy studios hop on to the AI bandwagon and manage to actually make something they can show the world, more production houses have a reason to follow suit. AI’s potential to speed production timelines up while keeping costs down is one of the main things that has kept studios interested in utilizing the technology. Shareholders would absolutely love it if production houses could put out more movies while spending less money, but doing that by using AI tools would almost certainly put a significant portion of the entertainment workforce out of jobs.

What may be keeping Disney and other studios from rushing to take Google up on its offers is the way that people have reacted to seeing AI used in the production of films like Spider-Man: Brand New Day. Fans were dismayed to find AI-generated images in Brand New Day’s official artbook, and the negative reaction might have been even more intense had people known about the technology’s use before the film hit theaters. It’s impossible to know for sure whether awareness about AI’s presence in Brand New Day’s production would have kept it from making $2 billion at the box office. But it stands to reason that none of the studios is eager to be the first to learn what happens when they release a project that’s presented as being the product of Google’s AI tools.

Though Google has everything to gain from Hollywood embracing AI, the studios have to be mindful of how endorsing this technology could leave them out on a limb. And as much as Google might be presenting its products as the solution to all of the entertainment industry’s issues, the AI industry needs Hollywood more than Hollywood needs more slop.

Tech.title: Anthropic launches Claude Fable 5.1 and says it’s up to 45 percent cheaper for agentic work
Tech.content:
is a news writer covering all things consumer tech. Stevie started out at Laptop Mag writing news and reviews on hardware, gaming, and AI.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Anthropic says its newest AI models, Fable 5.1 and Mythos 5.1, address criticisms from customers about price, data retention, and overzealous safeguards. The company claims Claude Fable 5.1 offers stronger performance than Fable 5, but costs around 25 percent less typically and up to 45 percent less for complex agentic tasks, thanks to reduced pricing on cached data that was already processed and stored.

Along with the announcement, a slew of early impressions popped up, including from Every CEO Dan Shipper, who claims, “It’s the strongest coding model we’ve used, but now it’s fast, token-efficient, and crucially actually speaks like a normal person.”

Box CEO Aaron Levie is another early access believer, saying that his company’s agent with Fable 5.1 picked up on subtleties and ambiguities in data that Fable 5 missed in the same test. Meanwhile, Lisan al Gaib points out that on benchmarks, Mythos 5.1 with low reasoning scores the same as its predecessor set to Max reasoning.

Fable 5.1 also has “more precise safeguards” that Anthropic says are less likely to block basic biology questions than Fable 5, but Mythos 5.1 has the same biology restrictions as the previous model. Anthropic also explained its progress on data retention, saying that Enterprise Frontier Safeguards offer “complete privacy” by storing data on the customer’s cloud servers instead of its own, and will start rolling out later this fall.

Anthropic says it’s “now allowing Fable 5.1 to be used for identifying software vulnerabilities,” but it will still redirect some cybersecurity tasks to Opus models, like “penetration testing, exploit generation, and binary-based vulnerability scanning.” Claude Fable 5.1 is now available on all platforms, while Mythos 5.1 is available to Project Glasswing participants only.

Tech.title: Apple Maps follows Google in renaming Lake Ontario
Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Apple Maps has officially changed the name of Lake Ontario to Lake America, as reported earlier by Bloomberg. The company joins Google in re-labeling the Great Lake following an executive order signed by President Donald Trump in the midst of a trade dispute with Canada.

The Canadian version of Apple Maps still shows “Lake Ontario” when panning over the area, while international versions of the app show both names, according to Bloomberg. Google updated its map shortly after the name change went live in the US Geographic Names Information System (GNIS), but Apple waited a bit longer.

Tech.title: Lenovo’s 2-in-1 Yoga 7i is a great Labor Day deal at $750
Tech.content:
Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Best Buy is celebrating Labor Day all week long with big deals, including a deep discount on the Lenovo Yoga 7i 2-in-1, taking its original $1,1199.99 price down to $749.99. It’s a capable configuration for the price, with a Core 7 Ultra 256V processor, 16GB of LPDDR5X memory, and a 512GB SSD. The IPS touchscreen has a 1920 x 1200 resolution with a 60Hz refresh rate, good enough for scrolling, taking notes, or catching up on YouTube videos. It can be tough to find a laptop at this price that doesn’t cut corners, and this model fits well within our criteria for a laptop suited for school and casual use.

Notably, this model is a 2-in-1 and features a 360-degree hinge, letting you fold the device all the way around to use it like a tablet, or prop it up on a surface for watching content. With an advertised battery life of up to 12.5 hours per charge, you shouldn’t have any issues getting through a full day of classes and studying, or just mucking about on Reddit.

Tech.title: OpenAI delayed its new model’s development after the Hugging Face hack
Tech.content:
is The Verge’s senior AI reporter. An AI beat reporter for more than five years, her work has also appeared in CNBC, MIT Technology Review, Wired UK, and other outlets.

After an unreleased OpenAI model wreaked enough havoc to make international headlines, OpenAI delayed the development of a different unreleased model suite, Astra, in order to shore up its safety work, the company wrote Tuesday in a blog post.

In July, an unreleased OpenAI model broke out of its restricted environment, finagled its way into internet access, made it possible for AI agents to secretly conspire under the company’s nose using a secret message board, and hacked into the network of AI lab Hugging Face. The attack sparked weeks of discussion and controversy inside and outside the AI industry, and AI leaders treated it as a “warning shot” for the tech’s growing capabilities and the inadequacy of its safeguards.

OpenAI said as much in its blog post, writing that although Astra wasn’t involved in the Hugging Face attack, the company had chosen to delay “parts of Astra’s development and release while we strengthened and tested protections against cyber misuse and unauthorized model actions.” OpenAI also said that Astra was the first model it had ever designated as meeting its “ C critical cybersecurity capability threshold,“ meaning that it’s able to find and exploit security vulnerabilities in “many well-protected systems” without human guidance. That means it “requires stronger safeguards during development and before release,” OpenAI wrote.

OpenAI said that to prepare for Astra’s release — which the company has not yet provided a timeline for — the company trained it to “more reliably” say no to potentially harmful cyber requests and introduced new monitoring processes. These are likely part of the new safety guardrails that the company announced in a Hugging Face post-mortem last week, where it promised to better isolate models from the internet and to introduce “24/7 escalation and rapid response” for concerning incidents. (OpenAI didn’t find out about the Hugging Face attack until weeks after it occurred.)

Astra is significantly riskier than OpenAI’s current leading model, GPT-5.6 Sol, the company says, because it represents a big step forward in cybersecurity capabilities — specifically, it uses fewer tokens to do more work, and it’s better at finding security gaps and developing ways to exploit them. But the company also wrote that Astra was its “most aligned model to date” according to internal evaluations.

OpenAI also said it had developed a test inspired by the Hugging Face attack, in which it tried to entreat agents to compromise security infrastructure instead of solving a task. It said GPT-5.6 Sol took the bait in more than half of the tests, but Astra “made no such attempts.”

Tech.title: On first listen, the Sonos Beam Ultra sounds great
Tech.content:
is an editor covering deals and gaming hardware. He joined in 2018, and after a two-year stint at Polygon, he rejoined The Verge in May 2025.

Sonos unveiled a bunch of new stuff today at its open house event. There’s the $699 Beam Ultra soundbar and the $449 Ace Ultra headphones, plus several under-the-hood app updates (some coming sooner than others). While the show floor was a less than ideal venue to judge audio quality of either new product, a private demo in a smaller room provided a better hint as to what the Beam Ultra soundbar might be capable of.

With the 7.1.2 soundbar about six feet in front of the press, the team ran through a couple demos to show off its range, particularly with Dolby Atmos content. The opening minutes of Widow’s Bay subtly illustrates the Beam Ultra’s enhanced bass, improved vocal clarity and Atmos chops. There are a lot of small details that didn’t get lost in the mix, like walkie talkie chatter, extraneous sound effects that build the world, plus the eerie swelling of the score to amp suspense.

There’s only so much sound that can come out of such a relatively small soundbar, but I was impressed — both at how it sounded and how Sonos found the ideal room to bounce around the sound coming from its side- and top-firing drivers.

The Beam Ultra looks similar to the older Beams, except it has holes poked on its top for its upward-firing speakers to fire through.

Sonos then wirelessly paired two Play portable speakers to the Beam Ultra, then set them behind us as rear channels for a demo with Sinners (the electrifying “I Lied To You” scene). If you have a small-ish living room and don’t want to permanently mount rear satellites, this setup might suffice for you. It’s certainly loud enough. Pairing more speakers seemed to let the Beam Ultra focus more on delivering a balanced, full sound with better directional audio than its predecessor, the Beam Gen 2, which virtualizes its spatial audio effect (as in, it fakes it) due to lacking side- and upward-firing speakers.

My colleague John Higgins will spend a lot more time with the Beam Ultra in an upcoming review. My first impression was good, but that’s how press events usually go. You’re using these products with a pro at the wheel, and sometimes in more ideal circumstances than our homes allow. As someone who bought a Vizio Elevate SE system last year, I was surprised by how punchy the Beam Ultra sounded during the demos. Sometimes, it sounded a little too good, and the presence of Sonos subwoofers and extra speakers in the demo room was tough to ignore, despite the team assuring us they weren’t used. Nevertheless, I’m curious how it holds up in a home environment, and specifically how it sounds across a range of content when it’s the only Sonos speaker you have.

Sitting between the $499 (currently $399) Sonos Beam Gen 2 and the $1,099 (currently $899) Sonos Arc Ultra, the Beam Ultra splits the difference between the two in terms of hardware features. You’ll get a proper taste of Atmos content without spending close to $1,000, and without straying outside of the Sonos ecosystem. The Beam Ultra launches September 29th, and preorders are available now at Best Buy, B&H Photo, Sonos, and Amazon.

Photography by Cameron Faulkner / The Verge

Tech.title: Tim Cook did alright by the environment — but AI could upend his climate legacy
Tech.content:
Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

As he steps down from his post as Apple CEO today, Tim Cook leaves behind a mostly positive environmental record. As far as billionaire tech moguls and the environment go, Cook will likely be remembered as one of the better ones — certainly far from the worst. But it will become harder for the company to meet the climate goals Cook set in place as Apple tries to catch up in the AI race.

Under his watch, Apple set industry-leading goals for reducing the amount of pollution created by its products and suppliers. It has managed to keep its carbon footprint from growing while other tech giants see their emissions rise with the energy needs of AI.

Even so, Apple has faced a series of accusations that it misled customers with its sustainability claims. And many of the environmental problems the company has grappled with under Cook are poised to become even bigger with the explosion of generative AI.

“If Tim Cook wants his legacy to be of a company that held its climate commitments he may have chosen the right time to leave.”

“If Tim Cook wants his legacy to be of a company that held its climate commitments he may have chosen the right time to leave — right now against a dark backdrop the picture is comparatively rosy,” Rachel Kitchin, senior campaign manager at the environmental group Stand.earth, says in an email to The Verge. “Depending on the choices the company makes moving forward it may not stay that way.”

The company pumped out 15.3 million metric tons of gross carbon dioxide emissions in 2025, according to the company’s latest environmental report. That’s about as much as the pollution from 40 gas-fired power plants over a year. In 2020, Apple set a goal of cutting its carbon emissions by 75 percent by the end of the decade (compared to its emissions in 2015). So far, it has reduced its emissions by 60 percent, which Apple touted in its announcement of Cook’s transition to executive chairman. Apple’s carbon pollution shrank each year since 2021 before flatlining over the past year, “holding constant from 2024 even in a year of significant business growth,” the company said in a press release.

Cook was clear during his tenure that the company’s move toward cleaner energy wouldn’t come at the cost of that growth. “I want to see that it pencils out, because I want other people to copy it. And I know they’re not going to copy a decision that’s not a good economic decision,” Cook told CBS News of its renewable energy investments in 2023. Meanwhile, Google’s and Microsoft’s greenhouse gas emissions have ballooned in recent years as generative AI demands more data centers and chip manufacturing.

Apple set itself apart with high standards it created for its suppliers, garnering approval from environmental groups that typically have a lot of negative things to point out about Big Tech companies. A 2023 report by Stand.earth assessed Apple, Dell, Google, HP, Microsoft, and Nvidia and found that Apple was the only one at the time that had set a 100 percent renewable electricity target for its suppliers.

In 2025, Apple earned a B+ rating from Greenpeace East Asia for its push for more renewable energy along its supply chains. “It’s a sharp contrast to companies such as Nvidia, whose supply chain is also concentrated in East Asia but has no clear renewable energy target or concrete support for them,” Avex Li, supply chain project lead at Greenpeace East Asia, says in an email.

“Apple needs more transparency and should invest more directly in new renewable capacity, particularly in Taiwan and South Korea, where much of its chip supply chain is concentrated and access to renewable energy remains constrained,” Li writes, adding that the company doesn’t disclose suppliers’ total electricity consumption nor the overall share powered by renewable energy.

When reached for comment, Apple spokesperson Sean Redding pointed The Verge to its most recent environmental progress report and its prior statements on Cook’s transition.

With growing demand for more advanced chips and cloud infrastructure, “AI will be the defining test of Apple’s climate commitments,” Li says. “To preserve Tim Cook’s environmental legacy, the company will need to show that AI growth can be accommodated within its existing climate commitments through absolute emissions reductions, additional renewable energy investment, and longer-lasting products.”

Tech.title: Larry Page’s flying car company Pivotal loses its CEO
Tech.content:
The CEO of a flying car company backed by Larry Page has left the company.

Ken Karklin, who was Pivotal’s CEO for more than four years, left the role this week, according to a press release. Pivotal said Karklin is “pursuing new endeavors” but didn’t offer any other information about the executive’s departure from the electric vertical takeoff and landing (eVTOL) firm.

“Leading Pivotal has been the privilege of my career. Together, we’ve moved beyond the promise of light eVTOL and proved it out in practice,” Karklin said in a statement. “This industry has moved past prototypes and press releases; it’s now operating in the real world, under real constraints, with real consequences for the future of Advanced Air Mobility. As I turn to new endeavors, I do so knowing the foundation we built here will help carry this industry forward.”

Karklin will be replaced on an interim basis by Mike Ross, an aviation executive who joined Pivotal’s board of directors in November 2025. Karklin did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Karklin’s departure comes two years after Pivotal started sales of Helix, its first lightweight electric personal aircraft. The single-seat aircraft doesn’t require a pilot’s license to fly and starts at around $200,000.

“Ken’s leadership over the past four years has been instrumental in bringing Pivotal to where it is today. Our team, our priorities, and our roadmap remain steady through this transition,” Ross said in a statement. “I’ve had the honor of working closely with Ken as a Board member and watching Pivotal’s disciplined approach to safety, engineering, and accessibility deliver on the vision of electric VTOL flight. I look forward to working with the team and guiding the company forward as we bring our fourth-generation Helix aircraft to market.”

Pivotal has also spent years developing an aircraft called BlackFly that is aimed at defense and first-responder use cases. Last month, BlackFly was used to respond to an emergency in North Carolina for the first time ever. The company says it beat an ambulance responding in parallel to the call by 20 minutes. BlackFly has flown more than 10,000 times, according to Pivotal.

Pivotal is one of a number of companies in the space that was selected for the Federal Aviation Administration’s eVTOL Integration Pilot Program, which was created to increase testing of these types of aircraft around the country.

Tech.title: Reliance’s JioHotstar takes its streaming empire global — without sports
Tech.content:
JioHotstar, the streaming platform controlled by Indian conglomerate Reliance Industries, is taking its brand outside India for the first time and will replace Hotstar in the U.K., Canada, and Singapore as it begins a wider global push.

The streaming service will launch with more than 160,000 hours of entertainment content but without the live sports that have helped drive its massive audience in India, including the Indian Premier League (IPL), Women’s Premier League (WPL), and Indian national cricket matches. JioStar said it is not offering sports at launch because of existing content deals but did not rule out adding them in the future.

The absence of sports at its global debut marks a significant difference from JioHotstar’s offering in India, where the company says it has more than 500 million monthly active users and sports is a major audience draw. The service streams some of India’s biggest cricket events alongside the English Premier League; tennis tournaments, including Wimbledon and the U.S. Open; and domestic leagues for sports such as kabaddi and hockey.

JioStar confirmed to TechCrunch that starting September 2, Hotstar will “cease to exist” in the U.K., Canada, and Singapore, with JioHotstar replacing it. Hotstar users in the three markets will no longer be able to access the service through the Hotstar app, though their existing login credentials will work on JioHotstar, the company said. The JioHotstar app will be available in all three markets through the App Store and Google Play Store on mobile devices, as well as on connected TVs.

For years, Hotstar has operated internationally, including in the U.K. and Canada. It also previously had a stand-alone service in the U.S. before shutting it down in 2021. However, JioHotstar is not launching in the U.S. as part of this initial international rollout. The company plans to expand into additional overseas markets over time.

JioHotstar will launch with a trove of Indian films, TV originals, and reality shows like “Bigg Boss,” along with live TV channels under the Star banner such as Star Plus, Colors, Star Vijay, Asianet, Star Jalsha, and Star Pravah. The company said its content is available in 12 languages, including English, Hindi, Gujarati, Malayalam, Kannada, and Marathi, with dubs and translations also available.

In 2024, Reliance merged its media assets with Disney to form an $8.5 billion joint venture. As part of the deal, streaming services Hotstar and JioCinema merged to create JioHotstar for Indian consumers. At the time, the two services accounted for 85% of the streaming audience in India.

Data from India’s Ministry of External Affairs suggests that across the three countries where JioHotstar is launching, the service could have a target audience of more than 4 million people. Some of its content could also appeal to the broader South Asian diaspora.

“South Asian audiences have a deep connection with Indian entertainment across languages, generations, and households. At the same time, audiences globally are increasingly seeking stories and cultures beyond their own. We see an opportunity to build for this broader, underserved global audience — not simply export an Indian streaming service to new markets,” JioStar’s Head of International Business, Amit Malhotra, said.

JioStar has priced JioHotstar at £19.99 (about $27) quarterly and £69.99 (around $95) annually in the U.K. In Canada, subscriptions cost CA$19.99 (about $14) quarterly and CA$49.99 (around $36) annually, while in Singapore they cost SG$29.98 (about $24) and SG$69.98 (around $55), respectively. The prices are similar to what Hotstar charges, but JioHotstar will offer only entertainment content at launch. Customers who want sports may have to pay extra for another service.

By comparison, JioHotstar subscriptions in India start at ₹79 (about $0.80) a month for viewing on a single mobile device and go up to ₹2,199 (around $23) a year for its top-tier plan.

Tech.title: Apple follows Google in adopting Trump’s ‘Lake America’ name
Tech.content:
Apple has followed Google’s lead and officially changed the name of Lake Ontario to “Lake America” on its Apple Maps service less than a week after President Trump ordered the change.

Apple Maps users in the United States will begin to see Lake America, not Lake Ontario — one of the five Great Lakes in North America — when using the website or mobile app. The change will only be shown to users in the United States. Apple Maps users in Canada will continue to see Lake Ontario, while those outside the two countries will see both names.

The change is in response to an executive order signed by Trump on August 27 that gave the Interior Department 30 days to update the lake’s name in the U.S. geographic naming service and other federal databases.

“In recognition of this flourishing economic resource and its critical importance to our Nation’s economy and its people, I am directing that the Lake officially be renamed as Lake America,” the order reads.

Trump’s directive — and Apple’s and Google’s compliance — has escalated an already strained relationship with Canada after trade talks between the two countries broke down.

Apple did not respond to a request for comment. Google Maps explained its reasoning for the change, noting in its announcement last week that it updates names to reflect changes in official government sources such as the Geographic Names Information System (GNIS).

However, not every map service has adopted that same policy. MapQuest said that it would not change the name of Lake Ontario on its maps, choosing to continue using the name that people are familiar with. (It also did not change the name of Gulf of Mexico to Gulf of America last year.)

Apple’s and Google’s actions over the name of this lake have driven a significant boost in users to MapQuest. Downloads of the so-called OG of mapping services have skyrocketed, pushing the iOS app to the No. 1 position in the U.S. App Store’s Top charts. That even put MapQuest ahead of perennial chart-topper ChatGPT as of September 1.

MapQuest also reached the No. 6 position overall in Google’s Play Store across both apps and games. And the company doesn’t appear to be budging. It posted on X a GIF of an apple, with the line “Them Too.” In another post showing a screenshot of MapQuest as the No. 1 downloaded app, the company wrote. “The people have spoken. We are working.”

There is precedent to Apple’s and Google’s deference to Trump. Last year, both of these tech companies changed the name of the Gulf of Mexico to Gulf of America after that name-changing order by Trump.

Tech.title: AfterQuery reportedly becomes Y Combinator’s fastest-ever unicorn, now valued at $3.2B
Tech.content:
In Brief

AI training-data startup AfterQuery has reportedly raised a round that valued it at $3.2 billion. This just five months after announcing its $30 million Series A at a $300 million valuation in April.

That’s more than a 10x increase in less than half a year and, according to Y Combinator partner Gustaf Alströmer, the fastest that any startup has gone from launch to unicorn status in the accelerator’s history. AfterQuery’s founders, today 22 and 23 years old, attended Y Combinator’s Winter 2025 cohort, just 18 months ago.

In April, the San Francisco startup said it had reached an annualized revenue run rate of $100 million and that it was working with many of the biggest labs. It has named companies such as Nvidia, Legora, and the Korean AI lab Motif Technologies as customers.

AfterQuery is among the new crop of startups following in the footsteps of Mercor and Scale that employ knowledge professionals like doctors, lawyers, and other specialists to do model training. However, rather than ensuring that models answer questions accurately, AfterQuery trains models and agents on how to work like professionals would to complete tasks — what the company describes as “encoding the patterns, decisions, and reasoning of the world’s best practitioners.”

Forbes first reported on the round. AfterQuery could not be immediately reached for comment.

Tech.title: OpenAI’s Astra model is on the way — and very good at breaking into computer systems
Tech.content:
OpenAI shared new details on its forthcoming Astra model, which the company said is the first large language model to meet its “critical cybersecurity threshold,” in preparation for its imminent release.

“We plan to make Astra available soon,” OpenAI’s blog post reads, “but access to its most advanced cybersecurity capabilities will be more limited.”

The frontier lab determined that Astra is capable of finding unknown security flaws in computer systems, and exploiting them without a person’s guidance. That’s similar to the concerns Anthropic raised about its Mythos model earlier this year, and OpenAI is taking comparable precautions as it prepares to roll out the Astra.

Without any third-party confirmation, it is difficult to evaluate OpenAI’s claims about safety or preparedness. The company said it would preview the model with a group of testers but did not say who they were or how they would be chosen. It’s not clear if OpenAI is working with the U.S. government to evaluate the model ahead of release.

OpenAI noted that Astra scored a perfect score on ExploitBench, an evaluation of an LLM’s ability to hack into known system vulnerabilities. In a modified version of the test developed by OpenAI engineers, the model discovered and exploited two zero-day vulnerabilities, the company said.

To ensure that its models are neither exploited by bad actors nor capable of bad behavior itself, OpenAI said it had already begun improving the model’s harness to detect abuses and prevent jailbreaks.

For Astra, however, the company invested in unspecified new techniques designed to make the model safer. OpenAI has also started identifying “accounts assessed as higher risk” and restricting the model’s responses to their prompts, though it also doesn’t say how. Finally, though the company describes Astra as its “most aligned model to date,” it will deploy the model with additional chain-of-thought monitoring to spot and stop bad behavior.

Preparations for the release of Astra come as the industry reacts to OpenAI agents breaking out of a training environment and accessing private data on Hugging Face, a popular model and benchmark distribution platform.

For Astra, OpenAI said it designed a test to tempt the new model to replicate the actions of the rogue agents in the Hugging Face incident, which collaborated to access the open internet despite safeguards applied by OpenAI researchers. They said Astra did not attempt to break out of its testing environment in these experiments.

Yona Shavit, a former OpenAI employee who now works on AI resilience at the OpenAI Foundation, wondered on social media whether Astra’s unwillingness to break the rules may have resulted from knowing what was expected of it or trying to fool researchers.

And for all these new details, it’s still difficult to know exactly what Astra is capable of or if OpenAI is taking the right measures to ensure safety. The company said it expects to release more evaluations of the model and further safety information when it is launched widely to the public.

At that point, however, the cat will be out of the bag.

Tech.title: Google’s Android update tackles motion sickness, accessibility, and more
Tech.content:
On Tuesday, Google announced it’s rolling out five new updates designed to make Android phones more accessible, useful, and personalized. Announced in a blog post, the features include those aimed at reducing motion sickness, helping blind and low-vision users navigate their surroundings, remembering where users leave important items, and another that adds new ways to personalize Google Messages.

While some of the features see Google playing catch-up to Apple, which already offers similar features for iPhone users, others specifically leverage Gemini to provide various improvements.

The most interesting update is “Motion Assist,” a feature designed to help people who experience motion sickness while using their phones in a moving vehicle. It adds a bubble overlay to the screen that moves in response to the vehicle’s motion, helping reduce the disconnect between what users see on their screens and what their bodies feel.

The concept isn’t entirely new, however. Apple introduced “Vehicle Motion Cues” in 2024, which uses animated dots around the edges of the display that move in response to a vehicle’s motion.

Users can set “Motion Assist” to turn on automatically, add it to Quick Settings, and customize the bubble’s shape, color, and transparency. Google says this feature is available to Android 17 users.

Image Credits:Google

Google is also introducing “Guided Vision,” a feature designed with blind and low-vision users in mind. It combines the phone’s camera with Gemini to help with tasks such as reading small print on a food label, viewing a menu in a dark restaurant, or identifying objects around the house.

The feature can also provide voice guidance when the camera isn’t positioned correctly, telling users to move the phone, pan around, or center an object. Guided Vision is coming to phones running Android 9 and newer in countries where Gemini is available.

Image Credits:Google

Another update gives Gemini a new way to help users remember where they put important items. A “remembered items” section in Find Hub will allow users to tell Gemini where they’ve stored something. For example, a user could say they put their passport in a bedroom drawer, and Gemini can save that information in Find Hub. Users can also attach a photo to make the item easier to identify later.

Additionally, Google is adding a Google Keep integration to Google Messages, allowing people to share and edit grocery lists, vacation notes, and other information directly within a conversation.

Image Credits:Google

Plus, Google Messages is getting more personalization options. Users will be able to customize individual chats with backgrounds, photos, and colors, Google says. The text bubbles will automatically match.

Apple added a similar custom background feature to Messages last year.

Tech.title: X says attackers are targeting user accounts after the launch of X Money
Tech.content:
Attackers are attempting to target X users following the launch of X Money. After numerous X users reported receiving unsolicited password reset emails, a representative said the social media company was actively investigating the issue but had not yet found evidence that the hacks were successful.

On Tuesday, X product engineer Mridul Singhai posted to the social network that the company was looking into users’ complaints about the mass password reset attempts.

“Attackers appear to believe that, now that @XMoney is widely available, they can gain unauthorized access to accounts,” he wrote. “We are actively investigating the issue and, so far, have found no evidence of any breaches. We apologize for the multiple emails and appreciate your patience as we work to resolve this.”

X Money is X’s newly launched payments service, which includes a bank card and other benefits. For X, the service could make it easier for creators to collect payments on the platform, further facilitating X’s digital economy.

Of course, money changing hands has a tendency to attract bad actors, which is what X says may be happening here.

Attackers appear to believe that, now that @XMoney is widely available, they can gain unauthorized access to accounts. We are actively investigating the issue and, so far, have found no evidence of any breaches.



We apologize for the multiple emails and appreciate your patience… https://t.co/zf1pRWbqBX — Mridul Singhai (@singhai) September 1, 2026

X has not posted details to one of its official company accounts as of the time of writing, and has not yet responded to our press inquiry about the matter.

However, X general counsel James Burnham wrote a threatening post, saying, “The legal and security teams @X will stop at nothing to identify, locate, and hold criminally accountable any person anywhere on or off earth who attempts to victimize our platform’s users.”

As the attacks continue, users are warning each other about the problem and reminding others to enable two-factor authentication, if it’s not already enabled, to protect their accounts. X’s chatbot Grok has also replied to some posts with the steps on how to do so, while also confirming that the attackers are “mass-triggering” the form for password resets using public usernames.

“No confirmed system breach or mass takeovers,” the AI bot said.

Tech.title: John Ternus hypes ‘huge launch next week’ in first memo as Apple CEO
Tech.content:
In Brief

John Ternus has officially taken the reins as Apple CEO, succeeding Tim Cook, who held the role for 15 years.

The company’s former senior vice president of Hardware Engineering, Ternus enters the CEO role at a critical time for Apple. On September 9, the company will host its annual iPhone event, which is rumored to include the launch of Apple’s first foldable iPhone. Apple is also expected to roll out its new-and-improved Siri AI more broadly, which marks an important opportunity for the company to position Siri as an equal to chatbots like OpenAI’s ChatGPT or Anthropic’s Claude.

“We have a huge launch next week that’s going to be phenomenal,” Ternus wrote in a memo to staff on Tuesday, according to Bloomberg. “I’m just as excited about what lies beyond that, including the incredible products already in the works and the ones we haven’t even imagined yet that we’ll dream up and create together.”

Apple is rumored to be working on several new products, like camera-equipped AirPods, smart glasses, and a touchscreen laptop.

“I take enormous comfort in handing the helm to someone as brilliant and wonderful and capable as John,” Tim Cook wrote to staff on his last day as CEO. “Few people understand what it takes to build products that change the world the way John does and I could not be more excited for his leadership.”
